title: Data Science Interview Notes
text:
How to use this book
This book turns my course review and interview-preparation notes into a connected set of explanations. Each chapter begins with a concrete question, works through a small example, then develops the mathematical assumptions and practical limits. The interview questions at the end are prompts for practice, not transcripts of actual interviews.
The chapters draw on two source documents: an IDS 2–13 review sheet covering probability, statistical inference, regression, classification, and unsupervised learning; and my longer lecture notes on ensemble trees, clustering, causal inference, and time series. Where a source statement was too broad or incorrect, the chapter explains the corrected condition. Worked numbers explicitly identified as examples are teaching data.
The book is maintained alongside my English portfolio and 中文个人网站.

title: Probability, Random Variables, and Distribution Shape
text:
Learning goals
After this chapter, you should be able to define a probability space, calculate a conditional probability, explain what a random variable actually is, and distinguish raw, central, and standardized moments. Only elementary algebra is assumed.
crumbs: 2  Probability, Random Variables, and Distribution Shape

title: Probability, Random Variables, and Distribution Shape
text:
Intuition
Inference asks what a limited observation says about an uncertain process. Probability supplies the rules for that uncertainty. A deterministic implication such as “if it rained, the pavement is wet” may fail as a description of the world because other conditions affect wetness, such as evaporation or a roof. Logic remains valid given its premises; probability helps represent uncertain premises and observations.
Imagine a lock that displays one digit. The sample space is \(\Omega=\{0,1,\ldots,9\}\). One observed digit \(\omega\) is an outcome. An event is a set of outcomes, such as \(A=\{0,2,4,6,8\}\). For this finite example, the event collection is the power set \(\mathcal F=2^\Omega\). More generally, \(\mathcal F\) is a sigma-algebra; it need not contain every subset of an infinite sample space. A probability measure \(P:\mathcal F\to[0,1]\) completes the probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\).
crumbs: 2  Probability, Random Variables, and Distribution Shape

title: Probability, Random Variables, and Distribution Shape
text:
Worked example
Suppose the ten lock digits are equally likely. Let \(A\) mean “even” and \(B\) mean “at least five.” Then \(P(A)=5/10\), \(P(B)=5/10\), and \(A\cap B=\{6,8\}\) has probability \(2/10\). The union rule gives
\[
P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)=0.5+0.5-0.2=0.8.
\]
Once we learn that the digit is even, our relevant sample space is restricted to the five even digits. Two satisfy \(B\), so
\[
P(B\mid A)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(A)}=\frac{0.2}{0.5}=0.4.
\]
The multiplication rule reverses this calculation: \(P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B\mid A)\). Because \(0.4\ne P(B)=0.5\), these particular events are not independent. Independence would require \(P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)\).
Now define \(X(\omega)=1\) for an even digit and \(0\) otherwise. The mapping \(X:\Omega\to\mathbb R\) is fixed; uncertainty comes from which \(\omega\) occurs. Here \(X\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(0.5)\), so \(E[X]=0.5\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=0.25\).
crumbs: 2  Probability, Random Variables, and Distribution Shape

title: Probability, Random Variables, and Distribution Shape
text:
Theory and assumptions

Axioms and calculation rules
Kolmogorov’s axioms say \(P(E)\ge0\), \(P(\Omega)=1\), and \(P(\bigcup_i E_i)=\sum_iP(E_i)\) for pairwise disjoint events. Finite additivity follows. The subtraction in the union formula prevents double-counting the intersection. Conditional probability requires \(P(A)>0\); independence is a separate property, not a consequence of conditioning.


Moments describe a distribution
For a continuous \(X\) with density \(f\), the \(k\)th raw moment is \(E[X^k]=\int x^kf(x)\,dx\). The \(k\)th central moment is \(E[(X-\mu)^k]\); the standardized moment divides by \(\sigma^k\) when \(\sigma>0\). For discrete variables, replace the integral by a sum. The zeroth raw moment is \(1\), the first raw moment is the mean \(\mu\), and the second central moment is the variance \(\sigma^2\). The third and fourth central moments, after standardization, describe skewness and kurtosis. Kurtosis concerns tail weight together with the distribution’s center and shoulders, so it is not a simple standalone “tail probability.” A center-of-mass analogy makes the mean intuitive: observations farther from the balancing point have greater leverage on it.


Normal approximation, Edgeworth, and Cauchy
A normal distribution is fully specified by its mean and variance:
\[
f(x)=\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\!\left[-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right].
\]
Under appropriate independence or weak-dependence and finite-variance conditions, sums of many contributions can be approximately normal. This does not imply every quantity assembled from many causes is normal. An Edgeworth expansion refines a normal approximation for a standardized statistic using higher cumulants, including skewness and kurtosis; it is an asymptotic correction whose accuracy depends on regularity conditions, not a universal replacement for the normal law.
The standard Cauchy distribution has \(f(x)=1/[\pi(1+x^2)]\). Its mean and variance do not exist: the positive and negative parts of the expectation integral diverge, even though a symmetric principal value can be written as zero. For independent standard Cauchy observations, the sample mean is again standard Cauchy. The usual finite-mean law of large numbers and finite-variance central limit theorem therefore do not apply. Its tails are far heavier than normal tails.
crumbs: 2  Probability, Random Variables, and Distribution Shape

title: Probability, Random Variables, and Distribution Shape
text:
Practice and pitfalls

State the sampling mechanism before assigning equal probabilities to outcomes; a lock digit is uniform only if the mechanism makes it so.
Distinguish an event \(A\subseteq\Omega\) from a random variable \(X:\Omega\to\mathbb R\) and its observed value \(X(\omega)\).
Do not write \(E[(X-\mu)^1]=\mu\); the first central moment is zero. Do not call an unstandardized fourth moment “kurtosis.”
A finite sample always has a numerical mean, even when the population mean is undefined. Its instability is the issue.
crumbs: 2  Probability, Random Variables, and Distribution Shape

title: Probability, Random Variables, and Distribution Shape
text:
Interview questions
What changes when you condition on an event? The denominator changes from all possible outcomes to outcomes in the conditioning event. I calculate \(P(B\mid A)=P(A\cap B)/P(A)\) only when \(P(A)>0\).
Is a random variable itself random? Formally it is a measurable function of an uncertain outcome. Once the outcome is fixed, its value is fixed.
Why might a normal approximation fail? Heavy tails, dependence, rare-event structure, or insufficient sample size can defeat the conditions or convergence rate. A Cauchy sample mean is a striking counterexample.
crumbs: 2  Probability, Random Variables, and Distribution Shape

title: Probability, Random Variables, and Distribution Shape
text:
Summary
Probability begins with outcomes, events, and a measure. Conditional probabilities change the reference event, while random variables turn outcomes into numerical quantities. Moments summarize distributions when they exist; heavy-tailed distributions remind us that they need not.

title: Descriptive Statistics, Association, and Visual Checks
text:
Learning goals
You should be able to select a center and spread measure for a data type, calculate Pearson and rank correlation, describe Chatterjee’s directional dependence coefficient, and explain why plotting data precedes interpretation. Review the probability chapter’s mean and variance first.
crumbs: 3  Descriptive Statistics, Association, and Visual Checks

title: Descriptive Statistics, Association, and Visual Checks
text:
Intuition
A summary is a deliberate compression. Squared-error loss favors the mean; absolute-error loss favors the median; a mode reports the most frequent category. No single number retains the shape of a dataset. The same caution applies to association: Pearson measures linear alignment, Spearman measures monotone rank alignment, and more general dependence measures ask whether knowing one variable helps predict another.
crumbs: 3  Descriptive Statistics, Association, and Visual Checks

title: Descriptive Statistics, Association, and Visual Checks
text:
Worked example
For \(x=(1,2,2,3,12)\), the mean is \(4\), the median and mode are both \(2\), and the population-style variance of these five values is
\[
\frac{(1-4)^2+(2-4)^2+(2-4)^2+(3-4)^2+(12-4)^2}{5}=16.4.
\]
The corresponding standard deviation is \(\sqrt{16.4}\approx4.05\). The mean absolute deviation around the mean is \((3+2+2+1+8)/5=3.2\). The median absolute deviation around the median, another statistic also abbreviated MAD, is \(\operatorname{median}(1,0,0,1,10)=1\). Naming the center and aggregation rule prevents ambiguity. The single value \(12\) pulls the mean and standard deviation much more than it moves the median.
For \(X=(1,2,3)\) and \(Y=(2,4,6)\), the sample Pearson correlation is \(1\): the centered coordinates are proportional. Changing \(Y\) from centimeters to inches changes covariance but leaves correlation \(1\).
crumbs: 3  Descriptive Statistics, Association, and Visual Checks

title: Descriptive Statistics, Association, and Visual Checks
text:
Theory and assumptions

Center and dispersion as loss choices
The minimizers of \(\sum_i(x_i-\theta)^2\), \(\sum_i|x_i-\theta|\), and \(\sum_i\mathbf1(x_i\ne\theta)\) are respectively the arithmetic mean, any median, and a mode (for a discrete sample). The last is a zero-one mismatch count, often called an \(L_0\)-style criterion; it is not a norm. Squaring heavily weights distant observations. For a population, \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=E[(X-\mu)^2]\) and \(\sigma=\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)}\). For a sample used to estimate population variance, the familiar unbiased formula uses \(s^2=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2/(n-1)\) rather than division by \(n\).


Covariance and three notions of association
Covariance \(E[(X-\mu_X)(Y-\mu_Y)]\) has units equal to the product of the variables’ units. Pearson correlation removes those units:
\[
r=\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)}{\sqrt{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2}}.
\]
It lies in \([-1,1]\) and captures linear association; nonlinear dependence can coexist with \(r=0\). Spearman’s \(\rho\) is Pearson correlation on ranks. With no tied ranks, \(\rho=1-6\sum_i d_i^2/[n(n^2-1)]\), where \(d_i\) is the difference of paired ranks. With ties, compute Pearson on the appropriately averaged ranks instead of using that shortcut. Spearman detects monotone patterns such as \(y=x^3\) and is less affected by the magnitude of outliers, although ranks can still be changed by unusual observations.
Chatterjee’s \(\xi\) is directional: \(\xi(X,Y)\) asks about dependence of \(Y\) on \(X\) and need not equal \(\xi(Y,X)\). In the no-tie sample construction, sort pairs by \(X\), let \(r_i\) be the associated rank of \(Y\), then compute
\[
\xi_n(X,Y)=1-\frac{3\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}|r_{i+1}-r_i|}{n^2-1}.
\]
Its population value lies in \([0,1]\), equals zero under independence, and equals one when \(Y\) is almost surely a measurable function of \(X\) (under the usual formulation). The finite-sample statistic can be negative and is not \(1\) even for a perfectly ordered finite sample. For \(n=5\) and ranks \((1,2,3,4,5)\) it is \(1-3(4)/24=0.5\). Ties require the tied-data definition; a coefficient alone does not establish a useful predictive model or causality.


Shape and visual diagnosis
A normal distribution has light tails relative to a Cauchy distribution, which lacks a finite mean and variance. Anscombe’s quartet shows that datasets can have nearly identical means, variances, Pearson correlations, and fitted linear regressions while exhibiting a line, a curve, an outlier-driven association, or a leverage point. Plot the observations and residuals before trusting a small set of summaries.
crumbs: 3  Descriptive Statistics, Association, and Visual Checks

title: Descriptive Statistics, Association, and Visual Checks
text:
Practice and pitfalls

Choose median and quantiles for highly skewed numerical data; keep mean and standard deviation when the estimand or downstream model explicitly concerns them.
Report sample size, units, missingness, and transformations with a correlation. A unit change leaves Pearson’s \(r\) unchanged under positive rescaling but changes covariance.
Correlation cannot settle direction of causation, common-cause confounding, or a spurious trend. A nonlinear curve can make both Pearson and Spearman near zero.
The no-ties Chatterjee formula and its finite-sample range differ from the idealized population interpretation; do not quote \([0,1]\) as an exact finite-sample guarantee.
crumbs: 3  Descriptive Statistics, Association, and Visual Checks

title: Descriptive Statistics, Association, and Visual Checks
text:
Interview questions
Why is the median more robust to one extreme value? The median depends on order, so moving the largest value farther away usually leaves it unchanged. Squared deviations make the mean and standard deviation react strongly.
When would Pearson be near zero despite dependence? If \(X\) is symmetric around zero and \(Y=X^2\), positive and negative \(X\) values cancel in covariance, although \(Y\) is determined by \(X\).
Does \(r=1\) mean \(X\) causes \(Y\)? No. It means the observed points lie on a positive-slope line, assuming nonzero variance. A common cause or data construction may explain the line.
crumbs: 3  Descriptive Statistics, Association, and Visual Checks

title: Descriptive Statistics, Association, and Visual Checks
text:
Summary
Summary statistics answer distinct questions and discard distinct information. Explain the chosen loss or relationship, then inspect the actual data geometry before claiming a pattern.

title: Scientific Reasoning and Hypothesis Testing
text:
Learning goals
You should be able to separate deduction from inference to a plausible explanation, identify a logical fallacy, frame null and alternative hypotheses, and interpret a p-value without reversing its conditional probability. This chapter builds on conditional probability.
crumbs: 4  Scientific Reasoning and Hypothesis Testing

title: Scientific Reasoning and Hypothesis Testing
text:
Intuition
Deduction derives a conclusion from stated premises. In modus ponens, \(H\Rightarrow P\) and \(H\) imply \(P\). In modus tollens, \(H\Rightarrow P\) and \(\neg P\) imply \(\neg H\). The tempting reverse—\(H\Rightarrow P\) and observing \(P\), therefore \(H\)—is affirming the consequent. Many explanations could predict the same observation. Scientific abduction instead compares explanations given evidence and assumptions; it is useful without being a logical proof.
Karl Popper’s falsifiability criterion asks whether a theory makes predictions that could conflict with evidence. In real studies, a conflict can also arise from measurement error or a mistaken auxiliary assumption, so one failed observation rarely refutes an entire research program by itself. Confirmation bias, illustrated by the Wason selection task, makes us seek supporting cases when disconfirming cases would be more informative.
crumbs: 4  Scientific Reasoning and Hypothesis Testing

title: Scientific Reasoning and Hypothesis Testing
text:
Worked example
Suppose a product team hypothesizes that a new checkout increases conversion. A randomized trial specifies \(H_0:p_{\rm new}=p_{\rm old}\) and \(H_1:p_{\rm new}\ne p_{\rm old}\). The primary outcome, assignment unit, sample size, and two-sided test are fixed before observing outcomes. If the resulting valid p-value is \(0.03\), then, assuming \(H_0\) and the test’s design assumptions, a test statistic at least as extreme as the observed one would occur with probability \(0.03\). At a prespecified \(\alpha=0.05\), reject \(H_0\).
That calculation does not say there is a 3% probability that \(H_0\) is true, a 97% probability the feature helps, or a 3% probability of the exact dataset. The estimated effect, interval, practical impact, and trial quality still matter. A nonsignificant result means the data did not meet the rejection rule; it does not establish equality.
crumbs: 4  Scientific Reasoning and Hypothesis Testing

title: Scientific Reasoning and Hypothesis Testing
text:
Theory and assumptions

The testing decision
Choose hypotheses and a statistic \(T\) before evaluating evidence. Under \(H_0\), calculate a reference distribution that accounts for the study design. For a two-sided statistic, a p-value often has the form \(P_{H_0}(|T|\ge|T_{\rm obs}|)\); the exact “as extreme” rule depends on the test. Compare it with a prespecified threshold \(\alpha\). If the null distribution and assumptions are correct, \(\alpha\) controls the long-run probability of rejecting a true null, not the probability that any particular rejected null is false.


Logic and scientific limits
The source notes connect null testing to proof by contradiction. That is a useful intuition, but statistical rejection is probabilistic: outcomes rare under \(H_0\) can still occur when \(H_0\) is true. Rejecting a simple null gives evidence against that null in the specified model; it does not uniquely prove the chosen alternative. Likewise, a high p-value may reflect a small effect, high noise, poor measurement, or low sample size.
crumbs: 4  Scientific Reasoning and Hypothesis Testing

title: Scientific Reasoning and Hypothesis Testing
text:
Practice and pitfalls

Define what would count against the claim before examining outcomes. Pre-registration reduces analysis flexibility but does not rescue a poorly designed experiment.
Separate the scientific claim, the statistical model, and the decision rule. A flaw in randomization, missing-data handling, or assumptions can invalidate a technically correct calculation.
Account for repeated looks and multiple outcomes. Choosing the smallest p-value after inspection changes the false-positive behavior of the planned test.
crumbs: 4  Scientific Reasoning and Hypothesis Testing

title: Scientific Reasoning and Hypothesis Testing
text:
Interview questions
Why can’t many confirmations prove a hypothesis? Competing hypotheses may predict the same observations. I look for predictions that distinguish explanations and for data that could contradict them.
What does a p-value of 0.03 mean? Conditional on the null model and test design, the chance of a statistic at least as extreme as the observed one is 3%. It is not \(P(H_0\mid\text{data})\).
What do you conclude from \(p>0.05\)? I fail to reject the null at that threshold and inspect the interval and power before making a substantive claim.
crumbs: 4  Scientific Reasoning and Hypothesis Testing

title: Scientific Reasoning and Hypothesis Testing
text:
Summary
Hypothesis testing formalizes a question about data under a null model. Its decision is evidence-sensitive but neither a deductive proof nor a posterior probability of a hypothesis.

title: Sampling, Standard Error, and Experimental Design
text:
Learning goals
You should distinguish a population parameter from a sample statistic, derive the standard error of a mean, state the relevant law of large numbers and central limit theorem assumptions, and explain why random assignment matters for causal interpretation.
crumbs: 5  Sampling, Standard Error, and Experimental Design

title: Sampling, Standard Error, and Experimental Design
text:
Intuition
The population has an unknown feature such as \(\mu\) or \(\sigma\); a sample yields estimates such as \(\bar X\) or \(s\). Repeating the sampling procedure would produce different estimates. The distribution of those estimates is the sampling distribution. Standard error describes that distribution’s spread, whereas standard deviation describes spread among individual observations.
crumbs: 5  Sampling, Standard Error, and Experimental Design

title: Sampling, Standard Error, and Experimental Design
text:
Worked example
Assume independent identically distributed Bernoulli conversions with true probability \(p=0.10\). For \(n=400\) users, \(E[\hat p]=0.10\) and
\[
\operatorname{SE}(\hat p)=\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}=\sqrt{\frac{0.10(0.90)}{400}}=0.015.
\]
The individual Bernoulli standard deviation is \(\sqrt{0.09}=0.30\); the estimate’s standard error is only \(0.015\). Quadrupling the sample to \(1{,}600\) halves standard error to \(0.0075\), provided the independence and stable-population assumptions remain reasonable. For inference from observed data, substitute \(\hat p\) for unknown \(p\) and consider whether a normal approximation is adequate.
crumbs: 5  Sampling, Standard Error, and Experimental Design

title: Sampling, Standard Error, and Experimental Design
text:
Theory and assumptions

LLN, CLT, and SEM
For iid observations with finite mean \(\mu\), the weak law of large numbers gives \(\bar X_n\xrightarrow{P}\mu\). With finite variance \(\sigma^2\), the classical central limit theorem gives
\[
\frac{\sqrt n(\bar X_n-\mu)}{\sigma}\xrightarrow{d}N(0,1),\qquad
\operatorname{SE}(\bar X_n)=\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}.
\]
The CLT concerns the mean’s sampling distribution, not the distribution of raw observations. “Large enough” depends on skew, tails, dependence, and the question at hand; no universal cutoff makes the approximation exact. Independence is not identical to random sampling: a probability sampling design, dependence structure, or cluster design may require a different standard-error formula. In biased selection, accumulating more observations can make a precisely wrong estimate.


Three different kinds of variation
The population standard deviation \(\sigma\) measures individual dispersion; the sample standard deviation \(s\) estimates it from one sample; \(s/\sqrt n\) estimates the standard error of a sample mean under the iid model. Variance scales in squared outcome units, while either standard deviation is in original units. For dependent or clustered observations, effective information can be far below nominal \(n\).


Experiments and causal inference
In a randomized experiment, the independent variable is the assigned treatment and the dependent variable is the measured outcome. Random assignment makes baseline causes of the outcome comparable in expectation across groups, including unmeasured ones. It does not guarantee exact balance in one finite experiment or fix noncompliance, attrition, interference, or measurement errors. The randomization unit should match the unit exposed to treatment; shared households or teams may need cluster randomization and cluster-aware uncertainty.
Observational comparisons with self-selection do not obtain this protection automatically. An “A/B test” is genuinely randomized only if the allocation is random and the analysis respects the design. Random sampling supports generalization to a target population; random assignment supports a causal contrast within the study. One can have either, both, or neither.
crumbs: 5  Sampling, Standard Error, and Experimental Design

title: Sampling, Standard Error, and Experimental Design
text:
Practice and pitfalls

Describe the target population, sampling frame, inclusion mechanism, and likely selection bias before quoting a standard error.
Check whether repeated observations of one user or cluster are correlated; treating them as independent inflates effective sample size.
Predefine outcome, exposure window, assignment unit, and treatment contrast. Inspect imbalance and missing outcomes without assuming randomization failed whenever one covariate differs.
Report effect estimates and uncertainty, not only “significant” or “not significant.”
crumbs: 5  Sampling, Standard Error, and Experimental Design

title: Sampling, Standard Error, and Experimental Design
text:
Interview questions
Why does four times as much data halve a mean’s standard error? Under iid finite-variance sampling, \(\operatorname{SE}=\sigma/\sqrt n\), so multiplying \(n\) by four divides the denominator by two.
Does the CLT make skewed data normal? No. It approximates the distribution of suitably standardized sample means under its conditions; the raw data can remain skewed.
What is the difference between random sampling and assignment? Sampling concerns who enters the study and hence generalizability; assignment concerns which condition each study unit receives and hence causal comparability.
crumbs: 5  Sampling, Standard Error, and Experimental Design

title: Sampling, Standard Error, and Experimental Design
text:
Summary
The sampling mechanism determines whether a sample statistic informs a population parameter. The standard error quantifies sampling variation under a model, and valid causal claims additionally depend on treatment assignment and study conduct.

title: Classical Tests: z, t, Ranks, and Distributions
text:
Learning goals
You should know when to use z, Student, paired, pooled, and Welch tests; explain the roles of chi-square, Mann–Whitney, Kolmogorov–Smirnov, and Kruskal–Wallis tests; and check each test’s design assumptions. Review sampling distributions and null hypotheses first.
crumbs: 6  Classical Tests: z, t, Ranks, and Distributions

title: Classical Tests: z, t, Ranks, and Distributions
text:
Intuition
A significance test compares an observed discrepancy with discrepancies expected under a null model. A z test treats the standard error as known. A t test accounts for estimating spread from the sample, producing heavier reference tails at low degrees of freedom. Rank and empirical-distribution tests answer different questions when a mean comparison is not the target.
crumbs: 6  Classical Tests: z, t, Ranks, and Distributions

title: Classical Tests: z, t, Ranks, and Distributions
text:
Worked example
Suppose independent groups have observations \(A=(1,2,3)\) and \(B=(2,3,4)\). Their means differ by \(-1\); each sample variance is \(1\). Welch’s statistic is
\[
t=\frac{\bar x_A-\bar x_B}{\sqrt{s_A^2/n_A+s_B^2/n_B}}
=\frac{-1}{\sqrt{1/3+1/3}}\approx-1.225.
\]
The Welch–Satterthwaite degrees of freedom are \(4\) in this equal-size, equal-variance example. A two-sided \(t_4\) reference distribution gives a large p-value; the sample is too small to establish a mean difference reliably. The interpretation concerns means under independent sampling, not every aspect of the distributions.
For paired data, use within-pair differences before testing. If four before-minus-after differences are \((1,2,3,4)\), their mean is \(2.5\), their sample SD is \(\sqrt{5/3}\), and \(t=2.5/(\sqrt{5/3}/2)\approx3.873\) with \(3\) degrees of freedom. Treating these as eight independent measurements would discard the pairing.
crumbs: 6  Classical Tests: z, t, Ranks, and Distributions

title: Classical Tests: z, t, Ranks, and Distributions
text:
Theory and assumptions

Tests of means
With known population SD, the one-sample statistic is \(z=(\bar x-\mu_0)/(\sigma/\sqrt n)\). With unknown SD, replace \(\sigma\) by \(s\) to obtain \(t=(\bar x-\mu_0)/(s/\sqrt n)\), with \(n-1\) degrees of freedom for an exact normal-sample t test. Normality of the raw observations or pair differences matters for exact small-sample t calibration; at larger sizes, mean-based inference may be robust under suitable finite-variance conditions. Strong dependence or severe skew can still cause problems.
For two independent groups, the pooled test assumes equal population variances:
\[
s_p^2=\frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2+(n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1+n_2-2},\qquad
t=\frac{\bar x_1-\bar x_2}{s_p\sqrt{1/n_1+1/n_2}},\quad df=n_1+n_2-2.
\]
The paired test applies the one-sample t formula to differences \(d_i\), testing \(E[D]=0\) with \(df=n-1\). The Welch test avoids an equal-variance assumption:
\[
t=\frac{\bar x_1-\bar x_2}{\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1+s_2^2/n_2}},\qquad
\nu\approx\frac{(s_1^2/n_1+s_2^2/n_2)^2}{(s_1^2/n_1)^2/(n_1-1)+(s_2^2/n_2)^2/(n_2-1)}.
\]
Welch is often a sensible default for independent mean comparisons. Equal variance is required by the pooled test, not by all parametric methods.


Counts, ranks, and distribution functions








Question
Statistic and reference
Key condition




Do categorical counts fit prespecified probabilities?
Pearson \(\chi^2=\sum (O-E)^2/E\), approximately \(\chi^2_{k-1}\) for \(k\) fixed categories
Independent counts and sufficiently informative expected cells; estimated parameters reduce degrees of freedom.


Are two categorical variables associated?
Pearson chi-square on an \(r\times c\) table, approximately \(\chi^2_{(r-1)(c-1)}\)
Independent units and adequate expected counts; small sparse tables may need an exact method.


Do two independent ordered samples differ in stochastic position?
Mann–Whitney \(U\), a rank-sum statistic
Independent observations; a pure median-shift interpretation needs similar distribution shapes.


Are two distribution functions the same?
Two-sample KS \(D=\sup_x|F_n(x)-G_m(x)|\)
Independent samples; usual distribution-free calibration assumes a continuous null.


Do three or more independent groups differ in ranks?
Kruskal–Wallis \(H\), approximately \(\chi^2_{g-1}\)
Independent groups; tied ranks and small samples need appropriate correction/calibration.



For Mann–Whitney, if \(R_1\) is the rank sum of group 1, one common orientation is \(U_1=R_1-n_1(n_1+1)/2\) and \(U_2=n_1n_2-U_1\). Some texts reverse which group is counted; two-sided testing is unaffected. Without ties under its null, \(E[U_1]=n_1n_2/2\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(U_1)=n_1n_2(n_1+n_2+1)/12\). Exact enumeration is useful at small sizes; normal approximation improves with adequate data and a tie correction.
For a one-sample KS test, compare the empirical CDF to a fully specified CDF. Estimating that CDF’s parameters from the same data changes the null distribution; standard KS critical values then do not apply directly. Kruskal–Wallis uses total rank sum \(R_j\) within each group of size \(n_j\):
\[
H=\frac{12}{N(N+1)}\sum_{j=1}^{g}\frac{R_j^2}{n_j}-3(N+1),\qquad N=\sum_jn_j.
\]
crumbs: 6  Classical Tests: z, t, Ranks, and Distributions

title: Classical Tests: z, t, Ranks, and Distributions
text:
Practice and pitfalls

Ask which outcome and estimand matter: a difference in means, ranks, category probabilities, or entire distributions. A “nonparametric replacement for t” does not necessarily test the same null.
Pairing, clustering, repeated measurement, and missing data must shape the test. No distributional test repairs confounded treatment assignment.
A Mann–Whitney result is not automatically a median difference; unequal spread alone can generate a rank difference.
Chi-square and KS reference distributions may be poor with sparse cells, ties, or estimated parameters. Use exact or design-aware alternatives when needed.
crumbs: 6  Classical Tests: z, t, Ranks, and Distributions

title: Classical Tests: z, t, Ranks, and Distributions
text:
Interview questions
When would you choose Welch over pooled t? For two independent means when equal variance is not justified, particularly with different group sizes. Welch estimates each variance separately and adjusts degrees of freedom.
What does the Mann–Whitney test compare? It uses pairwise ordering or ranks. Under suitable conditions it tests equality of distributions; interpreting it specifically as a location or median shift requires additional shape assumptions.
Why are z and t different? Estimating an unknown SD adds uncertainty. The t reference has heavier tails, especially with few degrees of freedom.
crumbs: 6  Classical Tests: z, t, Ranks, and Distributions

title: Classical Tests: z, t, Ranks, and Distributions
text:
Summary
Choose a test from the question, outcome scale, grouping structure, and null model. Formula selection is the last step after checking independence, pairing, variance, and calibration.

title: Permutation Tests and Exchangeability
text:
Learning goals
You should be able to state the exchangeability requirement, enumerate a small exact randomization test, implement a Monte Carlo p-value in words, and distinguish permutation from bootstrap resampling.

title: Permutation Tests and Exchangeability
text:
Intuition
Under a null that makes group labels exchangeable, relabeling the observed outcomes creates alternative assignments compatible with that null. A permutation test compares the actual statistic with this design-based or model-based null distribution. It avoids selecting a normal or t reference distribution, but exchangeability is a substantive assumption, not a free pass around study design.

title: Permutation Tests and Exchangeability
text:
Worked example
Four fixed values are \((1,2,3,4)\). The observed groups are \(A=(1,2)\) and \(B=(3,4)\), so \(T_{\rm obs}=\bar A-\bar B=-2\). There are \(\binom42=6\) assignments of two values to \(A\). Their mean differences are \(-2,-1,0,0,1,2\). For a two-sided test using \(|T|\), two assignments are at least as extreme as the observation, so the exact randomization p-value is \(2/6=1/3\).
This calculation is exact for the stated assignment mechanism and a sharp no-effect null (or for a suitable exchangeable-sample null), with the analysis matching that mechanism. A one-sided test would use the corresponding signed tail. If treatments were assigned within strata or clusters, the six unrestricted shuffles would be the wrong reference set.

title: Permutation Tests and Exchangeability
text:
Theory and assumptions

Algorithm

Specify a scalar statistic \(T\) aligned with the effect of interest: a difference in means or medians, a ratio, or another prespecified measure.
Calculate \(T_{\rm obs}\) using original labels.
Generate assignments allowed by the null and study design, without replacement and while preserving group sizes where applicable.
Recalculate \(T\) under each assignment; use the proportion at least as extreme as \(T_{\rm obs}\) for an exact p-value.

For \(N\) observations divided into groups of \(n_1\) and \(n_2\), there are \(\binom N{n_1}=N!/(n_1!n_2!)\) distinct fixed-size label assignments. Exact enumeration quickly becomes impractical. If \(B\) random assignments are sampled, a common nonzero Monte Carlo estimate is
\[
\hat p=\frac{1+\sum_{b=1}^{B}\mathbf1\{|T_b|\ge|T_{\rm obs}|\}}{B+1},
\]
with an analogous signed-tail version. The addition of one treats the observed labeling as part of the reference set and avoids reporting zero from a finite simulation. The Monte Carlo estimate has simulation error; increasing \(B\) reduces that error but does not fix a wrong permutation scheme.


What exchangeability really buys
Random assignment justifies reshuffling treatment labels according to the original assignment design under a sharp null of no unit-level effect. For observational groups, unrestricted shuffling requires a defensible exchangeability null, which may fail under confounding or unequal distributions. Under a weaker null of equal means with unequal variances, naive label permutation need not control type I error, especially with unequal group sizes; a studentized statistic or other method may be needed.
Permutation draws without replacement from a fixed set of observed values and chiefly tests an assignment or independence null. Bootstrap draws with replacement from an empirical distribution and chiefly estimates sampling uncertainty. Neither solves selection bias.

title: Permutation Tests and Exchangeability
text:
Practice and pitfalls

Preserve blocked randomization, matching pairs, clusters, and time dependence in the resampling scheme.
Report the statistic, tail definition, number of assignments or simulations, and null being tested.
Use a statistic sensitive to the scientific question; flexibility to invent one after seeing the result recreates selection bias.
A permutation p-value can be exact conditional on design while an effect-size estimate remains uncertain. Report both.

title: Permutation Tests and Exchangeability
text:
Interview questions
Why can labels be shuffled? Under the relevant null and assignment mechanism, the allowed labelings are exchangeable. I verify that condition and mirror the actual design in the shuffle.
What differs from bootstrap? Permutation reassigns labels without replacement to construct a null distribution; bootstrap resamples observations with replacement to approximate an estimator’s sampling distribution.
When would ordinary permutation fail? If groups were self-selected, measurements are clustered, or equal-mean groups have unequal distributions, unrestricted labels may not be exchangeable.

title: Permutation Tests and Exchangeability
text:
Summary
Permutation testing is a powerful way to build a problem-specific null distribution. Its validity comes from exchangeability and faithful reproduction of the assignment or sampling design.

title: Replication, Effect Size, and Research Flexibility
text:
Learning goals
You should recognize common drivers of irreproducible findings, distinguish statistical from practical significance, calculate Cohen’s \(d\) and \(q\), and explain how preregistration and transparent reporting reduce analysis flexibility.
crumbs: 8  Replication, Effect Size, and Research Flexibility

title: Replication, Effect Size, and Research Flexibility
text:
Intuition
Given enough independent data, even a tiny nonzero effect can produce a small p-value. That result might be real but irrelevant to a decision. Conversely, a useful effect can look inconclusive in an underpowered study. An effect size reports the magnitude on a meaningful scale; uncertainty tells us how precisely that magnitude is known.
The replication crisis concerns findings that do not hold up when studies are repeated. Causes vary by field, but the source notes emphasize small samples, selective publication, flexible stopping, multiple unreported analyses, and incentives to publish novelty. Numerical replication-rate claims depend on definitions, time period, and sample of studies; a single percentage should not be carried forward as a universal fact.
crumbs: 8  Replication, Effect Size, and Research Flexibility

title: Replication, Effect Size, and Research Flexibility
text:
Worked example
Suppose a treatment raises an outcome by \(0.5\) units and the common SD is \(10\) units. Cohen’s \(d=0.5/10=0.05\), a small standardized difference. A very large experiment could identify that difference precisely, but whether \(0.5\) units matter must be judged in the outcome’s real-world units, costs, and stakeholder context.
Suppose two studies report correlations \(r_1=0.8\) and \(r_2=0.2\). Cohen’s \(q\) uses Fisher’s transform:
\[
z(r)=\operatorname{atanh}(r)=\tfrac12\log\!\left(\frac{1+r}{1-r}\right),\qquad
q=z(r_1)-z(r_2)\approx1.099-0.203=0.896.
\]
The raw difference \(0.6\) ignores how the bounded correlation scale behaves near \(\pm1\). The transform improves large-sample normal approximations for correlation, although interpretation still requires sampling uncertainty and study comparability.
crumbs: 8  Replication, Effect Size, and Research Flexibility

title: Replication, Effect Size, and Research Flexibility
text:
Theory and assumptions

Why repeated significance checks mislead
If an analyst inspects accumulating data after each user and stops the first time \(p<0.05\), the chance of ever crossing that threshold under a true null usually exceeds 5%. Testing many outcomes, subgroup definitions, covariate sets, or outlier rules and reporting only the successful one has a similar selection effect. HARKing means presenting a hypothesis developed after observing results as if it had been prespecified. The file-drawer problem occurs when studies with unexciting results are less visible. These mechanisms can exaggerate published effect sizes and undermine replication.


Standardized effects
For two independent groups with a meaningful common SD, Cohen’s \(d=(\mu_1-\mu_2)/\sigma\) at the population level; in a sample, use a stated SD estimator, often pooled \(s_p\). The sign depends on group order. A small-sample correction produces Hedges’ \(g\). The source cheat sheet’s qualitative labels and real-world comparison examples are at most heuristics: no universal \(d\) cutoff determines practical value or a particular individual’s benefit. Standardizing removes units but can hide whether \(\sigma\) differs across settings.
As a memory aid, the source calls \(|d|\approx0.1\) tiny, \(0.3\) small, \(0.5\) moderate, \(1\) large, and \(2\) huge. These are descriptions of standardized separation for its examples, not domain-independent decision thresholds; an effect much smaller than \(0.1\) can still matter at scale or for a high-stakes outcome.
Fisher’s transform \(z(r)=\operatorname{atanh}(r)\) is defined for \(|r|<1\). Cohen’s \(q\) is the difference of two such transformed correlations. The sampling distribution of \(r\) can be skewed near its boundaries and its variance depends on the population correlation. Under independent bivariate-normal sampling, Fisher’s \(z\) has approximate standard error \(1/\sqrt{n-3}\). Dependent correlations need covariance-aware inference; \(q\) itself is not a test statistic or proof that associations differ.


Better evidence practices
Pre-register the primary question, outcome, exclusion criteria, sample-size or stopping rule, and planned analysis. Make exploratory analyses explicit, adjust or model multiplicity when appropriate, and report effect estimates with intervals and design limitations. An independent replication should use a comparable estimand and enough precision to distinguish a meaningful effect from negligible effects.
crumbs: 8  Replication, Effect Size, and Research Flexibility

title: Replication, Effect Size, and Research Flexibility
text:
Practice and pitfalls

A small p-value does not quantify the size, usefulness, or probability that an effect is real.
A failed replication need not prove fraud or exactly zero effect; populations, implementation, measurement, and uncertainty can differ. Compare estimates and intervals.
Cohen’s \(d\) is a standardized mean difference, not a promised “change for each person.” Cohen’s \(q\) compares correlations on Fisher’s scale, not raw probability differences.
Decide a minimum effect of interest before interpreting whether an interval is practically narrow.
crumbs: 8  Replication, Effect Size, and Research Flexibility

title: Replication, Effect Size, and Research Flexibility
text:
Interview questions
What is p-hacking? It is using flexible data collection or analysis choices to preferentially obtain a small p-value without accounting for those choices. It inflates false-positive risk and selected effect estimates.
Why report Cohen’s \(d\) if the p-value is significant? The p-value depends on sample size and noise. \(d\) describes mean separation in SD units; I also report the original-unit effect and an interval for practical interpretation.
How would you improve replicability? I would prespecify the primary analysis, ensure adequate power, disclose all planned outcomes and exclusions, share reproducible code where appropriate, and seek independent replication.
crumbs: 8  Replication, Effect Size, and Research Flexibility

title: Replication, Effect Size, and Research Flexibility
text:
Summary
Credible evidence requires attention to magnitude, uncertainty, design, and selection of analyses. Effect sizes help, but no single statistic substitutes for transparent study practice.

title: Power, Confidence Intervals, Bootstrap, and Jackknife
text:
Learning goals
You should distinguish type I and II errors, calculate a simple standard-error-based interval, interpret frequentist coverage, relate power to sample size and effect magnitude, and choose between bootstrap and jackknife resampling.
crumbs: 9  Power, Confidence Intervals, Bootstrap, and Jackknife

title: Power, Confidence Intervals, Bootstrap, and Jackknife
text:
Intuition
Power is the probability of rejecting \(H_0\) when a specified alternative is true. A low-powered study often produces a wide interval, making both a nonzero effect and a practically negligible effect compatible with the data. Confidence intervals foreground a range of effects under a procedure; resampling estimates the procedure’s variability when an analytic formula is inconvenient.
crumbs: 9  Power, Confidence Intervals, Bootstrap, and Jackknife

title: Power, Confidence Intervals, Bootstrap, and Jackknife
text:
Worked example
Suppose a sample mean is \(100\), population SD is known to be \(20\), and \(n=100\) independent observations satisfy conditions for a normal approximation. The standard error is \(20/\sqrt{100}=2\), so a 95% z interval is
\[
100\pm1.96(2)=[96.08,103.92].
\]
For a point-null difference of zero, an interval narrow enough to lie inside a prespecified negligible-effect region—say \([-5,5]\) in effect units—could support a practical equivalence claim via the appropriate equivalence procedure. A wide interval crossing zero gives less information; “not significant” alone cannot distinguish these situations.
For resampling, take observations \((1,2,3)\) with mean \(2\). One size-three bootstrap draw with replacement might be \((1,1,3)\), whose mean is \(5/3\); many such draws form an empirical distribution of means. The three leave-one-out jackknife means are \(2.5,2,1.5\). Their mean is \(2\), giving jackknife variance \((3-1)/3[(0.5)^2+0^2+(-0.5)^2]=1/3\) and standard error \(\sqrt{1/3}\approx0.577\).
crumbs: 9  Power, Confidence Intervals, Bootstrap, and Jackknife

title: Power, Confidence Intervals, Bootstrap, and Jackknife
text:
Theory and assumptions

Type I, type II, and power








Decision
\(H_0\) true
Specified alternative true




Reject \(H_0\)
Type I error, rate \(\alpha\)
Correct detection, power \(1-\beta\)


Do not reject \(H_0\)
Correct non-rejection, rate \(1-\alpha\)
Type II error, rate \(\beta\)



Power depends on the alternative effect, variance, sample size, threshold, sidedness, and design. Lowering \(\alpha\) while holding other factors fixed usually reduces power. Increasing sample size narrows the standard error. Pairing can improve precision when within-pair outcomes are positively correlated, but poor pairing or attrition can erase the gain.
For an approximate two-sided one-sample z test of a known-SD mean difference \(\delta\), target power \(1-\beta\) gives
\[
n\approx\left[\frac{(z_{1-\alpha/2}+z_{1-\beta})\sigma}{\delta}\right]^2.
\]
At \(\alpha=0.05\), 80% target power, \(\sigma=20\), and \(\delta=5\), this is about \([(1.96+0.84)4]^2=125.44\), so round up to at least \(126\) one-sample observations before allowances for attrition or approximation. An equal-size two-arm comparison has a different variance and needs a larger per-arm number. The source’s shorthand “power \(\propto\) effect size \(\times\sqrt N\)” captures the signal-to-noise trend but is not a general power equation.


Confidence intervals and evidence of absence
A \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence procedure covers a fixed parameter in \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) of repetitions under its assumptions. Once an interval is observed, the frequentist parameter is not assigned a probability of being inside it. For an iid normal mean with unknown SD, use \(\bar x\pm t_{n-1,1-\alpha/2}s/\sqrt n\); a known-SD z interval uses \(\sigma\). Intervals from clustered data, ratios, bounded parameters, or skewed estimators need appropriate calibration.
Absence of evidence means the interval still includes effects large enough to matter. Evidence of practical absence requires an interval sufficiently precise to exclude effects outside a prespecified equivalence region, with a method suited to the claim. Simply crossing zero does not decide this issue.


Bootstrap and jackknife
The nonparametric bootstrap treats the observed empirical distribution as an approximation to the population. Repeatedly sample \(n\) observations with replacement, compute the statistic \(\hat\theta_b^*\), and use the distribution across draws to estimate standard error or an interval. A percentile interval takes suitable quantiles of \(\hat\theta_b^*\); skew, bias, boundaries, dependence, and small samples can make simple percentile intervals inaccurate. Alternatives include studentized or bias-corrected approaches when justified. Clustered or time-dependent observations need a resampling scheme that preserves dependence.
The jackknife deterministically removes one observation at a time. For leave-one-out estimates \(\hat\theta_{(i)}\) and their mean \(\bar\theta_{(.)}\),
\[
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}_{\rm jack}(\hat\theta)=\frac{n-1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n(\hat\theta_{(i)}-\bar\theta_{(.)})^2.
\]
It also yields a bias estimate, \(\widehat{\operatorname{bias}}_{\rm jack}=(n-1)(\bar\theta_{(.)}-\hat\theta)\). Jackknife and bootstrap are distinct methods, not simply deterministic and stochastic versions of one another. Jackknife can perform poorly for nonsmooth statistics such as some quantiles; bootstrap is not automatically valid either.
crumbs: 9  Power, Confidence Intervals, Bootstrap, and Jackknife

title: Power, Confidence Intervals, Bootstrap, and Jackknife
text:
Practice and pitfalls

Define the minimum effect of interest and target power before data collection; a post hoc power number rarely adds more than the observed estimate and interval.
The sample cannot resample a truly absent rare event. Bigger samples reduce sampling variability but do not cure selection bias.
A bootstrap distribution approximates uncertainty conditional on the observed sampling mechanism. It does not replace randomization or a defensible target population.
Report the interval construction, resampling unit, repetitions, and treatment of ties or failures for reproducibility.
crumbs: 9  Power, Confidence Intervals, Bootstrap, and Jackknife

title: Power, Confidence Intervals, Bootstrap, and Jackknife
text:
Interview questions
What does 80% power mean? If a particular alternative effect and all design assumptions hold, the prespecified test rejects the null in about 80% of repeated studies.
Does a 95% confidence interval put 95% probability on this parameter being inside? Not in the frequentist interpretation. The procedure has 95% long-run coverage under its assumptions.
Why use bootstrap instead of a textbook formula? A complicated statistic may not have a convenient analytic standard error. I resample the correct unit and validate that the empirical distribution approximates the estimator’s sampling behavior.
crumbs: 9  Power, Confidence Intervals, Bootstrap, and Jackknife

title: Power, Confidence Intervals, Bootstrap, and Jackknife
text:
Summary
Power addresses whether a planned study can detect a meaningful effect. Intervals show the precision of an estimate. Bootstrap and jackknife estimate uncertainty from observed data, subject to the original data’s quality and the statistic’s regularity.

title: Bayesian Updating, Bayes Factors, and Predictive Value
text:
Learning goals
You should calculate a posterior with Bayes’ rule, distinguish likelihood from probability and maximum likelihood from Bayesian estimation, interpret a credible interval, explain a Bayes factor, and derive the positive predictive value of a significant finding.
crumbs: 10  Bayesian Updating, Bayes Factors, and Predictive Value

title: Bayesian Updating, Bayes Factors, and Predictive Value
text:
Intuition
Bayes’ rule updates prior uncertainty when data arrive. A frequentist parameter is conventionally a fixed unknown quantity and probability refers to a repeatable procedure or random data. A Bayesian model assigns a probability distribution to the unknown parameter conditional on the model and prior. Neither interpretation turns poor data into strong evidence.
For an event \(A\) and observation \(B\) with \(P(B)>0\),
\[
P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(B\mid A)P(A)}{P(B)}
=\frac{P(B\mid A)P(A)}{P(B\mid A)P(A)+P(B\mid\neg A)P(\neg A)}.
\]
The numerator combines a prior \(P(A)\) and a likelihood of the evidence \(P(B\mid A)\); the denominator is the marginal probability of the evidence, which normalizes the posterior.
crumbs: 10  Bayesian Updating, Bayes Factors, and Predictive Value

title: Bayesian Updating, Bayes Factors, and Predictive Value
text:
Worked example

Updating a conversion probability
Suppose \(7\) of \(10\) independent trials succeed. Under a Bernoulli model, the likelihood as a function of the unknown success probability \(p\) is proportional to \(p^7(1-p)^3\); its maximum is the MLE \(\hat p=7/10=0.7\). With a \(\operatorname{Beta}(2,2)\) prior, conjugate updating gives \(p\mid D\sim\operatorname{Beta}(9,5)\), whose posterior mean is \(9/14\approx0.643\). A 95% posterior credible interval contains 95% of this model-conditional posterior mass; its endpoints are posterior quantiles, not \(\hat p\pm1.96\) standard errors.
The prior matters at this sample size. A uniform \(\operatorname{Beta}(1,1)\) prior gives \(\operatorname{Beta}(8,4)\) and mean \(2/3\), while a concentrated \(\operatorname{Beta}(20,20)\) prior gives \(\operatorname{Beta}(27,23)\) and mean \(0.54\). Report such sensitivity when prior information is debatable.


Bayes factor for two point hypotheses
Compare \(H_0:p=0.5\) with \(H_1:p=0.7\) for the same \(7\) successes and \(3\) failures. The binomial coefficient cancels in the evidence ratio:
\[
BF_{10}=\frac{P(D\mid H_1)}{P(D\mid H_0)}
=\frac{0.7^7 0.3^3}{0.5^{10}}\approx2.28.
\]
With equal prior odds, posterior odds for \(H_1\) are \(2.28:1\) and \(P(H_1\mid D,H_0\text{ or }H_1)\approx2.28/3.28=0.695\). This posterior probability is conditional on treating the two point hypotheses as exhaustive and assigning equal prior probabilities.
crumbs: 10  Bayesian Updating, Bayes Factors, and Predictive Value

title: Bayesian Updating, Bayes Factors, and Predictive Value
text:
Theory and assumptions

Likelihood and MLE
For fixed \(\theta\), \(p(x\mid\theta)\) describes a sampling model for possible data \(x\). After observing \(x\), the same mathematical expression viewed as a function of \(\theta\) is the likelihood \(L(\theta;x)\). A likelihood is not generally a normalized probability distribution over \(\theta\). For iid data, \(L(\theta;x_{1:n})=\prod_i p(x_i\mid\theta)\); independence must be justified, not assumed by notation. Maximum likelihood selects the \(\theta\) that maximizes this function, often by maximizing its log.
Bayesian updating uses a prior density \(\pi(\theta)\) and posterior \(\pi(\theta\mid D)\propto p(D\mid\theta)\pi(\theta)\). The normalizing constant is \(p(D)=\int p(D\mid\theta)\pi(\theta)\,d\theta\). A 95% credible interval \(C(D)\) satisfies \(P(\theta\in C(D)\mid D)=0.95\) under this model. It differs from a frequentist 95% confidence interval, whose guarantee concerns coverage over repeated samples. Neither interval is guaranteed to be well-calibrated if its model is badly misspecified.


Bayes factors and prior odds
For hypotheses \(H_1,H_0\), posterior odds equal Bayes factor times prior odds:
\[
\frac{P(H_1\mid D)}{P(H_0\mid D)}
=\underbrace{\frac{p(D\mid H_1)}{p(D\mid H_0)}}_{BF_{10}}
\frac{P(H_1)}{P(H_0)}.
\]
For a composite hypothesis, \(p(D\mid H_j)=\int p(D\mid\theta_j,H_j)\pi_j(\theta_j)\,d\theta_j\): the marginal likelihood averages likelihood over a proper model-specific prior. A Bayes factor is therefore not simply a ratio of likelihoods evaluated at each model’s MLE, except in the point-hypothesis example above. Conventional verbal scales such as “anecdotal” or “strong” evidence are arbitrary aids, not scientific cutoffs; the value and prior assumptions should be reported directly.
The source’s mnemonic scale labels \(BF_{10}=1\) neutral, roughly \(1\)–\(3\) weak or anecdotal support for \(H_1\), \(10\)–\(30\) strong support, and values above \(100\) extreme support. Reciprocals express support for \(H_0\): about \(1/3\)–\(1\) weak support and below \(1/100\) extreme support. Intermediate ranges are not magical gaps or universal thresholds. Posterior odds also depend on prior odds, so even a large \(BF_{10}\) need not make \(H_1\) probable when its prior probability is very low.


Positive predictive value of a significant result
Consider many prespecified tests where an effect is truly present with base-rate probability \(\pi\), power is \(1-\beta\), and the false-positive rate for no effect is \(\alpha\). Bayes’ rule gives the proportion of significant findings arising from true effects:
\[
PPV=P(\text{effect true}\mid\text{significant})
=\frac{(1-\beta)\pi}{(1-\beta)\pi+\alpha(1-\pi)}.
\]
Writing prior odds \(R=\pi/(1-\pi)\) yields the cheat sheet’s formula \(PPV=(1-\beta)R/[(1-\beta)R+\alpha]\). If \(\pi=0.01\), power \(=0.80\), and \(\alpha=0.05\), then \(PPV=0.008/(0.008+0.0495)\approx0.139\). Even a nominally significant result may have low predictive value when the base rate is low. Sensitivity or power is \(TP/(TP+FN)\); specificity is \(TN/(TN+FP)=1-\alpha\) in this stylized binary setup; PPV or precision is \(TP/(TP+FP)\); accuracy is \((TP+TN)/(TP+FP+FN+TN)\).
This is a model for a collection of tests, not a generally valid posterior probability for one particular study. Publication selection, multiple testing, heterogeneous effects, and ambiguous definitions of “true effect” alter its inputs. A p-value alone does not specify \(\pi\) and cannot determine \(PPV\).
crumbs: 10  Bayesian Updating, Bayes Factors, and Predictive Value

title: Bayesian Updating, Bayes Factors, and Predictive Value
text:
Practice and pitfalls

Choose priors from substantive knowledge and check sensitivity. “More data” tends to reduce prior influence under identifiable, well-specified models, but neither framework automatically becomes reliable at a particular sample size.
Keep \(P(D\mid H)\) distinct from \(P(H\mid D)\); Bayes’ rule needs a prior and evidence under competing possibilities to reverse the conditioning.
State whether a Bayes factor compares point or composite hypotheses, which priors define the composite models, and whether stopping or selection was part of the design.
Do not treat a conventional Bayes-factor label or a significant p-value as a decision rule without costs, prior plausibility, and effect magnitude.
crumbs: 10  Bayesian Updating, Bayes Factors, and Predictive Value

title: Bayesian Updating, Bayes Factors, and Predictive Value
text:
Interview questions
What is the difference between likelihood and posterior? Likelihood scores parameter values by how well they predict the observed data but is not a probability distribution over parameters. Multiplying by a prior and normalizing produces the posterior.
How does a credible interval differ from a confidence interval? The credible interval carries model-conditional posterior probability for the parameter. A frequentist confidence procedure has long-run coverage for a fixed parameter under its assumptions.
Why can a positive significant finding be unreliable? If true effects are rare, false positives among many null tests can outnumber detected true effects. Power, type I error, base rates, and selection practices jointly determine predictive value.
crumbs: 10  Bayesian Updating, Bayes Factors, and Predictive Value

title: Bayesian Updating, Bayes Factors, and Predictive Value
text:
Summary
Bayesian inference updates explicit prior assumptions with a sampling model. Bayes factors compare predictive evidence between hypotheses, and predictive-value calculations show why base rates matter when interpreting “positive” findings.
crumbs: 10  Bayesian Updating, Bayes Factors, and Predictive Value

title: Linear Regression: Projection, Interpretation, and Assessment
text:
Learning goals
Explain a linear model, derive OLS as a projection, interpret regression to the mean, and assess fit without confusing training performance with generalization. This chapter covers the regression foundations and assessment material in IDS 11.
crumbs: 11  Linear Regression: Projection, Interpretation, and Assessment

title: Linear Regression: Projection, Interpretation, and Assessment
text:
Intuition
A regression model describes how an outcome varies with predictors. Hypothesis testing can ask whether a coefficient is zero; regression additionally supplies an estimated magnitude and predictions. The two tools complement each other.
The general linear model is
\[Y_i=\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_jX_{ij}+\epsilon_i.\]
“Linear” means linear in coefficients: a model containing \(X^2\) is still linear in its coefficients. Do not confuse the general linear model with the broader generalized linear model family, which includes logistic regression. Indicator variables connect this framework to ANOVA.
Coefficients are attractive because they make a compact model interpretable. Simplicity is useful when it reflects the problem; a simple misspecified model is not automatically scientifically preferable.
crumbs: 11  Linear Regression: Projection, Interpretation, and Assessment

title: Linear Regression: Projection, Interpretation, and Assessment
text:
Worked example
For \(x=(0,1,2)\) and \(y=(1,2,2)\), \(\bar x=1\) and \(\bar y=5/3\). The slope and intercept are
\[\hat\beta_1=\frac{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)}{\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2}=\frac12,\qquad
\hat\beta_0=\bar y-\hat\beta_1\bar x=\frac76.\]
Predictions are \((7/6,5/3,13/6)\) and residuals are \((-1/6,1/3,-1/6)\). Therefore \(\mathrm{SSE}=1/6\), \(\mathrm{SST}=2/3\), \(R^2=3/4\), and training \(\mathrm{RMSE}=\sqrt{1/18}\approx0.236\). Residuals sum to zero, and their inner product with \(x\) is zero.
For a separate regression-to-the-mean illustration, suppose \(r=0.42\). A predictor two standard deviations above its mean predicts an outcome only \(0.84\) standard deviations above its mean. This is a conditional prediction under the linear model, not a force making every individual move toward average.
crumbs: 11  Linear Regression: Projection, Interpretation, and Assessment

title: Linear Regression: Projection, Interpretation, and Assessment
text:
Theory and assumptions

Why squared error?
OLS minimizes \(\|y-X\beta\|_2^2\). Signed residuals alone cancel; absolute error avoids cancellation but has a kink at zero and targets a conditional median. Squared error is differentiable, penalizes large errors strongly, and targets a conditional mean. Other losses produce different optimal fits.
Differentiating gives
\[-2X^\top(y-X\hat\beta)=0,\qquad X^\top X\hat\beta=X^\top y.\]
If columns have full rank, \(\hat\beta=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y\). Geometrically, \(X\hat\beta\) projects \(y\) onto the column space of \(X\), leaving an orthogonal residual. With rank deficiency, coefficients are not unique, though fitted projections are; use a pseudoinverse or a regularized model. Numerically, QR or SVD is preferable to explicitly forming an inverse.


Which assumptions serve which goal?
Computing the least-squares fit requires no Gaussian errors. Conditional mean correctness, \(E[\epsilon\mid X]=0\), supports coefficient unbiasedness under appropriate sampling. Full rank supports identification. Homoskedastic uncorrelated errors yield the classical variance \(\sigma^2(X^\top X)^{-1}\) and Gauss–Markov efficiency. Normal errors support exact small-sample classical tests; robust or clustered uncertainty estimates address different dependence structures.
A multiple-regression coefficient describes the linear association holding included predictors fixed. It is not a causal effect simply because many variables were included: omitted confounders, post-treatment adjustment, measurement error, and selection still matter.


Assessing predictions
\[R^2=1-\frac{\sum_i(y_i-\hat y_i)^2}{\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2},\qquad
\mathrm{RMSE}=\sqrt{\frac1n\sum_i(y_i-\hat y_i)^2}.\]
The decomposition \(\mathrm{SST}=\mathrm{SSR}+\mathrm{SSE}\) and nonnegative training \(R^2\) hold for unpenalized OLS with an intercept. In simple regression that fit has \(R^2=r_{XY}^2\); in multiple regression it equals \(\operatorname{Corr}(y,\hat y)^2\) when nondegenerate. These identities do not transfer indiscriminately to held-out data, no-intercept fits, or regularized predictions. Test \(R^2\) can be negative, meaning worse squared error than its mean baseline. RMSE retains outcome units; \(R^2\) describes relative improvement.
crumbs: 11  Linear Regression: Projection, Interpretation, and Assessment

title: Linear Regression: Projection, Interpretation, and Assessment
text:
Practice and pitfalls
Plot residuals against fitted values and time; curvature suggests missing functional structure, a funnel suggests heteroskedasticity, and temporal patterns suggest dependence. Examine influential observations before treating a coefficient as stable. Predicting beyond observed covariate support is extrapolation.
Adding predictors cannot increase the optimized training SSE, but can worsen future error. The curse of dimensionality is particularly severe for flexible local models; it does not mean every parametric regression requires exponentially many observations. Correlated columns make coefficients unstable. With an intercept, encoding every category creates the dummy-variable trap; omit a reference category or use an appropriate constraint.
crumbs: 11  Linear Regression: Projection, Interpretation, and Assessment

title: Linear Regression: Projection, Interpretation, and Assessment
text:
Interview questions
Why are residuals orthogonal to predictors? This is the first-order condition of the squared-error minimization, not evidence that real-world causes have been eliminated.
Can a high \(R^2\) prove causation? No. Fit is compatible with confounding, reverse causality, and leakage.
Why is a zero training RMSE suspicious? A sufficiently flexible model may interpolate noise. Evaluate predictions on observations excluded from model selection.
crumbs: 11  Linear Regression: Projection, Interpretation, and Assessment

title: Linear Regression: Projection, Interpretation, and Assessment
text:
Summary
OLS is a projection with a clear objective. Distinguish algebraic properties of the fitted sample, assumptions for inference, and the separate evidence needed for causal claims and generalization.

title: Regularization and Cross-Validation
text:
Learning goals
Explain the bias–variance tradeoff, derive ridge shrinkage, contrast L1 and L2 geometry, and tune complexity without test-set leakage.

title: Regularization and Cross-Validation
text:
Intuition
A flexible model can chase accidental patterns. Regularization charges for complexity, accepting some bias to reduce sensitivity to the particular training sample. Under squared prediction loss, expected error decomposes into squared bias, variance, and irreducible noise. This decomposition describes repeated training samples, not three numbers observable from one training score.
Ridge spreads weight across correlated predictors. Lasso can make coefficients exactly zero. Elastic net combines both behaviors. Selection of a feature does not establish that it is causal or uniquely important.

title: Regularization and Cross-Validation
text:
Worked example
Take centered one-dimensional data with \(\sum x_i^2=4\) and \(\sum x_iy_i=8\). OLS gives \(\hat\beta=2\). For the objective \(\sum(y_i-x_i\beta)^2+\lambda\beta^2\), ridge with \(\lambda=4\) gives \(\hat\beta=8/(4+4)=1\).
For the lasso objective \(\sum(y_i-x_i\beta)^2+\lambda|\beta|\), the same data give
\[\hat\beta=\frac{\operatorname{sign}(8)(8-\lambda/2)_+}{4}.\]
Thus \(\lambda=4\) gives \(1.5\) and \(\lambda\ge16\) gives zero. The factor of two depends on whether the loss is written as SSE, half-SSE, or average half-SSE. Always state the convention before comparing penalty parameters.

title: Regularization and Cross-Validation
text:
Theory and assumptions
For centered predictors and outcome, ridge solves
\[\min_\beta\|y-X\beta\|_2^2+\lambda\|\beta\|_2^2,
\qquad \hat\beta=(X^\top X+\lambda I)^{-1}X^\top y.\]
If \(X=UDV^\top\), its fitted signal uses factors \(d_j^2/(d_j^2+\lambda)\). Directions with little information shrink most, explaining why ridge stabilizes collinearity. As \(\lambda\to\infty\), penalized slopes approach zero. With an unpenalized intercept the prediction approaches the training outcome mean.
Lasso replaces the squared norm by \(\|\beta\|_1\). In two dimensions its constraint region is a diamond, whose corners lie on coordinate axes; a loss contour can touch a corner, producing a zero coefficient. Ridge’s smooth ball generally shrinks rather than selects. Elastic net uses
\[\frac{1}{2n}\|y-X\beta\|_2^2+\lambda\left[\alpha\|\beta\|_1+\frac{1-\alpha}{2}\|\beta\|_2^2\right].\]
Here \(\alpha=1\) is lasso and \(\alpha=0\) is ridge under this convention. Strongly correlated features can make lasso selection unstable; adding L2 encourages more stable grouped behavior, without magically identifying the “true” feature.

title: Regularization and Cross-Validation
text:
Practice and pitfalls

Reserve a final test set using a split matching deployment: time, entity, or independent rows.
On the remaining data, cross-validate candidate penalties and feature choices. Fit scaling, imputation, feature selection, and PCA inside each training fold.
Select the penalty using the validation metric, optionally choosing a simpler model within one standard error of the best score.
Refit on development data and evaluate once on the untouched test set.

Standardize features before coefficient penalties so units do not decide which variable is expensive. Keep the intercept unpenalized unless there is a deliberate alternative model. Use nested cross-validation when reporting cross-validation performance after extensive tuning without a separate test set.
Do not call a repeatedly inspected tuning set a test set. Report both training and validation performance to distinguish underfitting from overfitting. Ridge improves conditioning, but neither ridge nor lasso repairs omitted-variable bias automatically.

title: Regularization and Cross-Validation
text:
Interview questions
Why can a biased estimator predict better? Lower sampling variance can more than compensate for additional squared bias.
Does lasso always choose the correct variables? No. Selection depends on signal strength, feature correlations, sample size, and penalty; assess stability.
Why scale inside each fold? A transform learned from validation observations leaks information about their distribution into training.

title: Regularization and Cross-Validation
text:
Summary
Penalty strength is a modeling choice selected with held-out evidence. Ridge stabilizes, lasso sparsifies, and elastic net combines shrinkage and selection. Preserve a final evaluation boundary.

title: Logistic Regression and Classification Metrics
text:
Learning goals
Derive logistic loss, interpret odds ratios, calculate classification metrics, and choose assessment measures appropriate to prevalence and decision costs.
crumbs: 13  Logistic Regression and Classification Metrics

title: Logistic Regression and Classification Metrics
text:
Intuition
Classification predicts categories, often through estimated probabilities. Maximizing a margin is one approach, not the universal definition of classification. Logistic regression maps an unrestricted linear score into a probability:
\[\eta=\beta_0+x^\top\beta,\qquad p=\sigma(\eta)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-\eta}}.\]
Odds are \(p/(1-p)\) and log-odds are \(\log[p/(1-p)]=\eta\). A one-unit predictor increase multiplies conditional odds by \(e^{\beta_j}\), holding other variables fixed. It does not add \(\beta_j\) to probability.
crumbs: 13  Logistic Regression and Classification Metrics

title: Logistic Regression and Classification Metrics
text:
Worked example
If \(\eta=-2+0.8x\), then \(p(0)\approx0.119\) and \(p(1)\approx0.231\). The odds ratio is \(e^{0.8}\approx2.23\), while the probability difference is about \(0.112\). That probability difference changes with the starting value of \(x\).
Now evaluate 1,000 observations containing 100 positives. A threshold yields TP = 80, FN = 20, FP = 90, TN = 810.

crumbs: 13  Logistic Regression and Classification Metrics

title: Logistic Regression and Classification Metrics
text:
Theory and assumptions
For independent Bernoulli responses, maximizing \(\prod_i p_i^{y_i}(1-p_i)^{1-y_i}\) is equivalent to minimizing binary cross-entropy:
\[L=-\sum_i[y_i\log p_i+(1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)].\]
Entropy \(H(P)=-\sum_xP(x)\log P(x)\) measures uncertainty. Cross-entropy satisfies \(H(P,Q)=H(P)+D_{KL}(P\|Q)\); it is not a symmetric mathematical distance. The per-observation derivatives with respect to score are \(g=p-y\) and \(h=p(1-p)\), linking logistic regression to boosted trees. The marginal probability effect is \(\partial p/\partial x_j=\beta_jp(1-p)\).
Linear probability models can be fitted with OLS, but can predict outside \([0,1]\) and have heteroskedastic errors. Gaussian errors are not required merely to compute OLS. Logistic regression instead specifies a Bernoulli conditional distribution and linear log-odds; that specification can itself be wrong.

Thresholds and curves
Lowering a score threshold usually raises both TPR and FPR. ROC plots TPR against FPR across thresholds. AUROC is the probability a random positive outranks a random negative, counting ties as one-half. Its possible range is \([0,1]\): random ranking has expected 0.5, perfect ranking has 1, and reversed ranking can be below 0.5.
Precision depends on prevalence \(\pi\):
\[\mathrm{PPV}=\frac{\mathrm{TPR}\,\pi}{\mathrm{TPR}\,\pi+\mathrm{FPR}(1-\pi)}.\]
This explains why a low FPR may still produce many false alarms in rare-event detection. Precision–recall curves are valuable alongside ROC in such settings. NPV means the fraction of actual negatives among predicted negatives; it does not mean a non-significant experiment proves “no effect.” Calling recall “power” is an analogy to detection, not a replacement for statistical-test power.
crumbs: 13  Logistic Regression and Classification Metrics

title: Logistic Regression and Classification Metrics
text:
Practice and pitfalls
Choose thresholds on validation data using cost or capacity, not automatically 0.5. With calibrated probabilities and only false-positive cost \(C_{FP}\) and false-negative cost \(C_{FN}\), predict positive when \(p>C_{FP}/(C_{FP}+C_{FN})\). Calibration and ranking are different: a model can rank well and give inaccurate probabilities.
Avoid interpreting non-convergence under perfect separation as strong finite coefficients; unregularized logistic estimates can diverge. Use appropriate regularization and inspect separation. Preserve temporal or entity splits, evaluate subgroup performance, and recompute decision economics if prevalence changes.
crumbs: 13  Logistic Regression and Classification Metrics

title: Logistic Regression and Classification Metrics
text:
Interview questions
Why log-loss instead of squared error? It is the negative Bernoulli log-likelihood and directly scores probability predictions.
Can AUROC tell me my precision at 100 reviews per day? No. Evaluate the operating point, such as Precision@100, on a representative population.
Does a coefficient of 0.8 mean an 80% probability increase? No. It is a log-odds change; the odds multiply by about 2.23.
crumbs: 13  Logistic Regression and Classification Metrics

title: Logistic Regression and Classification Metrics
text:
Summary
Separate probability estimation, ranking quality, and the final decision threshold. Read confusion-matrix denominators carefully and keep prevalence visible.
