title: Support Vector Machines: Margins and Hinge Loss
text:
Learning goals
Explain geometric margins, derive hinge loss from slack constraints, and distinguish a linear soft-margin classifier from a nonlinear kernel model.
crumbs: 14  Support Vector Machines: Margins and Hinge Loss

title: Support Vector Machines: Margins and Hinge Loss
text:
Intuition
Many hyperplanes may separate two classes. A support vector machine chooses a separator with a large clearance from training observations. The points constraining that clearance are support vectors; moving a distant non-support point slightly need not change the boundary.
Use labels \(y_i\in\{-1,+1\}\) and one consistent score convention, \(f(x)=w^\top x+b\). The decision boundary is \(f(x)=0\). Rescaling \((w,b)\) leaves the boundary unchanged, so impose functional-margin constraints to define its scale.
crumbs: 14  Support Vector Machines: Margins and Hinge Loss

title: Support Vector Machines: Margins and Hinge Loss
text:
Worked example
In one dimension, negative examples are \(x=-2,-1\) and positive examples are \(x=1,2\). Set \(w=1,b=0\). Then every \(y_if(x_i)\ge1\), and the support vectors lie at \(-1\) and \(1\). The geometric margin between supporting planes is \(2/\|w\|=2\).
For a positive example at \(x=0.2\) under the same score, \(y_if(x_i)=0.2\) and hinge loss is \(0.8\). It is correctly classified but inside the margin. A positive example at \(x=-0.2\) has hinge loss \(1.2\) and is misclassified. Slack is therefore a measure of margin violation, not only a count of wrong labels.
crumbs: 14  Support Vector Machines: Margins and Hinge Loss

title: Support Vector Machines: Margins and Hinge Loss
text:
Theory and assumptions
The hard-margin optimization is
\[\min_{w,b}\frac12\|w\|^2\quad\text{subject to }y_i(w^\top x_i+b)\ge1.\]
The two supporting planes have scores \(+1\) and \(-1\), hence their separation is \(2/\|w\|\). Hard-margin feasibility requires linearly separable data and is brittle to outliers.
Soft margin introduces \(\xi_i\ge0\):
\[\min_{w,b,\xi}\frac12\|w\|^2+C\sum_i\xi_i,
\qquad y_if(x_i)\ge1-\xi_i.\]
For a fixed score, the smallest feasible slack is \(\xi_i=\max(0,1-y_if(x_i))\). Substitution yields regularized hinge-loss minimization. An equivalent convention uses \(\lambda\|w\|^2+n^{-1}\sum_i\xi_i\); larger \(C\) emphasizes training violations while larger \(\lambda\) emphasizes regularization.
A soft margin permits violations but does not by itself make the boundary nonlinear. Kernel methods replace dot products by \(K(x,z)=\langle\phi(x),\phi(z)\rangle\), implicitly fitting a linear separator in a transformed feature space. An RBF kernel uses \(\exp(-\gamma\|x-z\|^2)\); its length scale controls how local the boundary can become.
crumbs: 14  Support Vector Machines: Margins and Hinge Loss

title: Support Vector Machines: Margins and Hinge Loss
text:
Practice and pitfalls
Scale distance-sensitive features using training-fold statistics. Tune regularization and kernel parameters within cross-validation; large RBF \(\gamma\) can create very local, overfit boundaries. Kernel methods may be expensive for large sample sizes, while linear solvers are useful for high-dimensional sparse representations.
The decision score is not automatically a calibrated probability. If probabilities are required, fit and validate calibration without using the final test labels. Class weights change the optimization cost of errors and should reflect the objective, not be treated as an automatic cure for imbalance.
crumbs: 14  Support Vector Machines: Margins and Hinge Loss

title: Support Vector Machines: Margins and Hinge Loss
text:
Interview questions
Can a correctly classified point have nonzero hinge loss? Yes, if its functional margin is between zero and one.
What does increasing \(C\) do? It makes margin violations more expensive relative to the weight norm; the model may accept a narrower margin to fit training data.
How does SVM differ from logistic regression? Both can fit a linear decision boundary, but hinge loss emphasizes margin violations while log-loss estimates conditional class probabilities under its model.
crumbs: 14  Support Vector Machines: Margins and Hinge Loss

title: Support Vector Machines: Margins and Hinge Loss
text:
Summary
Hard margin maximizes separation under feasibility. Soft margin trades that separation against hinge penalties. Kernels introduce nonlinear geometry; they are a separate choice from allowing slack.

title: Decision Trees: From a Rule to CART

Learning goals

title: Decision Trees: From a Rule to CART
text:
Intuition
A decision tree routes an observation through questions such as “is this feature above a threshold?” until it reaches a leaf. Classification leaves estimate class proportions or a class label; squared-error regression leaves estimate a mean. Training asks which question most improves the fit, then repeats locally.
Trees capture nonlinearities and interactions without specifying product terms. An axis-aligned split can express a conditional relationship: work experience may matter only after a GPA split. However, an oblique boundary may require many rectangular regions.

crumbs: 15  Decision Trees: From a Rule to CART

title: Decision Trees: From a Rule to CART
text:
Theory and assumptions

Impurity and split search
For class proportions \(p_1,\ldots,p_K\),
\[I_G=1-\sum_kp_k^2,\qquad I_H=-\sum_kp_k\log_2p_k.\]
Gini is exactly the probability that two independent draws with replacement from the empirical class distribution disagree. Entropy measures expected information in bits, with \(0\log0=0\). Both are zero for pure nodes and largest for a uniform class mixture. Gini avoids logarithms; neither criterion is universally more accurate.
A candidate feature-threshold pair partitions a node into \(L,R\) and receives
\[\Delta=I_P-\frac{n_L}{n_P}I_L-\frac{n_R}{n_P}I_R.\]
Sort each feature, consider boundaries between distinct values, and accumulate class counts to evaluate candidate splits. A scan after sorting costs approximately \(O(nd)\) at a node; sorting itself costs more. A balanced tree can achieve an approximately \(O(nd\log n)\) training scale with suitable reuse, but this is not a guarantee for every implementation or highly unbalanced tree.


Why a regression leaf predicts the mean
For a leaf forced to predict a constant \(c\),
\[\frac{\partial}{\partial c}\sum_{i\in R}(y_i-c)^2=-2\sum_{i\in R}(y_i-c)=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad c=\bar y_R.\]
Its impurity is \(n_R^{-1}\sum_{i\in R}(y_i-\bar y_R)^2\). The split minimizes the sample-size-weighted child MSE. With absolute loss the optimal constant is a median instead.


Growth and pruning
CART recursively chooses the best admissible split, grows child trees, and stops when no split meets constraints. This is greedy optimization, not an exhaustive search over all trees.
Pre-pruning controls max_depth, min_samples_split, min_samples_leaf, min_impurity_decrease, and max_leaf_nodes. Post-pruning minimizes a criterion such as
\[R_\alpha(T)=R(T)+\alpha|\text{leaves}(T)|,\]
selecting \(\alpha\) with cross-validation along a pruning path. This can preserve an initially weak split whose descendants become useful. Available pruning controls depend on the implementation; post-pruning is not absent from modern tree libraries merely because defaults do not activate it.
crumbs: 15  Decision Trees: From a Rule to CART

title: Decision Trees: From a Rule to CART
text:
Practice and pitfalls
Deep trees often have low training bias and high variance; stumps may instead have high bias. A tiny perturbation can change an early split and the whole tree. Minimum leaf sizes stabilize estimates and prevent spurious near-certain probabilities from one observation.
Feature scaling is generally unnecessary for threshold-based tree geometry. Categorical handling and missing-value support are implementation-specific; numeric category codes do not automatically imply a meaningful order. Trees trained on squared error predict leaf averages, so a standalone tree cannot extrapolate beyond the observed response range.
crumbs: 15  Decision Trees: From a Rule to CART

title: Decision Trees: From a Rule to CART
text:
Interview questions
Why weight child impurities? Without sample weights, a tiny pure child could count as much as a large impure child.
Why are trees useful ensemble components? They are flexible and can be trained repeatedly; averaging reduces their instability, while additive boosting builds a stronger function from constrained trees.
Is a pure tree a good tree? Purity measures training fit. Generalization depends on complexity, data quality, and validation.
crumbs: 15  Decision Trees: From a Rule to CART

title: Decision Trees: From a Rule to CART
text:
Summary
CART turns rule selection into a greedy impurity-reduction problem. Understand the leaf loss and stopping rule before interpreting the resulting tree.

title: Random Forest: Averaging, Correlation, and OOB Evaluation
text:
Learning goals
Derive ensemble variance, calculate the out-of-bag probability, explain feature importance, and tune tree strength against correlation.
crumbs: 16  Random Forest: Averaging, Correlation, and OOB Evaluation

title: Random Forest: Averaging, Correlation, and OOB Evaluation
text:
Intuition
A deep tree can change sharply when its training sample changes. Bagging averages trees trained on bootstrap samples. Random forests add another source of randomness: at each split, search only a random subset of features. This prevents every tree from relying on the same strongest predictor at the top.
The trees are separately trainable, but their predictions are not statistically independent: they share the underlying dataset and signal.
crumbs: 16  Random Forest: Averaging, Correlation, and OOB Evaluation

title: Random Forest: Averaging, Correlation, and OOB Evaluation
text:
Worked example
Suppose each tree’s prediction at a point has variance \(\sigma^2=0.09\), with pairwise correlation \(\rho=0.2\). For \(B=100\) trees,
\[\operatorname{Var}(\bar f)=0.2(0.09)+\frac{0.8}{100}(0.09)=0.01872.\]
With infinitely many such trees, the variance floor is still \(0.018\). Lowering correlation is therefore often more valuable than adding another hundred nearly identical trees.
For eight indexed observations, a bootstrap sample might be \((1,1,3,3,5,7,8,8)\). Its OOB set is \(\{2,4,6\}\). Repeated observations count repeatedly during tree fitting. Observation 1 must not receive an OOB prediction from this tree. A new observation is evaluated by every tree, whereas each training observation’s OOB score uses only eligible trees.

GPA \(>3.55\) votes Y; otherwise N



For a new candidate with GPA \(3.8\), experience \(2\), and recommendation \(5\), all three illustrative rules vote Y, so the majority vote is Y. For training candidate 1, only Tree 2 is eligible for an OOB prediction; for candidate 2, Trees 1 and 3 are eligible. The original lecture example swaps these OOB memberships and uses GPA \(3.7\) with a strict \(>3.7\) rule while calling the vote Y. Those arithmetic details are corrected here. Three small trees also leave some rows with very few OOB votes, so the example illustrates mechanics rather than a reliable error estimate.
crumbs: 16  Random Forest: Averaging, Correlation, and OOB Evaluation

title: Random Forest: Averaging, Correlation, and OOB Evaluation
text:
Theory and assumptions
For equal marginal variances and common covariance \(\rho\sigma^2\),
\[\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(\bar f)
&=\frac{B\sigma^2+B(B-1)\rho\sigma^2}{B^2}\\
&=\rho\sigma^2+\frac{1-\rho}{B}\sigma^2.
\end{aligned}\]
This stylized calculation makes the strength–correlation tradeoff visible. Restricting features can lower correlation but also weaken individual trees.

Training and OOB prediction
For each tree, sample \(n\) rows with replacement, then at every node sample \(m\) candidate features and choose the best admissible split. Aggregate regression predictions by averaging. Classification may aggregate votes or averaged leaf class probabilities, depending on the algorithm and implementation.
The probability a given row is never selected is
\[P(\mathrm{OOB})=\left(1-\frac1n\right)^n\longrightarrow e^{-1}\approx0.368.\]
Thus a bootstrap sample contains about 63.2% distinct training rows on average; this is not a statement that two samples have exactly 63.2% overlap. For each row, average predictions from trees excluding it, then evaluate the loss. Too few trees can leave unstable or missing OOB predictions.
OOB evaluation is useful under an appropriate independent-row sampling setup. It does not emulate a future time period or a new organization, and repeated tuning against OOB scores still creates selection optimism. There is no universal theorem that its error is always slightly worse than five-fold CV.


Interpreting importance
Mean decrease in impurity sums sample-weighted impurity reductions attributed to a feature across trees. Many potential cutpoints can make a feature look important by chance, particularly on training data.
Permutation importance measures held-out performance degradation after shuffling a feature. It assesses dependence of this fitted predictor on that feature under a particular perturbation. Correlated substitutes can hide importance; shuffling can also create unrealistic combinations. Neither method proves causation or fair treatment.

title: Gradient Boosting: Learning an Update Function
text:
Learning goals
Move from residual fitting to general losses, derive the descent argument, and explain shrinkage, leaf optimization, early stopping, and the contrast with bagging.
crumbs: 17  Gradient Boosting: Learning an Update Function

title: Gradient Boosting: Learning an Update Function
text:
Intuition
Boosting adds a new function to repair the current model. For squared error this means fitting residuals. For other losses, the general quantity to fit is the negative derivative with respect to the current prediction score.
At training points, the model can be viewed as a vector \((F(x_1),\ldots,F(x_n))\). A negative gradient says how to change each entry. A tree learns a function of \(x\) approximating those desired changes so the update also has a defined value at new inputs.
crumbs: 17  Gradient Boosting: Learning an Update Function

title: Gradient Boosting: Learning an Update Function
text:
Worked example
For \(y=(10,20,30,25,15)\), the constant squared-error optimum is \(F_0=20\), giving residuals \((-10,0,10,5,-5)\). Suppose a feature split groups observations \((1,2,5)\) together and \((3,4)\) together. Their residual means are \(-5\) and \(7.5\). A stump predicts those updates. With learning rate \(\nu=0.1\), predictions become \((19.5,19.5,20.75,20.75,19.5)\).
For a classification example take \(x=(1,2,3)\), \(y=(1,0,1)\) and initialize the logit \(F_0=0\) for illustration. Probabilities are all 0.5 and negative gradients are \((0.5,-0.5,0.5)\). A three-leaf tree can fit these exactly using two thresholds. Updating by \(0.1\) gives logits \((0.05,-0.05,0.05)\) and probabilities approximately \((0.5125,0.4875,0.5125)\). One stump cannot isolate the middle observation from both endpoints.
crumbs: 17  Gradient Boosting: Learning an Update Function

title: Gradient Boosting: Learning an Update Function
text:
Theory and assumptions

Derive pseudo-residuals
For \(L(y,F)=\tfrac12(y-F)^2\), \(\partial L/\partial F=F-y\), so \(-g=y-F\) is the ordinary residual. For Bernoulli log-loss with \(p=\sigma(F)\), the chain rule gives \(g=p-y\). Subtracting a logit directly from a binary response is not the right update.



Loss convention
Negative derivative with respect to \(F\)




\(\tfrac12(y-F)^2\)
\(y-F\)


\(|y-F|\)
\(\operatorname{sign}(y-F)\) away from zero


Binary log-loss, \(y\in\{0,1\}\), \(p=\sigma(F)\)
\(y-p\)


\(\log(1+e^{-2yF})\), \(y\in\{-1,1\}\)
\(2y/(1+e^{2yF})\)



The last row uses a different label and score convention. Do not mix its factor of two with ordinary logit formulas.


Why the update can descend
For a small step \(\nu h\),
\[\mathcal L(F+\nu h)=\mathcal L(F)+\nu\sum_i g_ih(x_i)+O(\nu^2).\]
If \(h(x_i)=-g_i\), the linear term is \(-\nu\sum_i g_i^2\). A fitted tree only approximates that vector; it is a descent direction when \(\sum_i g_ih(x_i)<0\). A sufficiently small step or suitable line search is needed. First-order reasoning does not guarantee arbitrary finite steps decrease the actual loss, and it says nothing by itself about test loss.


Complete training cycle

Initialize \(F_0=\arg\min_c\sum_iL(y_i,c)\). For squared error use the mean; for nondegenerate binary log-loss use the empirical log-odds.
At round \(m\), compute \(r_{im}=-\partial_FL(y_i,F_{m-1}(x_i))\).
Fit a regression tree to \(r_{im}\), producing regions \(R_{jm}\).
Optionally optimize each leaf update on the original loss:

\[\gamma_{jm}=\arg\min_\gamma\sum_{x_i\in R_{jm}}L(y_i,F_{m-1}(x_i)+\gamma).\]

Set \(F_m(x)=F_{m-1}(x)+\nu\sum_j\gamma_{jm}\mathbf1\{x\in R_{jm}\}\), and retain the validation-selected iteration.

AdaBoost can be understood as stagewise additive modeling with exponential loss; this connects its reweighting mechanism to the broader boosting framework without making every implementation identical.

title: Gradient Boosting: Learning an Update Function
text:
Practice and pitfalls
Learning rate and number of trees must be tuned together. Smaller updates often improve performance but require more rounds. Use early stopping on a representative validation set, restoring the best iteration rather than the last one. Typical exploratory rates such as 0.01–0.1 are starting points, not requirements.
Shallow trees restrict the complexity of each added interaction. Depth, minimum leaf sizes, sampling, shrinkage, and stopping all regularize the model; it is inaccurate to say generic GBDT has no regularization. Boosting can chase mislabeled or extreme observations, especially under sensitive losses.

title: XGBoost: Deriving Leaf Weights and Split Gain
text:
Learning goals
Derive gradient and Hessian statistics, regroup them by leaf, solve for optimal leaf weights, calculate split gain, and connect the mathematics to engineering controls.
crumbs: 18  XGBoost: Deriving Leaf Weights and Split Gain

title: XGBoost: Deriving Leaf Weights and Split Gain
text:
Intuition
A gradient provides a direction; curvature describes how quickly that gradient changes. XGBoost’s tree objective uses a second-order approximation to calculate regularized leaf updates. It also charges for the number of leaves and their weight magnitudes.
Use \(f_m\) for the new tree and \(h_i\) for a scalar second derivative to avoid confusing a function with a Hessian entry. These updates are in score space; for binary logistic loss, probabilities follow after the sigmoid.
crumbs: 18  XGBoost: Deriving Leaf Weights and Split Gain

title: XGBoost: Deriving Leaf Weights and Split Gain
text:
Worked example
Take \(x=(1,2,3)\), \(y=(1,0,1)\), current logits zero, \(\lambda=1\), leaf penalty \(\gamma=0\), and shrinkage \(\nu=0.1\). Then
\[g=(-0.5,0.5,-0.5),\qquad h=(0.25,0.25,0.25).\]
For the split \(x\le1.5\), \(G_L=-0.5,H_L=0.25,G_R=0,H_R=0.5\). Its gain is
\[\frac12\left[\frac{0.25}{1.25}+0-\frac{0.25}{1.75}\right]\approx0.02857.\]
The split at \(2.5\) ties by symmetry. Selecting \(1.5\) gives \(w_L=0.4,w_R=0\). After shrinkage, logits are \((0.04,0,0)\) and probabilities approximately \((0.5100,0.5,0.5)\). Gradients cancel in the right leaf; later rounds can separate its conflicting labels.
crumbs: 18  XGBoost: Deriving Leaf Weights and Split Gain

title: XGBoost: Deriving Leaf Weights and Split Gain
text:
Theory and assumptions

1. State the objective
For a tree with \(T\) leaves and weights \(w_j\),
\[\mathcal O_m=\sum_iL(y_i,F_{m-1}(x_i)+f_m(x_i))+
\gamma T+\frac\lambda2\sum_jw_j^2.\]
\(\gamma\) charges for leaves and \(\lambda\) shrinks their outputs. Define
\[g_i=\partial_FL(y_i,F_{m-1}(x_i)),\qquad h_i=\partial_F^2L(y_i,F_{m-1}(x_i)).\]
Squared half-error gives \(g_i=F_i-y_i,h_i=1\). Binary log-loss gives \(g_i=p_i-y_i,h_i=p_i(1-p_i)\). A small Hessian is low local curvature; it does not imply low loss or a correct prediction. A confidently wrong prediction can have small Hessian and large gradient.


2. Taylor-expand, dropping constants
\[\widetilde{\mathcal O}_m=\sum_i\left[g_if_m(x_i)+\frac12h_if_m(x_i)^2\right]
+\gamma T+\frac\lambda2\sum_jw_j^2.\]
For a general smooth loss this is a local approximation. Squared error makes the quadratic expansion exact. The usual closed-form argument needs \(H_j+\lambda>0\); arbitrary custom losses need care when curvature is nonpositive.


3. Regroup by leaves
Let \(I_j\) contain the samples routed to leaf \(j\). Since \(f_m(x_i)=w_j\) in that leaf, define \(G_j=\sum_{i\in I_j}g_i\) and \(H_j=\sum_{i\in I_j}h_i\). Then
\[\widetilde{\mathcal O}_m=\sum_j\left[G_jw_j+\frac12(H_j+\lambda)w_j^2\right]+\gamma T.\]
Each leaf is now an independent scalar quadratic conditional on the tree structure.


4. Differentiate and substitute
\[G_j+(H_j+\lambda)w_j=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
w_j^*=-\frac{G_j}{H_j+\lambda}.\]
Substitution gives
\[\widetilde{\mathcal O}_m^*=-\frac12\sum_j\frac{G_j^2}{H_j+\lambda}+\gamma T.\]
This is the optimized surrogate contribution, not the full original loss. It enables comparison of candidate structures without separately optimizing every weight numerically.


5. Compare parent and children
Gain means parent objective minus child objective:
\[\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Gain}=\frac12\bigg[
&\frac{G_L^2}{H_L+\lambda}+\frac{G_R^2}{H_R+\lambda}\\
&-\frac{(G_L+G_R)^2}{H_L+H_R+\lambda}
\bigg]-\gamma.
\end{aligned}\]
Split only when the gain and other structural constraints permit it. With positive L2 regularization, the bracket need not be nonnegative: \(G_L=G_R=H_L=H_R=\lambda=1\) gives \(1/2+1/2-4/3=-1/3\). The two child penalties alter the comparison. Do not apply the unregularized Cauchy–Schwarz argument to this expression unchanged.
With an additional L1 term \(\alpha|w_j|\), the leaf solution becomes \(-\operatorname{sign}(G_j)(|G_j|-\alpha)_+/(H_j+\lambda)\) under this objective convention.
crumbs: 18  XGBoost: Deriving Leaf Weights and Split Gain

title: XGBoost: Deriving Leaf Weights and Split Gain
text:
Practice and pitfalls

Engineering ideas
Quantile or histogram candidates reduce the number of thresholds. Sparse-aware splitting learns a default direction by comparing missing values sent left versus right. Sorted column blocks and parallel scans improve throughput; cache-aware storage reduces memory stalls; external-memory approaches process data exceeding RAM. These are implementation mechanisms, distinct from the derivation of the objective. Histogram methods still accumulate changing gradient statistics during training.

Role

Shrinkage and total additive complexity

gamma

Start by constraining depth and child support; assess sampling and penalties; then tune rate and rounds together with validation-based stopping. Record objective and implementation settings before interpreting a parameter numerically.
XGBoost is a system implementing boosted models, whereas gradient boosting is a broader algorithmic framework. Avoid absolute comparisons claiming all other GBDT implementations lack regularization, missing-value handling, or second-order leaf updates. The official objective tutorial documents the regularized boosted-tree formulation.

Why sum gradients by leaf? All observations in a leaf receive the same update, so their quadratic contributions combine into sufficient statistics \(G_j,H_j\).
What happens when \(H_j\) is tiny? An unregularized Newton step can become large; L2, child support constraints, and shrinkage help control it.
Where does \(-\gamma\) in gain come from? Replacing one leaf by two adds one leaf penalty.

title: LightGBM: Histograms, Sampling, and Leaf Growth
text:
Learning goals
Explain how training reduces row and feature work, calculate GOSS weights, distinguish histogram construction from scanning, and control leaf-wise overfitting.
crumbs: 19  LightGBM: Histograms, Sampling, and Leaf Growth

title: LightGBM: Histograms, Sampling, and Leaf Growth
text:
Intuition
Boosted-tree training repeatedly searches for good splits. The central computational levers are the number of rows processed, the effective feature count, the number of candidate thresholds, and the order in which leaves are expanded. LightGBM’s original contributions target those levers rather than replacing the overall additive-tree idea.
No fixed speed ratio follows from an algorithm name. Data sparsity, hardware, bin counts, objectives, and tuning determine observed runtime and memory.
crumbs: 19  LightGBM: Histograms, Sampling, and Leaf Growth

title: LightGBM: Histograms, Sampling, and Leaf Growth
text:
Worked example

GOSS with an explicit sampling convention
With \(n=1000\), retain the largest-gradient fraction \(a=0.2\), or 200 rows. Draw \(bn=100\) rows from the remaining 800, where \(b=0.1\) is a fraction of the original sample size. Each sampled small-gradient row represents \(800/100=8\) rows, so multiply its contribution by \((1-a)/b=8\). The retained set has 300 rows.
If instead someone defines \(b\) as a fraction of the remaining rows, the weight is \(1/b\) and the sample size changes. Stating the convention prevents an otherwise plausible but wrong formula.


Bundling bins
Suppose feature A has nonzero bins 1–3 and feature B has nonzero bins 1–2, and they never coexist. Encode A’s bins as 1–3, B’s as 4–5, and all-zero as 0, while retaining feature/bin metadata. This stores sparse activity compactly. It is not equivalent to handing a generic tree an ordinal scalar and assuming every threshold preserves the original split semantics.
crumbs: 19  LightGBM: Histograms, Sampling, and Leaf Growth

title: LightGBM: Histograms, Sampling, and Leaf Growth
text:
Theory and assumptions

GOSS: retain influential gradients
Large absolute gradients indicate observations to which the current loss is sensitive. GOSS retains that group and subsamples smaller gradients. For a candidate region,
\[\widehat G=\sum_{i\in A}g_i+\frac{1-a}{b}\sum_{i\in B}g_i.\]
Appropriate weighting recovers a gradient total in expectation under the sampling design. Implementations using second-order statistics apply their corresponding weighted statistics. Because gain contains squares and ratios, unbiased gradient totals do not imply exactly unbiased gain estimates. Sampling is an approximation with its own variance, not a guarantee of unchanged accuracy.


EFB: reduce sparse feature work
Exclusive Feature Bundling groups features whose nonzero occurrences rarely overlap. A conflict graph connects features with simultaneous activity; finding an ideal grouping is difficult, so a greedy procedure constructs bundles with controlled conflicts. Perfect exclusivity can preserve bin information, while tolerating conflicts introduces approximation. The goal is reducing effective histogram-building feature work, not inventing a meaningful order among original categories.


Histograms and subtraction
Map continuous values to a limited number of bins. At a node, aggregate gradient and Hessian totals per bin; scan prefix sums to evaluate thresholds. Candidate scanning is \(O(Bd)\) for \(B\) bins and \(d\) features, but accumulating the histogram still depends on the node’s rows. Gradients change each boosting round, so this is not a one-time \(O(n)\) cost for the whole training process.
A child histogram can be obtained by subtracting its sibling histogram from the parent histogram. Building the smaller child’s statistics and obtaining the larger one by subtraction saves work. Fewer bins reduce memory and candidate count but can merge meaningful distinctions.


Leaf-wise growth
Depth-wise growth expands available nodes at a common depth; best-first leaf-wise growth chooses the currently most promising leaf by gain. The latter spends a limited leaf budget where it helps immediately, but can create a very deep branch. It is greedy, so there is no universal global-optimality guarantee for the final tree.
Control both total leaves and support within each leaf. A depth limit \(D\) permits at most \(2^D\) leaves, but setting fewer leaves does not alone bound every path’s depth. Tree-growth policies are configuration choices; modern systems can support more than one policy.


Categorical features
Categorical splitting aggregates gradient and Hessian sums for each category, \(G_c=\sum_{i:x_i=c}g_i\) and \(H_c=\sum_{i:x_i=c}h_i\). A useful second-order ordering score is \(G_c/H_c\) when \(H_c>0\); implementations can smooth or regularize this ratio for sparse categories. Sort categories by that score, then evaluate contiguous cut points with the actual split-gain formula. For illustrative scores \(-1,0.5,2\), only the two cuts in the ordered list need evaluation, rather than every binary partition. The optimal-grouping argument depends on the split objective and its assumptions; it is not an unconditional guarantee for every categorical regularizer or constraint.
This approach avoids expanding every category into an independent sparse binary feature in suitable situations. It still uses training labels through gradients and requires regularization, proper train/validation separation, and handling of rare or unseen categories. It is not a blanket guarantee against label leakage.
The LightGBM feature reference describes histogram construction, histogram subtraction, leaf-wise growth, and categorical split support. Verify enabled sampling and categorical settings rather than assuming every optional mechanism runs in every fit.

title: PCA and SVD: A Smaller Representation
text:
Learning goals
Distinguish unsupervised representation learning from prediction, derive principal components, relate PCA to SVD, and identify the limits of explained variance.
crumbs: 20  PCA and SVD: A Smaller Representation

title: PCA and SVD: A Smaller Representation
text:
Intuition
Unsupervised learning uses the observed features without a supervised outcome label. Dimensionality reduction seeks a compact representation; clustering seeks groups under a chosen notion of similarity. Neither task automatically reveals a unique true structure.
PCA rotates centered data into orthogonal directions, ordered by variance. Keeping only the first few directions compresses the data. The scores are uncorrelated in the fitted sample, but are not necessarily statistically independent or identifiable real-world latent causes.
crumbs: 20  PCA and SVD: A Smaller Representation

title: PCA and SVD: A Smaller Representation
text:
Worked example
For covariance matrix
\[S=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},\]
the first eigenvector is \(v_1=(1,1)^\top/\sqrt2\) with eigenvalue 3. The second is \(v_2=(1,-1)^\top/\sqrt2\) with eigenvalue 1. The first direction explains \(3/(3+1)=75\%\) of total variance.
A centered point \(x=(2,0)\) has scores \(z_1=\sqrt2\) and \(z_2=\sqrt2\). Keeping PC1 reconstructs \(\hat x=z_1v_1=(1,1)\). Its squared reconstruction error is \(\|(2,0)-(1,1)\|^2=2\). Compression keeps common movement and discards some contrast between variables.
crumbs: 20  PCA and SVD: A Smaller Representation

title: PCA and SVD: A Smaller Representation
text:
Theory and assumptions
Let \(X_c\) be the \(n\times d\) column-centered data matrix and \(S=X_c^\top X_c/(n-1)\). The first direction solves
\[\max_{\|v\|=1}v^\top Sv.\]
A Lagrange multiplier gives \(Sv=\lambda v\), and the largest eigenvalue achieves the maximum. Subsequent directions solve the same problem with orthogonality to earlier directions. Scores are \(Z=X_cV_k\) and reconstruction is \(\hat X=ZV_k^\top+\mathbf1\bar x^\top\). The explained-variance ratio of component \(j\) is \(\lambda_j/\sum_r\lambda_r\).
Any real rectangular matrix has an SVD. For centered data,
\[X_c=UDV^\top,\qquad S=V\frac{D^2}{n-1}V^\top.\]
Thus right singular vectors are PCA loading directions, squared singular values divided by \(n-1\) are variances, and PCA scores are \(UD\). Singular values themselves are not variances. Truncating to the \(k\) largest singular values yields the best rank-\(k\) approximation in Frobenius norm; the squared residual norm is \(\sum_{j>k}d_j^2\).
SVD also applies to uncentered image or document matrices, but uncentered truncated SVD and centered PCA are not identical procedures. The mean must be accounted for when reconstructing centered data.
crumbs: 20  PCA and SVD: A Smaller Representation

title: PCA and SVD: A Smaller Representation
text:
Practice and pitfalls
Center the data; scale when variable units should have comparable influence. Covariance-based PCA of dollars and percentages can be dominated by unit choices. Standardization changes the scientific question to variation measured relative to each feature’s scale.
Fit centering, scaling, and directions only on training data when PCA feeds a predictive pipeline. Select component count using reconstruction, explained variance, downstream validation, and interpretability. A low-variance direction can be highly predictive of the target, so retaining 95% variance is not a guarantee of retaining 95% predictive information.
PCA is linear and sensitive to outliers. Directions are only determined up to sign; repeated eigenvalues allow rotations within the tied subspace. Different sign choices across software runs need not indicate different fitted geometry. Near-tied components may be individually unstable even when their joint subspace is stable.

Interview questions
PCA or SVD? PCA is a statistical transformation of centered data; SVD is a general matrix decomposition that can compute it.
Are principal components independent? They are uncorrelated under the fitted covariance; independence needs additional conditions, such as an appropriate joint Gaussian model.
Why can PCA hurt classification? It optimizes variance or reconstruction without consulting the class label.

title: K-Means: Optimization, Initialization, and Choosing K
text:
Learning goals
Derive centroid updates and convergence, understand K-means++ sampling, calculate silhouette, use the gap statistic, and recognize geometric failure modes.
crumbs: 21  K-Means: Optimization, Initialization, and Choosing K

title: K-Means: Optimization, Initialization, and Choosing K
text:
Intuition
K-means compresses a cloud of points into \(K\) representative means. Each point belongs to its nearest mean; each mean moves to the average of its assigned points. The number \(K\) and the representation of distance are inputs to the modeling decision.
Its nearest-center regions are convex Voronoi cells. Compact, similarly spread clusters often fit this geometry, but “spherical equal-size clusters” are a useful suitability heuristic, not explicit distributional assumptions needed to run the algorithm.
crumbs: 21  K-Means: Optimization, Initialization, and Choosing K

title: K-Means: Optimization, Initialization, and Choosing K
text:
Worked example
Use six two-dimensional points \((1,1),(1,2),(2,1),(8,8),(8,9),(9,8)\). Initialize centers at \((1,1)\) and \((8,8)\). Nearest-center assignment creates the two obvious triples. The updated centers are \((4/3,4/3)\) and \((25/3,25/3)\). Each triple contributes \(4/3\) to within-cluster squared error, giving \(W_2=8/3\).
The lecture also deliberately starts with both centers near the first cluster, \(\mu_1=(1,1)\) and \(\mu_2=(2,2)\), to show why one assignment is not the result. Ties for \((1,2)\) and \((2,1)\) are assigned to center 2 in this illustration:

The next assignment is unchanged and the final objective is \(8/3\). This demonstration shows a poor start can recover on these points; it does not guarantee recovery on arbitrary data.
For a separate silhouette calculation use clusters \(\{1,2,3\}\) and \(\{10,11\}\). At point 1, within-cluster mean distance is \(a=1.5\) and nearest-other-cluster mean distance is \(b=9.5\). Hence \(s=(9.5-1.5)/9.5\approx0.842\). At point 3, \(a=1.5,b=7.5\), giving \(s=0.8\).
If clusters are wrongly assigned as \(\{1,2,10\}\) and \(\{3,11\}\), point 3 has \(a=8,b=10/3\), so \(s\approx-0.583\). It is closer on average to the other cluster than to its assigned partner.
crumbs: 21  K-Means: Optimization, Initialization, and Choosing K

title: K-Means: Optimization, Initialization, and Choosing K
text:
Theory and assumptions

Objective and alternating minimization
\[J=\sum_{i=1}^n\|x_i-\mu_{c_i}\|^2,\qquad c_i\in\{1,\ldots,K\}.\]
Holding centers fixed, choose \(c_i=\arg\min_k\|x_i-\mu_k\|^2\). Holding assignments fixed, differentiating with respect to \(\mu_k\) yields the within-cluster mean. Both steps weakly decrease \(J\), which is bounded below by zero. With consistent tie handling and nonempty clusters, assignments stabilize at a local solution; this does not prove a global optimum.
K-means++ chooses the first center randomly, then samples each new center with probability proportional to the squared distance \(D_i^2\) from its nearest existing center. This spreads initial centers across uncovered regions. Run multiple initializations and compare the final objective; smart initialization still does not guarantee the global minimum.


Choosing K
Elbow: plot optimized inertia versus \(K\) and look for diminishing returns. Optimal inertia cannot increase when an extra center is allowed, but imperfect optimization can make empirical runs look nonmonotone. An elbow may be ambiguous or absent.
Silhouette: for a nonsingleton point, let \(a_i\) be average distance to other members of its cluster and \(b_i\) the minimum average distance to another cluster. Then
\[s_i=\frac{b_i-a_i}{\max(a_i,b_i)},\qquad \bar s=\frac1n\sum_i s_i.\]
Values approach one for good separation, zero near overlap, and become negative for questionable assignment. Singleton clusters conventionally receive zero, not a perfect score of one; the apparent formula with \(a=0\) is not used for that case. At least two nontrivial cluster labels are required for the usual dataset score. Numerical thresholds such as 0.5 are context-dependent guides, not universal evidence of real clusters.
Gap statistic: compare observed dispersion to a specified no-cluster reference distribution. For \(B\) simulated reference datasets,
\[\operatorname{Gap}(K)=\frac1B\sum_{b=1}^B\log W_K^{*(b)}-\log W_K.\]
The customary uncertainty adjustment is \(s_K=\operatorname{sd}(\log W_K^{*(b)})\sqrt{1+1/B}\). Choose the smallest \(K\) satisfying
\[\operatorname{Gap}(K)\ge\operatorname{Gap}(K+1)-s_{K+1}.\]
This is not simply maximizing the gap. Simulate in an appropriate bounding region, possibly using principal-coordinate directions; the reference distribution is a modeling choice, not an objectively universal absence of structure. Repeated simulations and fits add considerable computational cost.
Usefulness: assess stability, interpretability, and whether the groups support intended actions. If operational constraints require four segments, document that as a constrained design choice rather than claiming a metric uniquely discovered four natural kinds.


Complexity
Assignment evaluates \(nK\) distances of cost \(O(d)\), giving \(O(nKd)\). Updating sums and means costs \(O(nd+Kd)\). With \(I\) iterations, ordinary Lloyd training costs \(O(InKd)\), excluding initialization and repeated restarts. Exact silhouette calculations can be substantially more expensive because they involve many pairwise distances.
crumbs: 21  K-Means: Optimization, Initialization, and Choosing K

title: K-Means: Optimization, Initialization, and Choosing K
text:
Practice and pitfalls
Standardize when units should contribute comparably, handle outliers deliberately, and avoid interpreting numeric category IDs as Euclidean quantities. Empty clusters need a specified reinitialization policy. A pipeline using PCA must verify that the retained dimensions preserve the relevant grouping information.
Elliptical clusters may work if sufficiently separated, but unequal orientation or variance can mislead isotropic distances. Concentric rings and interlocking moons cannot be represented as one convex nearest-center region per desired group. K-means may partition rings into wedges; it is not true that all fitted centers must remain at the origin. Consider GMM for covariance-shaped components, or density and graph methods for nonconvex groups.
A teaching segmentation workflow can standardize a 28-feature profile, inspect a six-component representation, and evaluate four candidate segments. Labels such as “high engagement” describe cluster summaries; they are not verified personal traits or risk scores. Any numerical quality claim must come from the actual fit, not from the illustrative source narrative.
crumbs: 21  K-Means: Optimization, Initialization, and Choosing K

title: K-Means: Optimization, Initialization, and Choosing K
text:
Interview questions
Why does Lloyd’s algorithm converge? Each alternating minimization lowers a bounded objective; it can still end in a poor local solution.
Why not choose the smallest inertia? Increasing \(K\) buys lower training distortion, eventually one center per point. The useful complexity needs a separate criterion.
Can I replace Euclidean distance with any distance? Not while assuming the ordinary mean update remains optimal. Use a method whose center update matches its objective.

Summary
K-means is simple because it alternates two easy optimizations. Its real modeling decisions are representation, geometry, initialization, and the meaning of \(K\).

text:
Intuition
Changing a distance function can change the best representative. A mean is natural for squared Euclidean loss, a medoid is an observed representative chosen under a supplied dissimilarity, and a unit vector summarizes a direction. Choosing a method means choosing that geometry and its computational cost together.

title: Clustering Variants: Medoids, Mini-Batches, and Directions
text:
Theory and assumptions

K-medoids and PAM
For medoid set \(M\subseteq\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\) with \(|M|=K\),
\[T(M)=\sum_i\min_{m\in M}d(x_i,m).\]
PAM initializes representatives, assigns observations, evaluates every medoid–nonmedoid swap, accepts the greatest strict decrease, and stops when none improves. For each observation cache the nearest and second-nearest medoid distances. If its closest medoid is removed, compare the second-nearest distance with its distance to the replacement; otherwise compare its current nearest distance with the replacement.
There are \(K(n-K)\) swaps. With cached distances, scanning \(n\) points per swap costs approximately \(O(nd)\) if a distance costs \(O(d)\), giving \(O(Kn(n-K)d)\) per round. A fully naive implementation rescanning all \(K\) centers adds another factor \(K\). Precomputed distances change the distance-cost accounting and can require \(O(n^2)\) memory.
Absolute or other less tail-sensitive dissimilarities can improve robustness relative to squared-error means, but being a medoid does not make any possible metric immune to outliers. Medoids work with meaningful edit, graph, or Jaccard distances when arithmetic means are undefined. CLARA fits PAM on samples and evaluates candidates more broadly; CLARANS samples the swap search rather than exhaustively enumerating it.


Mini-batch K-means
Use a small batch instead of all observations at each update. For an individual new point assigned to center \(k\), increment its count \(N_k\) and update
\[\mu_k\leftarrow\mu_k+\frac1{N_k}(x-\mu_k).\]
For a batch with \(b_k\) assigned points and mean \(\bar x_{bk}\), combining it with the previous \(N_k\) points gives
\[\mu_k^{\mathrm{new}}=\frac{N_k\mu_k+b_k\bar x_{bk}}{N_k+b_k}.\]
The batch-mean learning rate is \(b_k/(N_k+b_k)\), not simply \(1/(N_k+b_k)\) unless the batch contributes one point. Assignment work per batch is \(O(bKd)\). This reduces individual update cost, with stochastic optimization and possible distortion tradeoffs; there is no universal 10–100-fold speed gain or fixed percentage accuracy loss.


Spherical K-means
Normalize nonzero observations and centers to unit length. Assign by maximum cosine similarity, and update each center to the normalized sum of its assigned unit vectors:
\[\mu_k=\frac{\sum_{i:c_i=k}x_i}{\left\|\sum_{i:c_i=k}x_i\right\|}.\]
For unit vectors, squared Euclidean distance equals \(2(1-\cos\theta)\). Normalizing centers matters; normalizing observations alone and then running unrestricted ordinary means is not exactly the same procedure. Zero vectors and cancelling sums need explicit handling. This is useful for text or preference directions where magnitude is not the desired similarity signal.


Other geometry changes
K-modes uses categorical mismatch costs and category modes instead of numeric means. Kernel K-means performs squared-distance clustering in an implicit feature space; a nonlinear kernel can separate patterns unavailable to raw-space Voronoi cells. Spectral clustering builds an affinity graph, embeds observations using graph-Laplacian eigenvectors, and clusters the embedding. Graph construction, affinity scale, and connectivity are substantive choices, and dense pairwise representations can be costly.
crumbs: 22  Clustering Variants: Medoids, Mini-Batches, and Directions

title: Clustering Variants: Medoids, Mini-Batches, and Directions
text:
Practice and pitfalls
For small noisy datasets or unusual dissimilarities, consider medoids. For large numerical datasets with compact groups, mini-batches provide incremental updates. For document directions use an appropriate normalized representation. For curved connected groups inspect density or graph methods.
Do not exchange an objective’s distance without updating its center rule. Evaluate multiple seeds, sensitivity to scaling, segment stability, and computation. With streaming mini-batches, cumulative averages can adapt too slowly after drift; a deliberate forgetting policy changes the model and should be validated.

Can a medoid be a fictional average observation? No. It must be one of the observed representatives under the defined problem.
Why spherical clustering for text? It emphasizes vector direction, reducing the influence of magnitude when magnitude is not informative about topic.

title: Gaussian Mixtures and Expectation–Maximization
text:
Learning goals
State the mixture generation process, derive E and M steps, hand-calculate an update, and explain why monotone likelihood is not a global convergence guarantee.

title: Gaussian Mixtures and Expectation–Maximization
text:
Intuition
A GMM imagines that each observation first chooses a component, then draws from that component’s Gaussian distribution. Unlike K-means, it provides a probability of membership in every component. Covariance matrices allow components to be tilted and elongated.
A component is a statistical modeling device. Its label does not necessarily correspond to a meaningful human category; component labels can be permuted without changing the fitted density.

title: Gaussian Mixtures and Expectation–Maximization
text:
Worked example
For \(x=(1,2,8,9)\) initialize two equal-weight components with means \((0,10)\) and variances \((4,4)\). For component 1,
\[\gamma_{i1}=\frac{1}{1+\exp(((x_i-0)^2-(x_i-10)^2)/8)}.\]
The responsibilities at 1 and 2 are approximately 0.999955 and 0.999447; at 8 and 9 they are approximately 0.000553 and 0.000045. Symmetry gives effective counts \(N_1=N_2=2\).
Treating these near-hard responsibilities as \((1,1,0,0)\) for a transparent approximation yields updated weights \((0.5,0.5)\), means \((1.5,8.5)\), and variances \((0.25,0.25)\). Exact soft arithmetic gives means about \((1.5018,8.4982)\) and variances about \((0.2629,0.2629)\). The distinction matters when demonstrating exact EM rather than its hard-assignment approximation.

title: Gaussian Mixtures and Expectation–Maximization
text:
Theory and assumptions

The generative model
\[z_i\sim\operatorname{Categorical}(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_K),\qquad
x_i\mid z_i=k\sim\mathcal N(\mu_k,\Sigma_k),\]
with \(\pi_k\ge0\) and \(\sum_k\pi_k=1\). The marginal density is \(p(x)=\sum_k\pi_k\mathcal N(x;\mu_k,\Sigma_k)\). Observed-data log-likelihood is
\[\ell(\theta)=\sum_i\log\left[\sum_k\pi_k\mathcal N(x_i;\mu_k,\Sigma_k)\right].\]
The logarithm of a sum couples the parameters, preventing a single direct closed-form joint maximum. If component assignments were observed, ordinary within-component Gaussian estimates would be easy.


E-step: Bayes’ rule
Holding current parameters fixed,
\[\gamma_{ik}=P(z_i=k\mid x_i)=
\frac{\pi_k\mathcal N(x_i;\mu_k,\Sigma_k)}{\sum_j\pi_j\mathcal N(x_i;\mu_j,\Sigma_j)}.\]
Each row sums to one. The numerator is a joint density; the denominator normalizes across components. Use log-density arithmetic and log-sum-exp in numerical implementations to avoid underflow.


M-step: weighted maximum likelihood
Set \(N_k=\sum_i\gamma_{ik}\). Then
\[\pi_k^{\mathrm{new}}=N_k/n,\qquad
\mu_k^{\mathrm{new}}=\frac{\sum_i\gamma_{ik}x_i}{N_k},\]
\[\Sigma_k^{\mathrm{new}}=\frac1{N_k}\sum_i\gamma_{ik}
(x_i-\mu_k^{\mathrm{new}})(x_i-\mu_k^{\mathrm{new}})^\top.\]
These maximize the expected complete-data log-likelihood: weights come from the simplex-constrained optimization, and means and covariances from weighted Gaussian MLE. The covariance divisor is the effective count, not an unbiased-estimation correction.


What EM guarantees
Jensen’s inequality constructs a likelihood lower bound. The E-step makes it touch the current likelihood; an exact M-step raises the bound. Hence observed likelihood does not decrease. However, an unconstrained Gaussian-mixture likelihood is not bounded above: a component can collapse on a single observation with covariance approaching zero, giving an arbitrarily large density.
Regularize or constrain covariance, use several initializations, inspect tiny effective counts, and monitor convergence. Even with a well-behaved bounded problem, the algorithm need not find a global optimum. Adding a covariance floor is a numerical regularization mechanism; it is not automatically identical to a fully specified Bayesian prior.


Relation to K-means
With common covariance \(\sigma^2I\) and fixed positive mixture weights, as \(\sigma\to0\) the closest mean dominates the responsibility away from distance ties. Responsibilities become hard and the mean update becomes a K-means update. Finite-variance general GMM is not simply K-means with probabilities attached.
Full covariance uses \(d(d+1)/2\) parameters per component, in addition to \(d\) mean parameters and mixture weights. Diagonal, spherical, and tied covariance choices trade flexibility for stability and computation. Compare AIC/BIC with parameter counts appropriate to the covariance form; evaluate held-out density and interpretability as well.

title: Gaussian Mixtures and Expectation–Maximization
text:
Practice and pitfalls
Use GMM for overlapping or elliptical probabilistic components when those assumptions are useful. It can be slower and less stable than K-means, especially with high-dimensional full covariances. K-means initialization often provides reasonable initial means but does not eliminate local optima.
Do not interpret high responsibility as a calibrated class probability unless a component-to-class meaning is justified. Gaussian density modeling, hard segmentation, and anomaly detection are different downstream uses requiring their own validation.

title: Gaussian Mixtures and Expectation–Maximization
text:
Interview questions
Why does EM use soft assignments? It computes conditional expectations of missing membership indicators under the current model, then fits with those weights.
Does increasing likelihood prove a good solution? No. There can be local solutions and covariance-collapse degeneracies.
How is GMM different from DBSCAN? GMM fits a parametric mixture density; DBSCAN connects locally dense neighborhoods and can leave noise unassigned.

title: Gaussian Mixtures and Expectation–Maximization
text:
Summary
EM alternates probabilistic membership and weighted parameter fitting. Its monotonicity is valuable, but covariance control and independent evaluation remain necessary.

title: DBSCAN, OPTICS, and Density Connectivity
text:
Learning goals
Distinguish core, border, and noise points; execute density expansion; choose neighborhood parameters; and explain the motivation for OPTICS and HDBSCAN.
crumbs: 24  DBSCAN, OPTICS, and Density Connectivity

title: DBSCAN, OPTICS, and Density Connectivity
text:
Intuition
DBSCAN defines a group by connected dense neighborhoods instead of distance to a common center. A cluster can bend into a crescent or ring as long as a chain of sufficiently dense neighborhoods connects it. Sparse points need not be forced into a group.
It avoids specifying \(K\), but replaces that choice with a neighborhood radius and minimum local support. The number of clusters remains sensitive to those choices and to the feature representation.
crumbs: 24  DBSCAN, OPTICS, and Density Connectivity

title: DBSCAN, OPTICS, and Density Connectivity
text:
Worked example
Take one-dimensional points \(\{0,0.1,0.2,0.3,0.4,2\}\) with \(\varepsilon=0.11\) and \(\mathrm{MinPts}=3\), counting each point itself. Points 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3 have three neighbors including themselves and are core points. Points 0 and 0.4 have only two neighbors but touch a core, so they are border points. Point 2 is noise.
Starting from core 0.1 absorbs 0 and 0.2. Core 0.2 expands to 0.3, which absorbs 0.4. The endpoints are 0.4 apart, greater than \(\varepsilon\), yet belong to the same cluster via a core chain. Border points join but do not expand the chain.
crumbs: 24  DBSCAN, OPTICS, and Density Connectivity

title: DBSCAN, OPTICS, and Density Connectivity
text:
Theory and assumptions
Define \(N_\varepsilon(p)=\{q:d(p,q)\le\varepsilon\}\). A point is core if \(|N_\varepsilon(p)|\ge\mathrm{MinPts}\). A noncore point within a core neighborhood is border; all remaining points are noise.
To grow a cluster, inspect an unvisited point. If it is core, enqueue its neighbors and repeatedly expand core neighbors. If it is not core, mark it provisional noise; it may later be absorbed as border. Do not assume a temporary noise mark is irreversible. A border point touching two components may receive a traversal-dependent assignment, while core connectivity defines the stable dense components.

Parameters and complexity
Small \(\varepsilon\) fragments groups and increases noise; large \(\varepsilon\) merges them through bridges. Small minimum support admits accidental groups; large support suppresses small groups. A sorted neighbor-distance plot can suggest a radius, but ensure its neighbor count matches whether self is included.
Spatial indexes can make low-dimensional sparse-neighborhood queries approximately \(O(n\log n)\) overall in favorable cases. Brute-force distance work is \(O(n^2d)\); dense neighborhoods or high dimensions can make time quadratic and implementations storing all neighborhoods can also require quadratic memory. It is therefore inaccurate to state either that DBSCAN is always quadratic or always \(n\log n\).


OPTICS
OPTICS creates an ordering with reachability information that exposes cluster structure across a range of density levels. The core distance of a point is the radius needed to include the specified minimum number of neighbors. Reachability from core point \(o\) to \(p\) is
\[\operatorname{reachability}(p\mid o)=\max\{\operatorname{core\_distance}(o),d(o,p)\}.\]
Valleys in a reachability plot suggest dense groups separated by higher-distance transitions. A later extraction rule selects clusters from this ordering. OPTICS is not simply DBSCAN magically finding a perfect separate epsilon for each point: it still needs support, distance, and extraction choices.


HDBSCAN
HDBSCAN constructs a hierarchy using density-related connectivity, typically through mutual-reachability distances and a spanning-tree structure, then selects stable groups from a condensed hierarchy. Minimum cluster size and support influence the result. It is useful to consider when densities vary, but does not guarantee meaningful clusters in arbitrary high-dimensional noise.
The clustering reference discusses DBSCAN, OPTICS, HDBSCAN, and implementation-specific scalability. Choose and measure the actual implementation rather than transferring a complexity claim across algorithms.
crumbs: 24  DBSCAN, OPTICS, and Density Connectivity

title: DBSCAN, OPTICS, and Density Connectivity
text:
Practice and pitfalls
Scale or weight features so neighborhoods reflect meaningful similarity. In high dimensions, distances can concentrate and local-density distinctions weaken. A single global radius can merge a sparse group while preserving a dense one, or preserve the sparse group only by merging dense neighbors.

Interview questions
Can border points connect two DBSCAN clusters? They cannot expand a cluster; connectivity must pass through core points.
Why can DBSCAN recover moons? It follows locally dense chains rather than requiring one convex nearest-center region.
Does no predefined K mean no tuning? No. Radius, support, metric, and representation determine the answer.

title: Isolation Forest: From Short Paths to Useful Alerts
text:
Intuition
Anomaly detection asks which observations are unusual under a reference pattern. Global anomalies are unusual overall; contextual anomalies are unusual given a time or group; collective anomalies are unusual as a sequence or combination. Isolation Forest mainly targets unusual multivariate tabular patterns. Temporal context usually needs grouping, seasonal adjustment, or window features first.
An unusual point surrounded by empty space can be separated by a few random cuts. A point inside a dense group usually requires more cuts. The forest averages this isolation difficulty instead of directly estimating a Gaussian distance or a neighbor density.

title: Isolation Forest: From Short Paths to Useful Alerts
text:
Worked example
Consider \(\{1.0,1.1,1.2,1.3,1.5,1.7,2.0,9.5\}\). A uniform first cut in \([1,9.5]\) falls between 2 and 9.5 with probability
\[\frac{9.5-2}{9.5-1}=\frac{7.5}{8.5}\approx0.882.\]
That event immediately isolates 9.5. For subsample size eight, \(c(8)=2H_7-14/8\approx3.436\). If average corrected paths are 1.4 for 9.5 and 3.8 for 1.3, their anomaly scores are
\[s(9.5)=2^{-1.4/3.436}\approx0.754,\qquad
s(1.3)=2^{-3.8/3.436}\approx0.465.\]
The path lengths here are illustrative forest averages, not a claimed measured simulation result. The larger score ranks 9.5 as more unusual.
crumbs: 25  Isolation Forest: From Short Paths to Useful Alerts

title: Isolation Forest: From Short Paths to Useful Alerts
text:
Theory and assumptions

Build and score a tree
For each tree, subsample \(\psi\) training observations. At a node, randomly choose a splittable feature, choose a split uniformly between its local minimum and maximum, and recurse. Stop at a singleton, an indistinguishable group, or a height cap often based on \(\lceil\log_2\psi\rceil\).
For a leaf containing \(m\) training observations after a path of \(e\) edges, use the corrected path \(h=e+c(m)\), where
\[c(m)=2H_{m-1}-\frac{2(m-1)}m\quad(m\ge2),\qquad c(1)=0.\]
For large \(m\), \(H_{m-1}\approx\log(m-1)+\gamma_E\), so the reference depth grows logarithmically. This baseline comes from average unsuccessful-search paths in binary search trees. It adjusts for samples not fully isolated at the depth limit.
Average corrected paths over \(T\) trees and normalize:
\[\bar h(x)=\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^Th_t(x),\qquad s(x;\psi)=2^{-\bar h(x)/c(\psi)}.\]
Paths far below the baseline give scores near one; baseline paths give 0.5; longer paths give scores below 0.5. This is a ranking transformation, not a calibrated probability of fraud or idleness. A universal 0.5 alarm threshold does not follow.


Sampling and computational cost
Subsampling makes trees fast, diversifies the forest, and can reduce masking by large populations. A small subsample may also miss legitimate rare subgroups. Typical exploratory sizes such as 256 represent a speed–resolution tradeoff, not a theoretical optimum.
With logarithmic average paths, training is approximately \(O(T\psi\log\psi)\), scoring \(n\) observations is \(O(nT\log\psi)\), and tree storage is \(O(T\psi)\). These expressions abstract away feature-processing and implementation overhead. Training cost can remain bounded with fixed subsample size while full-population scoring still grows with \(n\).
crumbs: 25  Isolation Forest: From Short Paths to Useful Alerts

title: Isolation Forest: From Short Paths to Useful Alerts
text:
Practice and pitfalls

A cloud-resource candidate pipeline
The following adapts the source’s project workflow as a teaching design, without claiming measured employer results.

Align monitoring, inventory, and billing to resource-by-day observations. Respect delayed billing availability.
Build only past-looking 7/30/90-day features: mean, P95, maximum, variability, trend, nonzero days, persistent low use, and missingness.
Keep missing indicators; an absent measurement is not zero utilization. Require enough observed history and compare similar resource types and environments.
Form a union of Isolation Forest candidates, robust univariate alerts, and explicit low-utilization rules:

\[\mathrm{Candidate}_i=\mathbf1\{s_i>\tau\}\lor\mathbf1\{|z_i^{\mathrm{robust}}|>u\}\lor\mathrm{LowUtilRule}_i.\]

Use cost downstream to prioritize review value. A high price is not evidence of idleness.
Obtain human labels, optionally train a supervised ranker, and evaluate the final review pipeline at a fixed capacity. The forest score alone must not trigger an unsupported claim of savings or classification accuracy.

Persistent low use can be common, hence statistically ordinary. Explicit rules cover that failure mode; the forest covers unusual combinations. Any measured performance from a downstream ranker or human review must not be attributed to Isolation Forest alone.


Thresholds, labels, and drift







Control
Interpretation




Tree count
Stability versus cost


Subsample size
Detail of normal structure versus speed


Feature subsampling
Diversity versus missing useful combinations


Contamination setting
Threshold calibration convention, not discovered truth


Top-K budget
Candidate volume matched to review capacity



Score direction varies by interface: inspect the implementation before sorting. Some return lower values for more abnormal observations. Validate direction with clear examples, and document any sign reversal.
With trusted labels, evaluate time-held-out recall, precision–recall behavior, and Precision@K. With only a review budget, track hit rate, candidate diversity, duplicates, and cost per useful alert. With almost no labels, use blinded spot checks, seed/window stability, comparisons and ablations against simple rules, then accumulate reviewed outcomes. Reviewing only the highest-ranked cases cannot estimate population recall without additional sampling assumptions.


Alternative methods and failure modes
Z-scores are interpretable for single-variable extremes but can fail under skew or heavy tails; robust location/scale helps. LOF compares local density with neighbors and may catch local anomalies missed globally. One-class SVM learns a boundary around a reference population but is sensitive to scale and kernel choices.
Isolation Forest does not require Euclidean standardization in the same way K-means does: independent positive affine feature scaling preserves the ideal random-cut geometry. Nevertheless skew, irrelevant features, missingness, and many sparse category indicators can affect usefulness. Dense anomalous groups can mask each other; new products or legitimate batch jobs can look unusual. Add context, monitor drift and repeated alerts, and never equate rarity with harm.

title: Isolation Forest: From Short Paths to Useful Alerts
text:
Interview questions
Why no distance calculation? Random partition path length measures how easily observations separate; empty surrounding regions create short paths.
Why divide by \(c(\psi)\)? Raw path lengths change with subsample size; the reference normalizes their scale.
Is contamination the true anomaly prevalence? No. It is a threshold-related assumption or setting, not label-based evidence.
How does this differ from Random Forest? Random forests optimize label-based splits and predict outcomes. Isolation trees use random features and thresholds, then score path lengths without target labels.
Why combine the model with rules? Statistical rarity and operationally undesirable behavior overlap imperfectly; each method covers different missed cases.

crumbs: 26  Potential Outcomes and Causal Identification

title: Potential Outcomes and Causal Identification
text:
Intuition
A causal question compares two interventions on the same population. If a customer receives a coupon, we observe spending with the coupon but cannot simultaneously observe spending without it. Predicting who spends most does not answer who spends more because of the coupon.
For person \(i\), define potential outcomes \(Y_i(1)\) and \(Y_i(0)\), assignment \(T_i\in\{0,1\}\), and pre-treatment covariates \(X_i\). Consistency gives
\[Y_i=T_iY_i(1)+(1-T_i)Y_i(0).\]
The individual treatment effect is \(Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)\). One outcome is missing for each person: the fundamental problem of causal inference. A model’s CATE prediction is an average among people with similar recorded characteristics; it does not reveal both outcomes for a particular person.
crumbs: 26  Potential Outcomes and Causal Identification

title: Potential Outcomes and Causal Identification
text:
Worked example

The coupon counterfactual
In a hypothetical pair of worlds, a customer would spend 100 with a coupon and 60 without it, so her effect is 40. If she receives the coupon we see 100, not 60. A nonrecipient spending 50 is not automatically a valid replacement for her missing 60: targeting may favor people who already intend to buy.
Suppose 40% of a population receives treatment, and the true subgroup effects are ATT = 8 and ATU = 3. Then
\[\operatorname{ATE}=0.4(8)+0.6(3)=5.\]








Estimand
Definition
Business question




ATE
\(E[Y(1)-Y(0)]\)
What would treating everyone change on average?


ATT
\(E[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid T=1]\)
What did the intervention change for recipients?


ATU
\(E[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid T=0]\)
What might expansion change for current nonrecipients?


CATE
\(\tau(x)=E[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid X=x]\)
Which observable groups benefit?



A high-frequency customer’s CATE might be 12 while a low-frequency customer’s is 1. These are hypothetical group averages, not measured individual effects. The identity ATE = \(P(T=1)\)ATT + \(P(T=0)\)ATU follows directly from total expectation.


Assignment versus behavior
A ranking experiment randomly assigns users to a new strategy. Its direct effect is the intention-to-treat (ITT) effect of assignment. Whether users actually click the resulting card is a later, self-selected behavior. Comparing clickers with nonclickers discards randomization.
A worked case in the source notes adds a score proportional to predicted click-through rate times predicted active return to a ranking policy. The transferable design lesson is to analyze the assigned policy at the randomization unit, with predeclared activity/order outcomes and platform guardrails. Those observations cannot identify the causal effect of clicking merely because the ranking assignment was randomized.
crumbs: 26  Potential Outcomes and Causal Identification

title: Potential Outcomes and Causal Identification
text:
Theory and assumptions

Consistency and SUTVA
Consistency connects the observed intervention to the specified potential outcome. The treatment must have sufficiently well-defined versions: “saw an advertisement” may hide one-second and thirty-second exposures with different effects.
SUTVA also rules out interference between units in its usual formulation. Coupons shared with friends, competition for limited inventory, driver supply changes, and recommendation-market equilibrium effects can affect untreated users. Cluster randomization or an explicit spillover model may address such questions, but changes the design and potentially the estimand.






Warning



Random assignment does not automatically guarantee SUTVA. It establishes a property of the assignment mechanism; interference and treatment versions still require design arguments.




Conditional exchangeability
\[\{Y(0),Y(1)\}\perp T\mid X.\]
Conditional on measured \(X\), treatment assignment provides no further information about either potential outcome. This concerns who gets treatment, not whether treatment works. A randomized drug can reduce pain even though assignment is independent of both potential pain scores.
Gym attendance and longevity illustrate failure: attendees may have better baseline health and higher income. Controlling recorded age, income, and health helps only if the remaining differences relevant to both attendance and longevity are addressed. Unrecorded motivation may still confound the comparison. Similarly, adjusting industry does not remove unmeasured diligence from an observational comparison of software adoption and productivity.
Exchangeability cannot generally be tested from observed outcomes because the missing potential outcomes remain missing. A causal diagram, timing audit, domain knowledge, negative controls, and sensitivity analysis support the argument; none proves it.


Positivity and overlap
\[0<e(x):=P(T=1\mid X=x)<1\]
is needed on the covariate support of the target population. A deterministic rule assigning all large sellers to support provides no untreated comparison for those sellers. Near-zero probabilities produce weak empirical information and unstable weights even when formal positivity holds.
Estimated probabilities close to zero or one can reflect overfitting, leakage, or genuine assignment rules. Plot both groups’ estimated score distributions and inspect relevant covariate strata. Restriction to common support changes the population being estimated. Another estimator cannot manufacture missing comparisons.


Identification step by step
For treatment \(t\) and supported \(x\),
\[\begin{aligned}
E[Y\mid T=t,X=x]
&=E[Y(t)\mid T=t,X=x] &&\text{consistency}\\
&=E[Y(t)\mid X=x] &&\text{exchangeability}.
\end{aligned}\]
Overlap makes both treatment-arm conditional regressions estimable on the target support. Subtracting identifies CATE, and averaging over the target covariate distribution identifies ATE:
\[\operatorname{ATE}=E_X\{E[Y\mid T=1,X]-E[Y\mid T=0,X]\}.\]
Identification is a population statement. Estimation adds finite data, modeling error, and uncertainty; a causal assumption does not guarantee a good finite-sample estimate.
crumbs: 26  Potential Outcomes and Causal Identification

title: Potential Outcomes and Causal Identification
text:
Practice and pitfalls

Specify eligibility, intervention versions, outcome window, and target population.
Draw a timeline and retain covariates measured before assignment or exposure.
Separate the assignment effect from compliance or engagement effects.
Audit spillovers, post-treatment selection, attrition, and missing outcomes.
Defend the identifying assumptions before fitting a flexible model.
Report effect size and uncertainty in absolute units and, where useful, relative units.

Do not claim that DiD or IV “fixes” an overlap problem without evaluating their different assumptions. Do not remove a real confounder simply to make treated and control score histograms look alike. Randomization balances baseline variables in expectation; realized imbalance and clustering still matter for precision and inference.
crumbs: 26  Potential Outcomes and Causal Identification

title: Potential Outcomes and Causal Identification
text:
Interview questions
Does ignorability mean treatment has no effect? No. It states that assignment is independent of potential outcomes conditional on covariates. The contrast between the two potential outcomes may still be large.
Why is CATE not an individual treatment effect? CATE averages over all unmeasured variation among units with the same recorded \(X\). Individual counterfactuals remain unobserved.
What does an A/B test identify when users can ignore the feature? The assignment or ITT effect. A treatment-on-the-treated interpretation needs additional compliance assumptions and an appropriate design, such as a valid encouragement instrument.
Can I verify no unmeasured confounding? Generally not. I explain the assignment mechanism, audit covariate timing, and report sensitivity to plausible omitted factors.

title: Potential Outcomes and Causal Identification
text:
Summary
A causal analysis starts with the intervention and estimand. Consistency, exchangeability, and overlap permit replacing missing potential outcomes with comparisons across observed people; they do not eliminate estimation error or resolve interference automatically.

title: Propensity Scores: Matching and Weighting
text:
Intuition
A live-shopping viewer may already have greater purchase intent than a nonviewer. Matching attempts to compare recipients with nonrecipients who had similar pre-treatment probabilities of treatment. The score is \(e(X)=P(T=1\mid X)\), not a prediction of purchase and not a measure of treatment benefit.
Reducing a high-dimensional \(X\) to a scalar score is useful only under the causal assumptions and an adequate estimated design. Two people with similar estimated scores need not have identical characteristics. Balance must be checked in the original covariates.
crumbs: 27  Propensity Scores: Matching and Weighting

title: Propensity Scores: Matching and Weighting
text:
Worked example

Build a design before comparing outcomes
Consider a pedagogical analysis of livestream exposure and subsequent ordering. Freeze age, city, historical GMV, and previous engagement before exposure. Do not include watch time measured after exposure as a baseline confounder.
Suppose three treated aggregate units and three equal-sized control aggregate units remain on common support:











Pair
Treated score
Control score
Treated outcome rate
Control outcome rate
Difference




1
0.30
0.31
0.08
0.07
0.01


2
0.50
0.48

0.08
0.01
