0.70
0.69
0.10
0.10
0.00



The outcome is an ordering rate within each aggregate unit; a user-level binary outcome would instead be 0 or 1. The matched average difference estimates an effect for these treated aggregate units, not an individual-user effect:
\[\widehat{\operatorname{ATT}}=(0.01+0.01+0)/3=0.006667,\]
or 0.667 percentage points, not 6.67 percentage points and not a 0.667% relative increase. Relative to the matched-control average \(0.08333\), the illustrative relative lift is 8%.


Balance is a separate calculation
If matched mean age is 32 versus 31 and the two sample variances are 100 and 100, absolute standardized mean difference is \(1/10=0.10\). If rematching yields 31.5 versus 31, it becomes 0.05. Also inspect variance ratios, empirical distributions, categorical proportions, tails, and meaningful interactions. A small score difference does not substitute for this inspection.


Weighting a rare treatment assignment
A treated user with \(e(X)=0.1\) receives ATE weight 10; one with \(e(X)=0.8\) receives weight 1.25. The first represents people of that covariate type who seldom receive treatment. A control with \(e(X)=0.9\) also receives weight 10 because untreated users of that type are rare. This is the source of both weighting’s correction and its instability.
crumbs: 27  Propensity Scores: Matching and Weighting

title: Propensity Scores: Matching and Weighting
text:
Theory and assumptions

The Rosenbaum–Rubin balancing argument
At a score value \(e(X)=p\), the probability of treatment is \(p\) for every covariate combination in that stratum. For any covariate set \(A\),
\[\begin{aligned}
P(X\in A,T=1\mid e(X)=p)
&=E[\mathbf 1\{X\in A\}e(X)\mid e(X)=p]\\
&=pP(X\in A\mid e(X)=p).
\end{aligned}\]
Thus \(T\perp X\mid e(X)\). Combining this balance with conditional exchangeability given \(X\) yields
\[\{Y(0),Y(1)\}\perp T\mid e(X).\]
The result concerns the true score. Approximation error, finite-sample matching, and limited common support remain practical issues.


Matching estimators
With one control match \(m(i)\) for each of \(n_T\) treated units,
\[\widehat{\tau}_{ATT}=\frac{1}{n_T}\sum_{i:T_i=1}[Y_i-Y_{m(i)}].\]
If treated units are discarded, this targets the retained treated population under the design assumptions, not automatically all original recipients. With \(K\) controls, replace \(Y_{m(i)}\) by their appropriately weighted average.








Design
Benefit
Cost or decision




1:1 nearest neighbor
Simple pair interpretation
May discard many controls or accept poor matches


K-nearest neighbors
More control information
More distant matches can increase bias


Caliper
Rejects implausibly distant pairs
Can discard treated units and alter the target


Kernel matching
Smoothly uses many controls
Bandwidth controls bias and variance


Replacement
Reuses excellent controls
Reuse creates dependence and lowers effective information


No replacement
Distinct controls
Results may depend on matching order



A common starting caliper is 0.2 standard deviations of the logit score, applied on the logit scale. It is not a raw probability difference of the same numerical size.


IPTW and its proof
The Horvitz–Thompson ATE estimator is
\[\hat\tau_{HT}=\frac1n\sum_i\left[\frac{T_iY_i}{\hat e_i}-\frac{(1-T_i)Y_i}{1-\hat e_i}\right].\]
With the true score and identification assumptions,
\[\begin{aligned}
E\left[\frac{TY}{e(X)}\right]
&=E_X\left[\frac{E[TY(1)\mid X]}{e(X)}\right]\\
&=E_X\left[\frac{e(X)E[Y(1)\mid X]}{e(X)}\right]
=E[Y(1)].
\end{aligned}\]
The control term similarly equals \(E[Y(0)]\). Estimated scores introduce estimation error; this population calculation is not a claim of exact finite-sample unbiasedness.
The Hájek alternative divides each weighted outcome sum by its arm’s weight sum before subtraction. For ATT weighting, treated weights are 1 and control weights are \(e(X)/(1-e(X))\). State the target and normalization rather than calling every weighted difference “ATE.”


Standard errors
Control reuse and matching uncertainty invalidate an independent two-sample standard error applied without regard to the design. A fixed number of nearest-neighbor matches gives a nonsmooth estimator for which the ordinary nonparametric bootstrap is generally invalid. Use an estimator-appropriate analytic matching variance or a justified alternative; do not promise that rerunning matching inside a naive bootstrap solves the issue. Abadie and Imbens (2008)
Weighting and smooth estimators have different inference options. Preserve clustering at the assignment or sampling unit and include nuisance estimation appropriately.
crumbs: 27  Propensity Scores: Matching and Weighting

title: Propensity Scores: Matching and Weighting
text:
Practice and pitfalls

Define treatment, outcome timing, eligibility, and ATT versus ATE.
Select baseline confounders and outcome predictors using substantive knowledge.
Fit a regularized logistic baseline; compare flexible alternatives through overlap and balance, not AUC alone.
Inspect common support and decide whether a restricted population answers the question.
Match or weight using a documented rule.
Examine balance in all covariates before examining the outcome contrast.
Estimate effect size with appropriate uncertainty, then conduct hidden-confounding and design sensitivity checks.

Balance failure sends the analysis back to the design step. Do not iterate based on whether the treatment effect becomes significant. A guideline such as \(|SMD|<0.1\) is useful, but does not prove exchangeability or guarantee balance of every relevant distributional feature.
Post-treatment mediators and colliders can bias adjustment in either direction. Pure treatment predictors may worsen weight variability without improving confounding control; removing a true confounder solely to improve overlap is not justified.
crumbs: 27  Propensity Scores: Matching and Weighting

title: Propensity Scores: Matching and Weighting
text:
Interview questions
Why not optimize propensity AUC? We need a useful balancing design. Near-perfect treatment prediction may expose nonoverlap, and a strong classifier can still leave covariate imbalance.
Does 1:1 PSM estimate ATE? Matching controls to treated units usually targets ATT for retained treated units. A different target requires a different design or weighting scheme.
Why inverse probability? It upweights observations underrepresented by the assignment mechanism, so weighted arm outcomes recover the target population expectation under the assumptions.
How would you present a project? Explain selection bias, freeze pre-treatment features, show overlap and balance, state the retained estimand, report absolute lift and CI, discuss unmeasured confounding, and separate observational evidence from randomized confirmation.

Summary
The true propensity score balances observed covariates. A credible implementation additionally needs common support, direct balance checks, an explicit estimand, and inference matched to its matching or weighting estimator.

crumbs: 28  Overlap, Polarized Scores, and Sensitivity Analysis

title: Overlap, Polarized Scores, and Sensitivity Analysis
text:
Intuition
A propensity histogram concentrated near zero for controls and one for treated units means comparisons are scarce. Sometimes a model memorized labels; sometimes the business assigned treatment deterministically. These require different responses. Making probabilities less extreme cosmetically does not create missing counterfactual information.
Even excellent balance addresses only recorded variables. Sensitivity analysis asks how strongly an omitted factor would need to affect assignment or outcomes to change a conclusion. It quantifies a vulnerability under a specified model; it does not certify the absence of that factor.
crumbs: 28  Overlap, Polarized Scores, and Sensitivity Analysis

title: Overlap, Polarized Scores, and Sensitivity Analysis
text:
Worked example

Extreme weights and effective information
For a treated observation with score 0.01, ATE weight is 100. Four other observations with weights 1 contribute much less. A common descriptive effective sample size is
\[ESS=\frac{(\sum_iw_i)^2}{\sum_iw_i^2}=\frac{104^2}{10000+4}\approx1.08.\]
Five records may therefore contain little weighted information. Stabilizing a treated weight by multiplying it by \(P(T=1)=0.2\) changes 100 to 20 but multiplies all treated weights by the same constant. Its within-arm ESS is unchanged; stabilization does not fix absent support.


Rosenbaum’s assignment-odds bound
Two matched people with the same observed covariates have treatment odds \(p_i/(1-p_i)\) and \(p_j/(1-p_j)\). A sensitivity model permits
\[\frac1\Gamma\leq\frac{p_i/(1-p_i)}{p_j/(1-p_j)}\leq\Gamma.\]
At \(\Gamma=1\), their assignment odds agree. At \(\Gamma=2\), probabilities 0.5 and \(2/3\) are possible: odds 1 versus 2. For probabilities 0.5 and \(5/6\), the odds ratio is 5.
For illustrative matched outcomes, suppose the worst-case p-value is 0.01 at \(\Gamma=1.5\), 0.04 at 2, and 0.06 at 2.1. The conclusion crosses a 5% significance threshold around 2.1. This says how much hidden assignment bias is allowed in this particular sensitivity model before the statistical conclusion becomes inconclusive. It is not a 2.1-fold treatment effect and does not establish that such bias is implausible.


An E-value calculation
For a risk ratio \(RR=0.08/0.04=2\),
\[E\text{-value}=RR+\sqrt{RR(RR-1)}=2+\sqrt2\approx3.414.\]
This is a risk-ratio sensitivity benchmark for an unmeasured confounder’s associations with treatment and outcome, conditional on measured covariates. It summarizes the minimum equal-strength association benchmark sufficient to explain away the point estimate under the bounding model. Unequal-strength combinations can also explain an estimate; it is too strong to claim that both associations must individually exceed 3.414 in every possible configuration.
For a protective \(RR<1\), use its reciprocal in the basic formula. Also calculate the E-value for the confidence-limit closest to the null; a large point-estimate E-value with a CI touching 1 is weak evidence of precision.
crumbs: 28  Overlap, Polarized Scores, and Sensitivity Analysis

title: Overlap, Polarized Scores, and Sensitivity Analysis
text:
Theory and assumptions

Balance as standardized mean difference
For covariate \(j\), compare matched treatment and control means on a common scale:
\[\operatorname{SMD}_j=\frac{\bar X_{Tj}-\bar X_{Cj}}{\sqrt{(s_{Tj}^2+s_{Cj}^2)/2}}.\]
For a binary covariate, the arm means are proportions and the corresponding variance estimates can use \(p_{gj}(1-p_{gj})\). Keep a chosen pre-match denominator fixed when comparing SMD before and after matching, so an apparent improvement is not produced by changing the scale. Also inspect categorical proportions, variances, and distribution plots: equal means alone do not establish distributional balance. A value such as \(|\mathrm{SMD}|<0.1\) is a diagnostic convention, not proof of ignorability.


A diagnostic sequence for polarized XGBoost scores

Audit timing and leakage. An exposure identifier or post-treatment action may almost encode the label.
Compare out-of-fold with training probabilities. Training-only separation suggests overfitting.
Inspect the assignment policy. Eligibility thresholds may produce genuine zero probabilities.
Check covariate support, not only one score plot. Aggregate histogram overlap can hide empty multivariate strata.
Evaluate balance and weight distributions. Report retained fractions, maximum weights, and ESS by arm.

Shallower trees, stronger leaf penalties, larger minimum leaf information, subsampling, and early stopping can reduce overfitting. Logistic regression or a GAM can be useful baselines. Hyperparameters from a study are starting points rather than transferable guarantees.


What each remedy actually does








Remedy
Purpose
Limitation




Regularization
Reduce fitted-score overfitting
Cannot overturn a deterministic policy


Calibration
Improve probability calibration on held-out data
Cannot restore real overlap


Trimming
Restrict to supported covariate regions
Changes the target population


Clipping/truncation
Limit numerical weight extremes
Alters the estimator and introduces bias tradeoffs


Stabilized weighting
Control some weight scaling behavior
Does not remove within-arm relative extremes


Caliper matching
Reject distant matches
May lose many treated units


DR/DML/TMLE
Reduce particular nuisance-model sensitivity
Still require the relevant identification and overlap assumptions



The often-used \([0.05,0.95]\) range is a sensitivity choice, not a universal rule. Report results and population composition under alternative sensible restrictions.
For an AIPW ATE score, with \(\mu_t(X)=E[Y\mid T=t,X]\),
\[\psi_i=\hat\mu_1(X_i)-\hat\mu_0(X_i)
+\frac{T_i[Y_i-\hat\mu_1(X_i)]}{\hat e_i}
-\frac{(1-T_i)[Y_i-\hat\mu_0(X_i)]}{1-\hat e_i}.\]
Under the causal assumptions, appropriate regularity, and overlap, its mean can be consistent if either the propensity or outcome regressions are correctly specified. This robustness is not permission to omit confounders. The partially linear residual-on-residual DML score has a different robustness structure.


Sensitivity checks answer different questions
Rosenbaum bounds assess departures in treatment-assignment odds within matched designs; implementations include paired and more general matched configurations. E-values use a risk-ratio bounding framework. Risk differences, odds ratios, and hazard ratios cannot all be inserted into the risk-ratio formula unchanged. Translation requires appropriate assumptions and transformations.
A pre-treatment placebo outcome cannot be affected by the later intervention. An estimated “effect” raises concerns about confounding or design errors. A nonsignificant placebo does not prove validity: it may have low power or miss the relevant bias pathway.

title: Overlap, Polarized Scores, and Sensitivity Analysis
text:
Practice and pitfalls
A useful report shows unadjusted and adjusted balance, support exclusions, the retained estimand, absolute effects and CIs, alternative design choices, and sensitivity to unmeasured confounding. Explain which omitted factors are plausible in context—shopping intent, payday timing, private targeting signals—and avoid assigning them numerical strengths without evidence.
Do not turn \(\Gamma\) thresholds into universal rules such as “above 3 is safe to launch.” Sensitivity varies with the outcome, matching design, test, and scientific context. Likewise, a high E-value does not repair selection bias, outcome measurement error, interference, or model misspecification automatically.
Business translation should preserve uncertainty: multiplying ATT by recipient count estimates an aggregate incremental outcome only when the retained target matches that recipient population and the intervention scales without changing effects or costs.
crumbs: 28  Overlap, Polarized Scores, and Sensitivity Analysis

title: Overlap, Polarized Scores, and Sensitivity Analysis
text:
Interview questions
My XGBoost scores are at 0 and 1. What next? I audit leakage and actual assignment rules, compare out-of-fold predictions with a regularized baseline, inspect support and balance, and then consider restriction or redesign. I do not promise calibration or DML will recover missing comparisons.
What does \(\Gamma^*=2.1\) mean? In the chosen sensitivity model, an unmeasured factor allowing roughly 2.1-fold differences in assignment odds can make the result statistically inconclusive under a worst-case allocation.
Why report the E-value for the CI as well? Robustness of a point estimate alone ignores sampling uncertainty. The confidence-limit calculation shows how little hidden confounding may be needed to move the compatible effect range to the null.

title: Difference-in-Differences and Event Studies
text: Learning goals

title: Difference-in-Differences and Event Studies
text:
Derive the two-group, two-period estimator and interpret every regression coefficient.
Explain parallel trends, unit and time fixed effects, and event-time normalization.
Recognize treatment-effect heterogeneity problems in staggered TWFE designs.

title: Difference-in-Differences and Event Studies
text:
Intuition
A city launches a seller incentive and GMV grows. Some growth might have happened anyway during a holiday. DiD subtracts the untreated comparison group’s change from the treated group’s change. Stable baseline differences cancel within groups; a common time change cancels across groups.
The causal argument is parallel untreated trends: without the policy, the treated group’s average change would match the comparison group’s change. This allows different initial levels. It does not allow an unaccounted city-specific demand shock coinciding with launch.

title: Difference-in-Differences and Event Studies
text:
Worked example

Four cells and four coefficients
A hypothetical livestream pop-up yields these ordering rates:

\[\widehat\tau_{DiD}=(0.09-0.05)-(0.06-0.04)=0.02.\]
The counterfactual treated post-period rate is \(5\%+2\%=7\%\). The actual 9% is 2 percentage points higher. A raw post comparison gives 3 pp; a treated-only before/after comparison gives 4 pp. Each retains a different unwanted component.



The control trend projects a treated counterfactual of 7%; the observed treated rate is 9%.


Fit
\[Y_{it}=\alpha+\beta G_i+\gamma P_t+\delta G_iP_t+\epsilon_{it}.\]
Here \(G_i\) marks the treated group, and \(P_t\) marks the post period. The four fitted cells are \(\alpha\), \(\alpha+\gamma\), \(\alpha+\beta\), and \(\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta\). Therefore \(\alpha=0.04\), \(\beta=0.01\), \(\gamma=0.02\), and \(\delta=0.02\). The interaction becomes causal only with the design assumptions.


A dynamic rollout
Relative to the last pre-launch period, suppose estimated differences in percentage points are:

Pre-period coefficients near zero are compatible with parallel trends but do not prove it. The post pattern suggests accumulation followed by partial decay. Confidence intervals are essential: the apparent difference between 1.8 and 1.3 may be noise. The example illustrates how an event study separates an immediate effect, delayed adoption, and novelty decay that one average coefficient would hide.

title: Difference-in-Differences and Event Studies
text:
Theory and assumptions

Identification
For two periods, the key condition is
\[E[Y_1(0)-Y_0(0)\mid G=1]=E[Y_1(0)-Y_0(0)\mid G=0].\]
Together with no anticipation, consistency, and an appropriate stable population/composition, DiD identifies the treated group’s post-period average effect. Untreated levels need not agree. The unobserved post-treatment counterfactual means parallel trends cannot be established simply by testing pre-period coefficients.
Time-varying confounders specific to the treated group, treatment spillovers, simultaneous interventions, differential measurement changes, and selective entry or exit can invalidate the comparison. For repeated cross-sections, changing group composition needs explicit attention.


Two-way fixed effects
For a panel,
\[Y_{it}=\alpha_i+\lambda_t+\delta D_{it}+\epsilon_{it}.\]
Unit effects absorb time-invariant unit characteristics; time effects absorb shocks common to all units. Remaining unit-specific time-varying differences do not disappear. Covariate adjustment can support a conditional parallel-trends argument, but adding arbitrary time trends or post-treatment covariates is not a mechanical repair.
Cluster standard errors at a level consistent with assignment and dependence, often the policy unit. Millions of users in a few treated cities do not create millions of independent policy assignments. Few clusters require suitable small-sample inference.


Event studies
If unit \(i\) first receives treatment at \(g_i\), an event-time representation is
\[Y_{it}=\alpha_i+\lambda_t+\sum_{k\ne-1}\beta_k\mathbf1\{t-g_i=k\}+\epsilon_{it}.\]
Omit a reference event time, commonly \(k=-1\), to normalize the comparisons. Never-treated units have no finite adoption time and their event indicators must be encoded accordingly. Plot the coefficient estimates with intervals and show which cohorts support long event horizons.
In a simple common-adoption setting, leads describe relative pre-period differences and lags describe the dynamic post contrast. Under staggered heterogeneous treatment effects, conventional TWFE event-study coefficients can be contaminated; their interpretation needs a suitable estimator.


Staggered treatment and heterogeneous effects
If one city adopts in March and another in July, conventional TWFE can use already-treated early adopters as controls for later adopters. Changes in the early adopters’ treatment effects then contaminate the control trend. The result need not equal the desired average of causal effects and can even reverse sign.
The Goodman–Bacon decomposition writes a standard TWFE coefficient as a weighted average of two-by-two comparisons. Its comparison weights are nonnegative in that decomposition; problematic comparisons can nevertheless imply negative weights on underlying heterogeneous group-time effects. Do not conflate those two weighting statements.
Alternatives include:

Callaway–Sant’Anna: estimate group-time ATT values using suitable never-treated or not-yet-treated comparisons, then aggregate for a defined target.
Sun–Abraham: estimate cohort-specific event-time effects and aggregate without the usual heterogeneous-effects contamination.
de Chaisemartin–D’Haultfœuille: use estimators designed for treatment-effect heterogeneity and appropriate clean comparisons.

Choice depends on the assignment structure, anticipation window, treatment reversals, available comparison cohorts, and desired aggregation. Estimator names are not substitutes for parallel trends.

title: Difference-in-Differences and Event Studies
text:
Practice and pitfalls
Record adoption dates, anticipation periods, clustering units, and concurrent policies before modeling. Plot raw outcomes alongside event-study contrasts. Check missing periods, changing denominators, and group composition. Report the point estimate, interval, population, time horizon, and aggregation weights.
A nonsignificant pretrend test can be underpowered. A significant pretrend is a warning, not an invitation to search for a time window that passes. Matching before DiD may improve comparability but still requires the conditional parallel-trends assumption. Synthetic control offers a different counterfactual construction, not an assumption-free fallback.

title: Difference-in-Differences and Event Studies
text:
Interview questions
What does the interaction coefficient mean? The treated group’s before/after change minus the control group’s change. It identifies the post-period ATT under parallel untreated trends and the remaining design assumptions.
Why are unit and time fixed effects insufficient? They remove stable unit differences and common shocks, not treatment-correlated unit-specific shocks that evolve over time.
Does an insignificant lead prove parallel trends? No. Pre-period data provide a diagnostic with limited power; the identifying counterfactual concerns the post period.
What breaks under staggered TWFE? Already-treated groups may become controls, and heterogeneous or changing effects contaminate comparisons. I estimate group-time effects using appropriate comparison cohorts and aggregate deliberately.

title: Difference-in-Differences and Event Studies
text:
Summary
DiD obtains a counterfactual change from a comparison group. Transparent timing, credible untreated trends, appropriate dependence-aware inference, and a heterogeneity-compatible estimator matter more than merely including two sets of fixed effects.

title: Synthetic Control
text: Learning goals

title: Synthetic Control
text:
Explain the donor pool, pre-treatment fit, convex weights, and post-treatment gap.
Calculate a synthetic outcome and understand why fit is necessary but insufficient.
Compare synthetic control with DiD and design meaningful placebo analyses.

title: Synthetic Control
text:
Intuition
When one city launches a policy, no single untreated city may be a convincing comparator. A synthetic control combines several untreated cities so that their pre-policy outcomes and predictors resemble the treated city’s. The post-policy gap is interpreted through the assumption that this relationship would have continued without treatment.
One treated city does not mathematically rule out DiD. Synthetic control is attractive when a weighted donor combination is more defensible than any single comparison; inference with very few treated units remains challenging for either approach.

title: Synthetic Control
text:
Worked example

Build a synthetic city
Suppose pre-policy optimization produces weights 0.42, 0.28, 0.20, and 0.10 on four donors. The weights are nonnegative and sum to one. A future untreated donor outcome vector is \((100,80,90,70)\) in consistent GMV units. Then
\[\widehat Y_t(0)=0.42(100)+0.28(80)+0.20(90)+0.10(70)=89.4.\]
If the treated city’s observed outcome is 98, the estimated time-\(t\) effect is \(98-89.4=8.6\), or about 9.62% relative to the synthetic level. This interpretation requires a credible untreated trajectory; the arithmetic alone does not identify a causal effect.


Check the fit
Suppose treated pre-period outcomes are \((70,75,80)\) and synthetic values are \((69,76,80)\). Pre-RMSPE is
\[\sqrt{[(70-69)^2+(75-76)^2+(80-80)^2]/3}=\sqrt{2/3}\approx0.816.\]
A post-period gap of 8.6 is large relative to this pre-fit error, but a coincident treated-city shock could still explain it. Reassigning “treatment” to donors and recomputing the entire procedure provides a distribution of placebo gaps. Compare post/pre error ratios and pre-fit quality, not only raw post gaps from donors of very different scale.

title: Synthetic Control
text:
Theory and assumptions

The optimization
Let \(X_1\) contain treated-unit pre-treatment predictors and outcome summaries, and let columns of \(X_0\) contain donor equivalents. Traditional synthetic control chooses
\[\widehat w=\arg\min_w (X_1-X_0w)'V(X_1-X_0w),\qquad w_j\ge0,\quad\sum_jw_j=1.\]
\(V\) weights predictor discrepancies. Alternatively, a simple teaching version minimizes squared pre-period outcome gaps directly. All tuning must use pre-treatment information; including treated post outcomes leaks the answer into the counterfactual.
For post-treatment periods,
\[\widehat\tau_t=Y_{1t}-\sum_j\widehat w_jY_{jt}.\]
The convex restriction avoids unrestricted extrapolation but means the treated unit may lie outside the donor pool’s convex hull. Poor pre-fit is then informative: the donor pool may not support the comparison.


Why pre-fit can help
Under suitable outcome models, a long and well-matched pre-period can align observed predictors and latent factor exposure. This supports extrapolating the untreated relationship forward. Perfect fit is neither guaranteed by the optimizer nor proof that the post counterfactual is correct.
Important conditions include no anticipation, no donor contamination or spillovers, stable measurement, no treatment-related donor selection, and no unmodeled shock uniquely affecting the treated unit after launch. A stable factor structure or another substantive counterfactual argument is still required. Synthetic control does not remove causal assumptions by “constructing parallel trends.”


Placebos and uncertainty
An in-space placebo applies the same design to untreated donor units. An in-time placebo moves the intervention into the pre-period. Leave-one-donor-out analysis reveals dependence on a single heavily weighted donor. All are diagnostics; their inferential interpretation depends on comparability and an assignment or sampling argument.
With few donors, placebo ranks are coarse. A donor with terrible pre-fit is not comparable to a well-fitted treated unit without adjustment or restriction. A standard independent-observation t-test on serially correlated post gaps is usually inappropriate.

title: Synthetic Control
text:
Practice and pitfalls







Situation
Design implication




Many treated and control units with credible common trends
DiD may offer a direct and transparent design


One or few treated units and a rich untreated donor panel
Synthetic control can construct a more suitable comparator


Weak pre-fit
Revise the donor pool/predictors or acknowledge insufficient support


Strong geography or seasonal differences
Match pre-period trajectories and relevant predictors carefully


Donors exposed indirectly to the policy
Exclude or explicitly model contamination



Normalize units and denominators, document donor exclusions, freeze the fitting period, and show weights alongside outcome plots. Compare absolute and relative gaps without confusing aggregate GMV effects with per-user effects.
The classic applications include the Basque Country study and California’s tobacco-control program. The methodological lesson is a transparent comparative case design; historical applications do not validate a new city’s counterfactual automatically.

title: Synthetic Control
text:
Interview questions
Why not choose the most similar single city? A convex combination can match multiple pre-treatment features better while making the donor contribution explicit.
Can synthetic control fix failed parallel trends? It can construct a different comparator, but requires adequate pre-fit and a credible stable untreated relationship. It is not a guaranteed repair.
What do placebo gaps tell you? Whether similar apparent effects arise when the same procedure is applied without the intervention, conditional on comparable fit and the study design.

title: Synthetic Control
text:
Summary
Synthetic control makes the counterfactual construction visible through donor weights and pre-fit. Its credibility rests on a stable untreated relationship, uncontaminated donors, and transparent sensitivity analyses.

text: Learning goals

title: Instrumental Variables, 2SLS, and LATE
text:
State relevance, independence, exclusion, and monotonicity separately.
Calculate the first stage, reduced form, Wald ratio, and two-stage estimate.
Interpret LATE for compliers and diagnose weak-instrument inference.

title: Instrumental Variables, 2SLS, and LATE
text:
Intuition
Viewing a livestream and ordering may share an unobserved cause: shopping intent. A valid instrument \(Z\) changes viewing while providing variation unrelated to that intent and affecting ordering only through viewing. The estimate uses the treatment variation induced by \(Z\).
A randomized encouragement is a candidate instrument, not automatically a valid one. A card can alter brand awareness, displace other content, or change shopping intent even without a view; those are possible exclusion violations.

title: Instrumental Variables, 2SLS, and LATE
text:
Worked example

Encouragement and the Wald ratio
Consider an explicitly hypothetical study of 1,000 users:

Encouragement \(Z=1\)
500

The first-stage effect is \(0.60-0.20=0.40\), and the reduced-form outcome effect is \(0.12-0.06=0.06\). Therefore
\[\widehat\beta_{Wald}=\frac{0.06}{0.40}=0.15.\]
The encouragement changes ordering by 6 percentage points. Under valid-IV and monotonicity assumptions, viewing changes ordering by 15 percentage points among compliers. Neither is a universal individual effect. The encouragement’s own policy value is directly represented by its reduced form, potentially adjusted for deployment costs.


See both regression stages
Stage one gives \(\widehat T=0.20+0.40Z\). The fitted treatment values are 0.20 and 0.60. Stage two fits an outcome line through \((0.20,0.06)\) and \((0.60,0.12)\), whose slope is 0.15. This reproduces the Wald estimate.
A direct observational regression of outcome on actual viewing may have a larger coefficient because it includes selection on shopping interest. Its magnitude cannot be decomposed into “true effect plus bias” numerically without additional information.

title: Instrumental Variables, 2SLS, and LATE
text:
Theory and assumptions

Four distinct requirements

Relevance: \(Z\) changes treatment probability, conditionally on included baseline controls if applicable.
Independence: \(Z\) is independent of relevant potential outcomes and treatment responses, or satisfies the appropriate conditional exogeneity argument.
Exclusion: holding treatment fixed, changing \(Z\) does not change the outcome. In potential-outcome notation, \(Y(t,z)=Y(t)\).
Monotonicity for binary LATE: \(T_i(1)\ge T_i(0)\); the encouragement does not reduce treatment for any unit.

Consistency and a suitable interference assumption are also needed. Exclusion and independence are conceptually different; writing one covariance restriction does not establish both. Monotonicity can fail if an intrusive recommendation deters some users, so it must be argued rather than assumed to hold in all industrial settings.


Compliance types

Under monotonicity, the first-stage difference equals the complier fraction. Independence and exclusion make the outcome difference equal to that fraction times the complier average effect:
\[\begin{aligned}
E[T\mid Z=1]-E[T\mid Z=0]&=P(C),\\
E[Y\mid Z=1]-E[Y\mid Z=0]&=P(C)E[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid C].
\end{aligned}\]
Dividing identifies LATE. In the example \(P(C)=0.4\). The effects for always-takers and never-takers are not identified by this contrast. Scaling to a different encouragement or a new population may change the complier group.


Two-stage least squares
With baseline controls \(X\), first regress \(T\) on an intercept, \(Z\), and \(X\), then regress \(Y\) on fitted \(T\), an intercept, and the same controls. More generally, 2SLS projects the endogenous regressors onto the instrument space.
Use an IV estimator’s variance calculation. Running two ordinary regressions and accepting the second regression’s naive standard errors ignores the generated-regressor structure and uses the wrong residuals for structural inference. Cluster or heteroskedasticity-robust inference may be needed.


Weak instruments
The Wald ratio divides by the first stage. If that denominator is close to zero, small sampling changes can produce very large estimate changes, nonnormal distributions, and unreliable conventional confidence intervals. Report first-stage coefficients and appropriate strength statistics.
The familiar first-stage \(F>10\) is a rough historical diagnostic, not a universal guarantee of strong identification, especially with heteroskedasticity, clustering, many instruments, or multiple endogenous variables. Stock–Yogo critical values have their own assumptions; use diagnostics appropriate to the design.
Potential responses are a more informative valid instrument, a better-designed encouragement, carefully justified LIML in suitable settings, or weak-IV-robust procedures such as Anderson–Rubin inference. A wide or unbounded interval is information about the design’s limits. Adding controls does not guarantee a stronger or more valid instrument.

title: Instrumental Variables, 2SLS, and LATE
text:
Practice and pitfalls
Historical candidate instruments illustrate the argument and its vulnerabilities:








Candidate

Rainfall and rides

The source notes include these as motivating examples; none should be described as valid merely because the story sounds external. In particular, weather is often a poor instrument for downstream travel outcomes because it directly changes them.
Report the treatment units, first stage, reduced form, LATE, confidence interval, compliance interpretation, and threats to exclusion. Distinguish “effect of offering the program” from “effect of participation for induced participants.”

title: Instrumental Variables, 2SLS, and LATE
text:
Interview questions
What makes an instrument valid? It must shift treatment, be exogenous under the design, and have no outcome pathway except treatment. Binary LATE also needs monotonicity and a nonzero complier fraction.
Why LATE rather than ATE? Only compliers change treatment when the instrument changes. Their outcome response identifies the ratio; always-taker and never-taker treatment effects remain outside it.
Is a first-stage F of 11 enough? It is not a universal certificate. I examine the relevant weak-identification diagnostics, covariance structure, number of instruments, and robust inference.
Would a random card with no purchase button guarantee exclusion? No. It might still affect awareness or displace content. The absence of a button is evidence about one pathway, not proof about all pathways.

title: Instrumental Variables, 2SLS, and LATE
text:
Summary
IV trades conditional exchangeability of treatment for a credible external variation argument. The output often targets compliers, and weak first stages or exclusion violations cannot be repaired by confident interpretation.

text: Learning goals

title: Double Machine Learning
text:
Distinguish the structural outcome function from the conditional outcome regression.
Derive residual-on-residual estimation, orthogonality, and a sufficient nuisance-rate condition.
Design a complete observational analysis with valid timing, uncertainty, and experimental follow-up.

title: Double Machine Learning
text:
Intuition
Historical activity can predict both a user’s exposure and future return. DML uses flexible models to subtract the predictable baseline from both treatment and outcome, then estimates the relationship between what remains. Sample splitting prevents the same observation from training its own nuisance prediction.
This improves estimation under a causal identification argument. It does not make exposure random, remove unmeasured interest, or repair an outcome window that overlaps exposure measurement.

\[\hat\theta=\frac{0.164}{0.82}=0.20.\]
For a binary outcome and binary treatment under a constant-effect partially linear model, this is a 0.20 probability-unit effect, or 20 percentage points. This tiny example teaches the arithmetic; four records are not sufficient for credible high-dimensional causal inference.


A return-search study, from question to action
The source case asks which touchpoints after an anchor-day search predict later active return-search. A reusable design has these steps:

Define a user-level eligible cohort at anchor day \(t_0\) and a precise active-return outcome, such as first qualifying return during \(t_0+2\) through \(t_0+7\).
Predefine a treatment window that ends before the outcome window; do not end exposure counting at the outcome itself. That creates outcome-dependent opportunity to receive exposure.
Group candidate actions: passive-search cards and query suggestions; search-result CTR/CVR, price visibility, product clicks and depth; video/livestream and marketplace exposure; experience and marketing measures. Decide which are treatments, mediators, or controls using the timeline rather than treating every available metric as a confounder.
Freeze controls from the preceding 30 days: demographics, purchasing power, city, activity, historical exposures/clicks/payments, lifecycle, and past search-result behavior.
Cross-fit treatment and outcome models. Estimate each action in meaningful units, or explicitly standardize before comparing coefficients. Simultaneous treatments require a joint causal model and residual treatment variation with adequate rank.
If effect modifiers are numerous, a sparse linear final effect model \(\tau(z)=\beta_0+z'\beta\) can summarize heterogeneity. Sparsity and suitable debiasing/inference conditions are additional assumptions.
Use the observational findings to prioritize hypotheses, then randomize promising strategy changes. The source distinguishes observational driver screening from a separate exposure-reversal experiment; a threshold observed in that experiment belongs to the randomized result, not to DML identification. Its specific operating value is omitted from this public teaching edition.

Possible negative associations between content consumption and return-search may suggest attention substitution, but dynamic recommendation and unrecorded interest are alternative explanations. State those limitations rather than turning screening results into proven mechanisms.

title: Double Machine Learning
text:
Theory and assumptions

Partially linear regression
\[Y=\theta_0T+g_0(X)+U,\qquad E[U\mid X,T]=0,\]
\[T=m_0(X)+V,\qquad E[V\mid X]=0.\]
Define the conditional outcome regression
\[\ell_0(X)=E[Y\mid X]=\theta_0m_0(X)+g_0(X).\]
The nuisance models fitted from \(X\) alone are \(\ell_0\) and \(m_0\), not \(g_0\) and \(m_0\). For binary treatment, \(m_0=e\) is the propensity; for continuous treatment it is a conditional mean.
Subtracting conditional expectations gives \(Y-\ell_0(X)=\theta_0[T-m_0(X)]+U\). Thus
\[\hat\theta=\frac{\sum_i\widetilde T_i\widetilde Y_i}{\sum_i\widetilde T_i^2},\quad
\widetilde Y_i=Y_i-\hat\ell_{-k(i)}(X_i),\quad
\widetilde T_i=T_i-\hat m_{-k(i)}(X_i).\]
This is a no-intercept least-squares slope. In linear regression it parallels the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell residualization theorem. Cross-fitted residuals need not have sample means exactly zero; the stated moment equation, rather than an automatic centering shortcut, defines this estimator.


Orthogonality
Use the score
\[\psi(W;\theta,\ell,m)=[Y-\ell(X)-\theta(T-m(X))][T-m(X)].\]
At the true nuisance functions, its expectation is zero. Its first derivative with respect to small nuisance perturbations is also zero: conditional mean-zero residuals cancel the first-order terms. Let \(a=\hat\ell-\ell_0\) and \(b=\hat m-m_0\). At \(\theta_0\), the remaining population perturbation includes
\[E[ab-\theta_0b^2].\]
Therefore a convenient sufficient rate condition for this parameterization is
\[\|\hat m-m_0\|_2\bigl(\|\hat\ell-\ell_0\|_2+\|\hat m-m_0\|_2\bigr)=o_P(n^{-1/2}),\]
along with moment, identification, and other regularity conditions. Both nuisance errors being \(o_P(n^{-1/4})\) is sufficient for this remainder. The additional squared treatment-regression error should not be omitted when stating the condition for this particular score.
Here \(o_P(n^{-1/2})\) means multiplying the error by \(\sqrt n\) makes it converge to zero in probability. A root-\(n\) target error shrinks by about tenfold with 100 times the data; an \(n^{-1/4}\) nuisance error shrinks only about 3.16-fold. Orthogonality prevents such nuisance error entering the target entirely at first order.


Cross-fitting and inference
For five folds, train nuisance models on four folds and predict the fifth, rotating until every observation has held-out predictions. Hyperparameter tuning belongs inside the relevant training portion. For repeated users or dependent clusters, split at the appropriate unit.
After solving the moment equation, use an influence-function/sandwich variance appropriate to the sampling structure. With independent observations and \(J=E[\widetilde T^2]\), a basic estimate has form
\[\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\theta)=\frac{n^{-1}\sum_i\hat\psi_i^2}{n\hat J^2}.\]
Cross-fitting removes an important overfitting dependence but does not itself guarantee nuisance quality, root-\(n\) inference, or causal identification.

title: Double Machine Learning
text:
Practice and pitfalls

Residualizing only the outcome leaves treatment’s predictable component in the final regression.
PLR-DML avoids explicit inverse propensity weights, but near-constant treatment conditional on \(X\) makes residual treatment variance vanish. There is still too little identifying variation.
DML is a framework, not an automatic synonym for doubly robust. AIPW-based ATE scores can have either-model-correct robustness; the PLR residual score must be assessed on its own terms.
With heterogeneous effects and binary treatment, a constant PLR coefficient generally averages effects with weights related to \(e(X)(1-e(X))\), not automatically the population ATE.
Pre-treatment covariates, no omitted confounding, correct temporal ordering, sufficient residual variation, and a suitable structural model remain necessary.

title: Double Machine Learning
text:
Interview questions
Why two models and two residuals? Both outcome and treatment contain predictable covariate-driven variation. Removing only one side leaves a confounded comparison and nuisance bias.
What does cross-fitting solve? It prevents each record from training the nuisance models used to predict that record, reducing own-observation overfitting bias.
Does DML solve endogeneity? Not unmeasured endogeneity by itself. A PLR analysis relies on the stated conditional mean/exchangeability argument; a valid-IV question needs an IV score or another appropriate design.
What did the return-search analysis establish? It screened potential drivers under observational assumptions. A separate randomized reversal design evaluated key strategy hypotheses and the reported overexposure threshold.

title: Double Machine Learning
text:
Summary
DML combines an orthogonal score with held-out nuisance predictions. Its precision argument relies on second-order remainder control, and its causal interpretation still depends on the design and estimand.

title: Uplift Modeling and Heterogeneous Effects
text:
Intuition
A customer who would buy anyway may have a high purchase score and almost no coupon uplift. Targeting should consider the incremental response, \(\tau(x)=E[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid X=x]\), and intervention cost.
For a binary purchase outcome, the potential-outcome types are:

crumbs: 33  Uplift Modeling and Heterogeneous Effects

title: Uplift Modeling and Heterogeneous Effects
text:
Worked example

Same baseline complexity, simple effect
Suppose untreated spending is a complicated function \(\mu_0(x)\), and \(\mu_1(x)=\mu_0(x)+5\). The effect function is simply 5 even though each outcome function is difficult to learn. A T-learner estimating the two functions with errors \(\varepsilon_0\) and \(\varepsilon_1\) gives
\[\hat\tau(x)=5+\varepsilon_1(x)-\varepsilon_0(x).\]
If the errors are independent with standard deviation 20 each, the difference has standard deviation \(\sqrt{20^2+20^2}\approx28.3\), dwarfing the effect. In general the variance also contains \(-2\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_0)\); independent training groups do not justify every unconditional independence claim automatically.


X-learner arithmetic
For a treated observation, actual spending is 100 and predicted untreated spending is 92, so its imputed effect is \(100-92=8\). For a control observation, predicted treated spending is 85 and observed spending is 80, so the imputed effect is \(85-80=5\).
After fitting effect models to many such observations, suppose \(\hat\tau_0(x)=6\), \(\hat\tau_1(x)=8\), and \(e(x)=0.25\). The propensity-weighted blend is
\[\hat\tau_X(x)=0.25(6)+0.75(8)=7.5.\]
These imputed outcomes contain prediction error and individual noise. They are training signals for a conditional average, not observed individual treatment effects.


Why an outcome tree may miss effect heterogeneity
Two customer groups can have the same observed average spending but treatment effects of 50 and 5. A regression tree focused on reducing outcome prediction error may not separate them. A causal tree or forest uses an effect-oriented splitting criterion to seek informative differences in treatment response.
crumbs: 33  Uplift Modeling and Heterogeneous Effects

title: Uplift Modeling and Heterogeneous Effects
text:
Theory and assumptions
All learners need consistency, exchangeability under the study design, and overlap on the prediction population. Flexible models do not exempt the analysis from these conditions.

T-learner
Fit \(\hat\mu_1(x)\) on treated observations and \(\hat\mu_0(x)\) on controls, then use
\[\hat\tau_T(x)=\hat\mu_1(x)-\hat\mu_0(x).\]
It is transparent and allows different outcome structures by arm. Separate fits may waste shared structure or make the smaller arm unstable. Good outcome prediction in both arms does not guarantee precise estimation of their small difference.


S-learner
Fit one model \(\hat\mu(x,t)\) and compare
\[\hat\tau_S(x)=\hat\mu(x,1)-\hat\mu(x,0).\]
It shares information across treatment groups. A regularized learner may ignore a weak treatment feature or its interactions, shrinking estimated effects toward zero. Explicit interactions or an appropriate treatment-effect model can help. A monotonicity constraint does not force a nonzero effect and is justified only by substantive knowledge; it is not a general solution to treatment-signal suppression.


X-learner

Fit outcome models \(\hat\mu_0,\hat\mu_1\).
Impute \(D_i^{(1)}=Y_i-\hat\mu_0(X_i)\) for treated observations and \(D_i^{(0)}=\hat\mu_1(X_i)-Y_i\) for controls.
Regress these pseudo-outcomes on \(X\) separately to obtain \(\hat\tau_1,\hat\tau_0\).
Blend them, often as \(e(x)\hat\tau_0(x)+(1-e(x))\hat\tau_1(x)\).

When controls greatly outnumber treated observations, the control outcome model can be especially accurate, making treated-unit imputed effects useful. The weighting emphasizes the corresponding effect estimate. Other weighting choices are possible. X-learning can exploit a simpler effect function and arm imbalance, but does not universally dominate T-learning.


R-learner
Let \(m(X)=E[Y\mid X]\) and \(e(X)=E[T\mid X]\). Fit these with cross-fitting and solve
\[\hat\tau_R=\arg\min_\tau\sum_i\left[(Y_i-\hat m(X_i))-(T_i-\hat e(X_i))\tau(X_i)\right]^2+\Lambda(\tau).\]
This generalizes Robinson residualization from a constant coefficient to a function. The residual treatment explains the residual outcome, with regularization acting directly on the effect function. Nuisance orthogonality reduces sensitivity to small nuisance errors under the appropriate rate conditions. Tiny treatment residuals mean little information; naively dividing by them to make pseudo-labels can be unstable.


Causal forests and honesty
Causal forests adapt tree-based neighborhoods to heterogeneous effects. Splitting criteria target effect information rather than only outcome fit; generalized versions solve local moment equations and can residualize confounding.
Honesty uses different subsamples to select splits and estimate leaf effects. This limits adaptive overfitting from choosing the partition and estimating its effects with the same outcomes. Predictions aggregate information across trees. Valid confidence intervals require the estimator’s sampling, overlap, regularity, and tuning conditions; honesty alone does not automatically make every forest asymptotically normal.

title: Uplift Modeling and Heterogeneous Effects
text:
Interview questions
How is uplift different from PSM? Uplift targets conditional effects for allocation; a conventional matched analysis often targets ATT. Both depend on a causal design, and matching can also be used within heterogeneous-effect analyses.
Why might X-learning help with imbalance? A well-estimated outcome function from the large arm provides counterfactual predictions for the small arm; the second stage exploits structure in the effect function.
What is honesty? Separate data choose tree partitions and estimate effects within them, reducing adaptive estimation bias.
Can purchase AUC select an uplift model? No. It evaluates outcome ranking, which can prioritize sure things. Use treatment-aware held-out gains and a policy experiment.

title: Evaluating Uplift: Gains, Qini, and Policy Value
text:
Construct a treatment-aware cumulative gain curve on a held-out sample.

Turn a ranking into a cost-aware policy and validate it experimentally.
crumbs: 34  Evaluating Uplift: Gains, Qini, and Policy Value

title: Evaluating Uplift: Gains, Qini, and Policy Value
text:
Intuition
An uplift model is useful when treating the highest-ranked users yields more incremental benefit than treating a random set of the same size. The all-user effect is the same endpoint for every ranking of a fixed evaluation sample; the model changes how quickly benefit accumulates as budget increases.
Outcome AUC cannot answer this question. A model can accurately find people who would purchase without intervention and still waste the entire treatment budget.
crumbs: 34  Evaluating Uplift: Gains, Qini, and Policy Value

title: Evaluating Uplift: Gains, Qini, and Policy Value
text:
Worked example

An oracle illustration
Imagine 100 users whose hypothetical effects sum to 50 units. A good ranking puts ten users averaging 0.95 effect first, giving 9.5 incremental units at 10% coverage. A random ranking has expected gain \(10(0.5)=5\). A reversed ranking might obtain only 0.5.
All rankings end at 50 at 100% coverage. These known-effect numbers illustrate the curve shape; ordinary data do not reveal all 100 individual effects. Real evaluation estimates gains from treatment and control observations.


A randomized evaluation calculation
In an independent experiment with treatment probability \(p=0.5\), define each unit’s transformed outcome
\[Z_i=\frac{T_iY_i}{p}-\frac{(1-T_i)Y_i}{1-p}.\]
For the top ten ranked users, suppose treated outcomes sum to 8 and control outcomes sum to 3. Estimated total incremental gain is \(8/0.5-3/0.5=10\) units. Dividing by all 100 evaluation users gives normalized gain 0.10; dividing by the ten selected users gives the selected group’s estimated average effect 1.0. These are different quantities with different denominators.
A small prefix can contain few observations from one arm and produce noisy gains. Do not treat a jagged empirical curve as a precisely known ordering of individual effects.
crumbs: 34  Evaluating Uplift: Gains, Qini, and Policy Value

title: Evaluating Uplift: Gains, Qini, and Policy Value
text:
Theory and assumptions

One explicit convention
Rank held-out observations by a model fitted without their outcomes, and let \(S_k\) be the top \(k\) fraction. With known randomized assignment probabilities \(p_i\), use
\[G(k)=\sum_{i\in S_k}\left[\frac{T_iY_i}{p_i}-\frac{(1-T_i)Y_i}{1-p_i}\right].\]
Conditional on the fixed ranking features and under randomization/consistency, its expectation is the total treatment effect among selected users. Define \(g(k)=G(k)/n\) for gain per member of the full evaluation population. Then \(g(1)\) estimates ATE and \(G(1)\) estimates \(n\times ATE\).
The random-ranking benchmark is the line \(kG(1)\) in expectation. Under this convention,
\[AUUC=\int_0^1G(k)\,dk,\]
and a baseline-adjusted area can be defined as
\[Qini=\int_0^1[G(k)-kG(1)]\,dk.\]
Libraries use different names, scales, and normalizations. Publish the equation, denominator, treatment-allocation assumptions, and baseline definition alongside the metric.


Relating common formulas
Another cumulative contrast is \(\sum_{S_k,T=1}Y-(n_T/n_C)\sum_{S_k,T=0}Y\). With constant assignment probability and a corresponding overall arm ratio, it is on a treatment-arm-scaled total rather than the full-population total scale. Dividing it by \(n\) does not make its endpoint \(n\times ATE\). This distinction corrects the inconsistent normalization in the source notes.
Prefix arm-count normalization is another convention and may be unstable when an arm count is zero. An IPW convention using known assignment probabilities avoids dividing by random prefix counts, though variance remains high for small prefixes or rare assignment.


Observational evaluation
If assignment is observational, a raw treated-control prefix contrast is generally confounded. Under conditional exchangeability and overlap, evaluate with suitable estimated propensity adjustment or a cross-fitted doubly robust score. Independent evaluation, correct covariate timing, and uncertainty still matter. In-sample ranking by noisy fitted effects creates optimism even when the original treatment was randomized.
crumbs: 34  Evaluating Uplift: Gains, Qini, and Policy Value

title: Evaluating Uplift: Gains, Qini, and Policy Value
text:
Practice and pitfalls
For a budget covering 30% of users, compare the gains at \(k=0.3\), not only the full-curve area. A model can have a good overall area and a poor ranking in the operational budget range.
If benefit is margin \(v\) per incremental conversion and treatment costs \(c(x)\), use a policy criterion such as \(v\hat\tau(x)-c(x)\), with explicit treatment and redemption cost assumptions. Highest conversion uplift is not necessarily highest net value. Negative-effect segments can make “treat everyone” worse than a restricted policy.
Validate the chosen policy in a new randomized test comparing the model-based allocation with a meaningful existing or random-allocation policy under the same budget. Report aggregate incremental value, guardrails, uncertainty, and exposure counts. A claim such as “targeting 20% saves 80%” applies to the number of interventions at equal per-user cost; it does not automatically mean 80% net-cost savings or unchanged revenue.
Use design-respecting bootstrap or influence-function uncertainty for a fixed trained policy when appropriate. If the entire policy is retrained in evaluation, account for that selection procedure separately. Preserve user/cluster dependence.
crumbs: 34  Evaluating Uplift: Gains, Qini, and Policy Value

title: Evaluating Uplift: Gains, Qini, and Policy Value
text:
Interview questions
Why do rankings share an endpoint? At 100% every ranking includes the same observations. Only the order changes, so the fixed-sample aggregate estimate is unchanged.
Is Qini the same as AUROC? No. ROC measures classification ranking; uplift gains compare treatment and control outcomes to measure incremental response.
What must accompany an AUUC number? The exact curve definition, normalization, dataset and assignment design, random baseline, uncertainty, and operational budget.
How do you choose the targeting cutoff? Optimize expected incremental value under the budget and cost structure on validation data, then test the fixed policy independently.

Evaluate uplift where the policy will operate. Keep total and per-person gains distinct, document metric conventions, and confirm the selected allocation with independent causal evidence.

crumbs: 35  CUPED and Experiment Variance Reduction

title: CUPED and Experiment Variance Reduction
text:
Intuition
Customers differ in baseline activity. Last month’s activity predicts some of this month’s activity even without treatment. Subtracting that predictable variation can make the difference between randomized groups more precise.
CUPED uses pre-experiment covariates to improve precision. Randomization supplies the identification argument; the adjustment does not turn a selected observational comparison into a randomized experiment.
crumbs: 35  CUPED and Experiment Variance Reduction

title: CUPED and Experiment Variance Reduction
text:
Worked example

Adjust two users
Suppose \(E[X]=10\), \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=25\), and \(\operatorname{Cov}(Y,X)=15\). Then \(\theta^*=15/25=0.6\).
A user with \(Y=18,X=15\) has adjusted outcome \(18-0.6(15-10)=15\). Another with \(Y=12,X=5\) has adjusted outcome \(12-0.6(5-10)=15\). Their different baseline activity explained the apparent outcome difference.


Precision in correlation units
If \(\rho=0.7\), residual variance is \(1-0.7^2=0.51\) of original variance: 49% reduction, not 51% reduction. Under comparable variance and design conditions, the same standard error would otherwise require about \(1/0.51=1.96\) times as many observations.

Read a small lift carefully
In a synthetic teaching example, suppose the control mean is 9.000 and the treatment mean is 9.007. Their absolute difference is 0.007 and relative difference is
\[9.007/9.000-1\approx0.000778=0.0778\%.\]
The example illustrates that very large experiments can detect small effects. Those means alone do not reproduce a CUPED standard error or adjusted p-value: one needs the relevant adjusted variance, covariance, counts, and platform estimand. A raw two-sample calculation and an adjusted platform test need not agree. A significant visit metric also does not imply significant orders, payment amounts, or every subgroup.
crumbs: 35  CUPED and Experiment Variance Reduction

title: CUPED and Experiment Variance Reduction
text:
Theory and assumptions

Derive the adjustment
Set
\[Y^*=Y-\theta(X-E[X]).\]
Since subtracting a constant does not change variance,
\[\operatorname{Var}(Y^*)=\operatorname{Var}(Y)+\theta^2\operatorname{Var}(X)-2\theta\operatorname{Cov}(Y,X).\]
Differentiate with respect to \(\theta\) and set the derivative to zero:
\[2\theta\operatorname{Var}(X)-2\operatorname{Cov}(Y,X)=0,
\qquad\theta^*=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y,X)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)}.\]
For \(\operatorname{Var}(X)>0\), the second derivative is positive. Substitution gives
\[\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Var}(Y^*)
&=\operatorname{Var}(Y)-\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y,X)^2}{\operatorname{Var}(X)}\\
&=\operatorname{Var}(Y)(1-\rho_{YX}^2).
\end{aligned}\]
This is a population linear-projection result. Estimated coefficients, arm heteroskedasticity, and finite-sample dependence affect the precise gain for an experimental difference estimator.


Why the effect is preserved
For a fixed adjustment coefficient,
\[\begin{aligned}
E[Y^*\mid T=1]-E[Y^*\mid T=0]
&=E[Y\mid T=1]-E[Y\mid T=0]\\
&\quad-\theta\{E[X\mid T=1]-E[X\mid T=0]\}.
\end{aligned}\]
Randomization and a pre-treatment \(X\) make the final population contrast zero. The observed adjusted difference need not equal the raw sample difference because realized baseline imbalance is precisely what is being adjusted. Estimating \(\theta\) from the same small sample adds finite-sample considerations.
With several covariates, the linear projection coefficient is \(\Sigma_{XX}^{-1}\Sigma_{XY}\) when nonsingular. More flexible baseline predictions can remove nonlinear predictable variation, but require suitable training/cross-fitting and valid inference to avoid overfitting-induced bias.


Relationship to regression and ANCOVA
The one-variable \(\theta^*\) is the population OLS slope of \(Y\) on \(X\). Comparing residualized outcomes resembles covariate-adjusted regression \(Y\sim T+X\).
However, residualizing only \(Y\) using a pooled regression and then comparing treatment means is not generally algebraically identical in a finite sample to the treatment coefficient in ANCOVA. Frisch–Waugh–Lovell residualizes both \(Y\) and \(T\) with respect to \(X\). The methods align under appropriate randomization/asymptotic conditions, but implementation and uncertainty should be stated explicitly.
crumbs: 35  CUPED and Experiment Variance Reduction

title: CUPED and Experiment Variance Reduction
text:
Practice and pitfalls
Use strongly prognostic pre-treatment variables, usually the same metric in a pre-period. Predefine that period and handle users with no history consistently; missing historical activity may itself be predictive. Do not condition on treatment-induced clicks, visits, or purchases.
Two reasons CUPED may not make a result significant are a genuinely small/zero effect and a weakly predictive baseline covariate. Limited sample size, noisy coefficient estimation, heterogeneous variance, or model misspecification can also limit gains.

Merely displaying both does not automatically double the hypothesis family, but selecting whichever p-value is significant does create a testing problem. Multiple outcomes or exploratory subgroups require an appropriate multiplicity strategy. Report per-randomization-unit lift, CIs, and guardrails rather than total count differences alone.

title: CUPED and Experiment Variance Reduction
text:
Interview questions
Why is \(\theta\) a regression slope? Minimizing adjusted outcome variance differentiates the same quadratic loss underlying a linear projection, giving covariance divided by variance.
Does CUPED change ATE? With a fixed pre-treatment adjustment in an RCT it preserves the population difference in expectation. The sample estimate can change because baseline imbalance is adjusted.
Is variance reduction \(1-\rho^2\)? That is the fraction retained. The fraction removed is \(\rho^2\).
Can I use machine learning? Yes, to predict baseline outcomes more flexibly with a design that controls overfitting and yields valid experimental inference. Better training fit alone is insufficient.

Summary
CUPED removes predictable baseline variation. Its value is narrower uncertainty around a properly identified experimental effect, with consistent reporting of adjusted inference and practical effect magnitude.

title: ARIMA and Seasonal ARIMA
text:
Read AR, MA, integration, and seasonal lag notation without confusing innovations with rolling averages.
Calculate simple forecasts, assess stationarity, and interpret ACF/PACF patterns.
Design temporal validation and residual diagnostics that respect a forecasting information set.

title: ARIMA and Seasonal ARIMA
text:
Intuition
Tomorrow’s GMV may depend on recent GMV and on recent surprises. An AR term uses past observations; an MA term uses past innovations. If the level drifts, differencing can expose a more stable process in changes. Seasonal terms repeat this logic at lags such as seven days or twelve months.
ARIMA is a statistical dependence model, not a causal explanation. Yesterday’s predictive information does not by itself identify what an intervention would do tomorrow.

title: ARIMA and Seasonal ARIMA
text:
Worked example

From levels to changes
For seven days of GMV \((100,102,105,103,106,108,110)\), first differences are
\[(2,3,-2,3,2,2),\qquad \overline{\Delta Y}=10/6\approx1.667.\]
The differences no longer show the same rising level, but six values cannot establish stationarity. A random-walk-with-drift baseline would forecast \(110+1.667=111.667\) next day if this estimated drift were used. Its uncertainty should reflect limited estimation data.


AR and MA predictions
For an AR(1) with \(c=20\), \(\phi=0.8\), and latest value 110,
\[\widehat Y_{t+1\mid t}=20+0.8(110)=108.\]
The stationary mean is \(20/(1-0.8)=100\), so the forecast moves toward 100. A second step gives \(20+0.8(108)=106.4\).
For an MA(1) with \(c=105\), \(\theta=0.3\), and latest inferred shock \(\hat\epsilon_t=5\),
\[\widehat Y_{t+1\mid t}=105+0.3(5)=106.5.\]
The unknown future innovation has conditional mean zero. Two steps ahead, this finite MA(1) shock no longer enters the mean forecast, so the forecast is 105. MA here means a moving average of innovations, not \((Y_t+Y_{t-1})/2\).


Reconstruct the level after differencing
Suppose a fitted ARIMA(1,1,1) has
\[W_t=0.5+0.4W_{t-1}+\epsilon_t+0.2\epsilon_{t-1},\qquad W_t=\Delta Y_t.\]
With latest difference 2 and inferred shock 1, next difference is \(0.5+0.4(2)+0.2(1)=1.5\). The next level forecast is \(110+1.5=111.5\). The following difference is \(0.5+0.4(1.5)=1.1\), because the future innovation is forecast as zero. Thus the two-step level forecast is 112.6.

title: ARIMA and Seasonal ARIMA
text:
Theory and assumptions

Notation and stationarity
\(Y_t\) is the observed value, \(\widehat Y_{t+h\mid t}\) an \(h\)-step forecast using information through \(t\), and \(\epsilon_t\) an innovation. Weak white noise has zero mean, constant finite variance, and zero serial covariance; independence is a stronger condition, not part of every white-noise definition. For the conditional-mean forecasts below, assume \(E[\epsilon_{t+1}\mid\mathcal F_t]=0\); weak white noise alone only supports the corresponding linear-prediction argument.
Weak stationarity requires constant mean and variance, and covariance depending on lag rather than calendar time. A trend, changing seasonal amplitude, or structural break can violate it. Differencing addresses certain nonstationary mean structures; a log or variance-stabilizing transform addresses a different issue. Deterministic trend regression and stochastic differencing are not interchangeable assumptions.
ADF tests a unit-root null under its selected deterministic/lag specification. KPSS tests a level- or trend-stationarity null under its specification. Failure to reject is not proof of the null, and breaks or low power can complicate both tests. Use plots, scientific context, and diagnostics alongside them.


AR(p)
\[Y_t=c+\sum_{j=1}^p\phi_jY_{t-j}+\epsilon_t.\]
The roots of \(1-\phi_1z-\cdots-\phi_pz^p\) must lie outside the unit circle for the usual causal stationary AR representation. In AR(1), \(|\phi|<1\) means shocks decay; \(\phi=1\) gives a random walk, and \(|\phi|>1\) gives an explosive recursion.
For a stationary AR with mean \(\mu\), \(c=\mu(1-\sum_j\phi_j)\). A differenced process can still have a nonzero mean or drift; differencing does not automatically set its constant to zero.


MA(q)
\[Y_t=c+\epsilon_t+\sum_{j=1}^q\theta_j\epsilon_{t-j}.\]
A finite linear combination of weak white noise with constant coefficients is weakly stationary. Invertibility is a separate condition ensuring an appropriate unique innovation representation from past observations; with this plus-sign convention, roots of \(1+\theta_1z+\cdots+\theta_qz^q\) lie outside the unit circle.
Innovations are not directly observed. Fitting infers them jointly with model parameters, often via likelihood/state-space methods. Forecasting uses estimated past innovations and zero conditional means for future innovations.


ARIMA(p,d,q)
Let \(LY_t=Y_{t-1}\) be the lag operator and \(W_t=(1-L)^dY_t\). Model \(W_t\) as ARMA:
\[W_t=c+\sum_{j=1}^p\phi_jW_{t-j}+\epsilon_t+\sum_{j=1}^q\theta_j\epsilon_{t-j}.\]
\(d=0\) models levels, \(d=1\) models changes, and \(d=2\) models changes in changes, \(Y_t-2Y_{t-1}+Y_{t-2}\). Use as much differencing as needed for the chosen process, not as much as possible. Over-differencing adds unnecessary noise and can create problematic moving-average behavior.


Seasonal ARIMA
Write SARIMA\((p,d,q)(P,D,Q)_s\), where lowercase orders refer to ordinary lags and uppercase orders to seasonal lags. Typical integer periods are 7 for weekly seasonality in daily data, 12 for annual seasonality in monthly data, and 4 for quarterly annual seasonality.
\[\Phi(L^s)\phi(L)(1-L^s)^D(1-L)^dY_t
=c+\Theta(L^s)\theta(L)\epsilon_t.\]
For example, \((1-L)(1-L^{12})Y_t=Y_t-Y_{t-1}-Y_{t-12}+Y_{t-13}\). Multiplying seasonal and ordinary AR polynomials also creates cross-lags; SARIMA is more than adding two isolated regressors.
A single seasonal period does not automatically capture both weekly and annual cycles. Annual patterns in daily data, leap years, moving holidays, and multiple seasonalities may call for calendar regressors, Fourier terms, decomposition, or other models. A fractional “365.25” is not a literal integer SARIMA lag.


ACF and PACF
ACF at lag \(k\) is \(\operatorname{Cov}(Y_t,Y_{t-k})/\operatorname{Var}(Y_t)\) for a stationary process. PACF removes the linear association mediated by intermediate lags; “direct” here is statistical rather than causal.

Sample plots are noisy estimates. “Cutoff” does not mean every later observed spike must lie inside a 95% band. Inspect seasonal lags as well as ordinary ones. Use AIC/AICc/BIC to compare appropriate candidates, then compare forecasts on rolling-origin holdouts. Automated order search does not remove the need to audit differencing, seasonal period, and residuals.

title: ARIMA and Seasonal ARIMA
text:
Practice and pitfalls
Fit transformations, model selection, and parameters using only data available at each forecast origin. Compare with naive, seasonal-naive, and drift baselines at the actual deployment horizon. Use MAE/RMSE and an appropriate scaled metric; MAPE is unstable with zeros and tiny denominators.
Inspect residual time plots, ACF, and Ljung–Box tests for remaining serial correlation. Ljung–Box tests autocorrelation through selected lags; a large p-value does not prove independence. A Q–Q plot assesses distributional tails relevant to model-based intervals. Residual normality is not necessary for every useful point forecast.
Prediction intervals often widen with horizon, but stationary-process uncertainty can approach a finite limit. Reconstructing levels after differencing accumulates uncertainty differently. Distinguish prediction intervals from confidence intervals for a conditional mean.
For a major-sale GMV forecast, known campaign dates can enter as regressors, while weekly seasonality and annual patterns need suitable modeling. Future regressor values must actually be known or forecast. Do not transfer an example’s claimed MAPE to a new dataset. Structural breaks can defeat an otherwise well-fitted historical model.
ARIMA offers interpretable linear dependence and strong short-horizon baselines. ETS emphasizes level/trend/seasonal states; decomposable trend/holiday approaches such as Prophet offer another model family. VAR/VECM concern multivariate dependence with their own stationarity/cointegration assumptions. Choose by temporal validation and the forecasting problem, not by a universal ranking.

title: ARIMA and Seasonal ARIMA
text:
Interview questions
What is MA(1)? A model using the current innovation and one past innovation, not a rolling mean of observed outcomes.
How do you select p, d, and q? Establish an appropriate stationary representation, use ACF/PACF and information criteria for candidate orders, and validate at realistic rolling forecast origins.
Can ADF prove stationarity? It can reject a specified unit-root null. That is not a blanket proof against every form of nonstationarity.
What about multiple seasonalities and promotions? Represent calendar information explicitly or choose a suitable multi-seasonal/decomposition model, then evaluate with future information restricted to what deployment knows.

title: ARIMA and Seasonal ARIMA
text:
Summary
ARIMA models observations and innovations after an appropriate transformation. Forecast quality requires correct timing, seasonal structure, residual checks, and comparisons with simple baselines; order selection alone is insufficient.

title: Exponential Smoothing and ETS
text:
Intuition
A forecast can maintain a small summary of the past: the current level \(\ell_t\), trend \(b_t\), and seasonal pattern \(s_t\). Each new observation updates these states. Recent data usually receive more weight, while older influence decays geometrically.
SES tracks a level; Holt adds a trend; Holt–Winters adds seasonality. ETS puts such forecasting methods in an error–trend–seasonality state-space framework, supporting likelihood estimation and prediction intervals.

Using unrounded intermediate states, SES forecasts 106.332 at every horizon. Holt forecasts 111.355 one day ahead, 112.887 two days ahead, and 120.548 seven days ahead. The corrected arithmetic avoids accumulating the source table’s intermediate rounding differences. Holt follows the rising series more directly, but seven points do not establish superior out-of-sample accuracy.


Damp the distant trend
With damping \(\phi=0.9\), the trend multiplier is \(\sum_{j=1}^h\phi^j\). It equals 0.9 at one step, about 3.686 at five, 5.862 at ten, and approaches 9 as \(h\) grows. Thus long-run trend contribution is bounded instead of increasing forever. A fitted damped model also damps the state updates; applying damping only to an undamped fit is merely a numerical illustration.


Reuse the correct seasonal state
For daily data with weekly period \(m=7\), let current time be \(t=10\). At horizon \(h=5\), use seasonal state \(s_8\), since day 15 and day 8 share a weekday. At \(h=10\), use \(s_6\), since day 20 and day 6 are two weeks apart. The rule \(k=\lfloor(h-1)/m\rfloor+1\) selects \(s_{t+h-mk}\) from the most recent observed cycle.

title: Exponential Smoothing and ETS
text:
Theory and assumptions

Simple exponential smoothing
\[\ell_t=\alpha Y_t+(1-\alpha)\ell_{t-1},\qquad\widehat Y_{t+h\mid t}=\ell_t.\]
Unrolling the recursion gives
\[\ell_t=\alpha\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}(1-\alpha)^jY_{t-j}+(1-\alpha)^t\ell_0.\]
The observation weights \(\alpha,\alpha(1-\alpha),\alpha(1-\alpha)^2,\ldots\) explain “exponential.” Large \(\alpha\) reacts quickly but follows noise; small \(\alpha\) smooths heavily. The initial state’s remaining weight matters early in a short series.
SES has flat multi-step point forecasts because it has no trend state. This does not imply zero future uncertainty. Parameters and initial states can be estimated by a suitable loss or likelihood; Gaussian additive-error formulations connect likelihood and squared errors, whereas other error models need not have the same objective.


Holt and damped Holt
\[\begin{aligned}
\ell_t&=\alpha Y_t+(1-\alpha)(\ell_{t-1}+b_{t-1}),\\
b_t&=\beta^*(\ell_t-\ell_{t-1})+(1-\beta^*)b_{t-1},\\
\widehat Y_{t+h\mid t}&=\ell_t+hb_t.
\end{aligned}\]
The level combines the observation with yesterday’s level-plus-trend prediction. The trend combines the latest level change with the previous trend. Damped Holt replaces the old trend contribution by \(\phi b_{t-1}\) in the state updates and uses
\[\widehat Y_{t+h\mid t}=\ell_t+\left(\sum_{j=1}^h\phi^j\right)b_t.\]
For \(0<\phi<1\), the sum is \(\phi(1-\phi^h)/(1-\phi)\) and converges to \(\phi/(1-\phi)\). At \(\phi=1\), ordinary Holt is recovered.


Additive Holt–Winters
With period \(m\) and component-form smoothing parameters,
\[\begin{aligned}
\ell_t&=\alpha(Y_t-s_{t-m})+(1-\alpha)(\ell_{t-1}+b_{t-1}),\\
b_t&=\beta^*(\ell_t-\ell_{t-1})+(1-\beta^*)b_{t-1},\\
s_t&=\gamma(Y_t-\ell_{t-1}-b_{t-1})+(1-\gamma)s_{t-m},\\
\widehat Y_{t+h\mid t}&=\ell_t+hb_t+s_{t+h-mk}.
\end{aligned}\]
The level removes the previous same-season effect from the observation. The seasonal update compares the observation with the nonseasonal prediction. The forecast adds level, extrapolated trend, and the corresponding historical seasonal state.
For example, if \(Y_t=125\), old level 100, old trend 2, old same-season effect 20, and \((\alpha,\beta^*,\gamma)=(0.3,0.2,0.1)\), then \(\ell_t=0.3(105)+0.7(102)=102.9\), \(b_t=0.2(2.9)+0.8(2)=2.18\), and \(s_t=0.1(23)+0.9(20)=20.3\).
Different texts parameterize the seasonal update using the new rather than prior level; parameters must be transformed appropriately before treating formulas as identical.


Multiplicative seasonality
For proportional seasonal variation, replace deseasonalizing subtraction by division:
\[\begin{aligned}
\ell_t&=\alpha(Y_t/s_{t-m})+(1-\alpha)(\ell_{t-1}+b_{t-1}),\\
s_t&=\gamma\frac{Y_t}{\ell_{t-1}+b_{t-1}}+(1-\gamma)s_{t-m},\\
\widehat Y_{t+h\mid t}&=(\ell_t+hb_t)s_{t+h-mk}.
\end{aligned}\]
The trend update remains the corresponding Holt update. An additive season might add 20 units every weekend; a multiplicative season might multiply the level by 1.2. Multiplicative models require suitable positive values and nonzero denominators. A log transform can turn proportional structure into additive structure, but back-transforming a mean forecast requires attention to bias.


ETS notation and innovations
ETS stands for Error, Trend, Seasonal, not three interchangeable component positions. Errors are additive or multiplicative; trend can be none, additive, damped additive, and in broader taxonomies multiplicative variants; seasonality can be none, additive, or multiplicative.

Interpretation
